title: Security Deposit Cap
bodyText: South Dakota caps a residential security deposit at one month's rent (SDCL 43-32-6.1). A larger deposit may be agreed between landlord and tenant only where special conditions pose a danger to the maintenance of the premises (e.g., a pet, waterbed, or similar elevated-risk factor) - this is a mutual-agreement exception, not a unilateral landlord right, so it should be documented as a negotiated term, not just charged.

title: Security Deposit Itemized Accounting & Bad-Faith Penalty
bodyText: Within 21 days after the tenancy ends and you receive the tenant's mailing address or delivery instructions, return the deposit or give the tenant a written statement of the specific reasons for withholding any of it. You may withhold only what is reasonably necessary to remedy the tenant's default in rent or other amounts due under the lease, or to restore the property to its condition at the start of the term, ordinary wear and tear excepted (SDCL 43-32-24). If a South Dakota tenant requests an itemized accounting of any withheld security deposit, the landlord must provide it within 45 days after termination of the tenancy - a separate, longer deadline than the 21-day return/withholding-notice window. A landlord who fails to comply with the deposit-return requirements forfeits all rights to withhold any portion of the deposit. Bad-faith retention of a deposit (including failure to provide the required written statement or itemized accounting) exposes the landlord to punitive damages up to $200, in addition to the forfeited deposit.

title: Self-Help Eviction Prohibited
bodyText: South Dakota law prohibits a residential landlord from unlawfully removing or excluding a tenant from the premises, or willfully diminishing services by interrupting electric, gas, water, or other essential service, as a way to force a tenant out. A tenant subjected to this may sue for an injunction, sue to recover possession, or terminate the rental agreement - and in any case may recover damages equal to two months' rent plus the return of any advance rent and deposit paid. A second statute can make a lockout cost much more. For forcibly ejecting or excluding a person from the possession of real property, the measure of damages is three times the sum that would compensate for the harm caused (SDCL 21-3-6). Whether a tenant can recover under both statutes is a question only case law could settle, so plan on the larger exposure.

title: Retaliation Prohibited
bodyText: A South Dakota landlord may not retaliate against a tenant by raising rent above fair market value, by decreasing electric, gas, water or sewer service, or by giving a notice to vacate that is not based on a breach of the lease, after any of three protected events: the landlord has received written notice, from the tenant or from a government agency, that the tenant complained to an agency responsible for enforcing a building or housing code violation that applies to the premises and materially affects health and safety, and the complaint is determined to have been reported in good faith; the tenant has given the landlord written notice of a condition requiring repair under SDCL 43-32-9; or the tenant has organized or joined a tenant's union or organization. Read the 180 days carefully. It is not a general window on the whole prohibition: SDCL 43-32-27 makes it a DEFENCE that the NOTICE TO VACATE was given more than 180 days after the protected event, and that defence is written for the notice-to-vacate limb alone. A retaliatory rent increase above fair market value, or a retaliatory cut to electric, gas, water or sewer service, carries no 180-day cut-off on the face of the statute. A landlord's failure to renew a written lease before or upon its expiration is not retaliation. A tenant harmed by retaliation gets the SDCL 43-32-6 remedies - injunctive relief, recovery of possession, or termination, plus damages equal to two months' rent and the return of any advance rent and deposit - and the court may award the tenant reasonable and customary attorney's fees on a verified itemized statement of costs and services (SDCL 43-32-28).

title: Domestic Abuse Contact Information Confidentiality
bodyText: If a tenant terminates under South Dakota's domestic-abuse/stalking early-termination provision and provides the landlord a forwarding address or other contact information, the landlord may not disclose that information to any person except with the tenant's consent or as required by law.

title: Entry Notice Requirements
bodyText: Except in an emergency or where it is impracticable, a South Dakota landlord must give the tenant reasonable notice of intent to enter and may enter only at reasonable times. Twenty-four hours' written notice is presumed reasonable unless the lease sets a different method or timing by mutual agreement. The notice must specify the date(s) of entry, a time period during normal business hours for the entry, the purpose of the entry, and a means by which the tenant may request to reschedule.

title: Month-to-Month Lease Modification Notice
bodyText: To modify the terms of a South Dakota month-to-month lease - including a rent increase - the landlord must give the tenant notice in writing at least 30 days before the expiration of the month, and the new terms take effect at the expiration of that month if the tenant continues to hold the premises. The notice itself, once served, operates to make the new terms, rent and conditions part of the lease; no separate agreement or signature is needed. A tenant who receives such a notice may instead terminate the lease effective the first day of the next month by providing the landlord notice of termination within 15 days after receiving the modification notice. The statute requires the LANDLORD's modification notice to be in writing but does not require the TENANT's responding notice of termination to be written, so do not treat an unwritten tenant response as ineffective.

title: Tenancy-at-Will Termination Notice
bodyText: Outside the modification-notice mechanics of a month-to-month lease, South Dakota law separately allows a landlord to terminate a residential tenancy at will (a tenancy with no agreed end date) by giving the tenant at least 15 days' written notice. If the tenancy is the residence of a tenant on active military service, or of an immediate family member (spouse or minor child) of a tenant on active military service, the landlord must instead give at least two months' written notice - unless the tenant has engaged in sustained conduct that is disruptive, illegal, destructive, negligent toward maintaining the property, or a material breach of the lease, or unless the landlord has sold the property or the property has passed into the landlord's estate. The notice must be in writing and served by delivering it to the tenant or to some person of discretion residing on the premises; if neither can be found with reasonable diligence, it may be served by affixing it to a conspicuous part of the premises where it can conveniently be read.

title: Eviction Grounds
bodyText: A South Dakota landlord may bring a forcible entry and detainer (FED) action against a tenant who: holds over after the lease term ends or fails to pay rent for three days after it is due; commits waste on the premises; or does or fails to do any act which, under the lease's own terms, operates to terminate the lease. (Additional grounds cover forcible/fraudulent entry and post-foreclosure or post-partition holdovers, which are not typical residential-lease scenarios.) For the lease-violation ground to be available, the lease itself must state that the specific violation terminates the tenancy - South Dakota law does not independently define which lease violations justify eviction.

title: Eviction Procedure
bodyText: South Dakota no longer requires a landlord to serve a separate statutory notice to quit before filing a forcible entry and detainer (FED) action - that requirement, formerly SDCL 21-16-2, was repealed effective 2024. A landlord may file once a FED ground exists, such as rent unpaid for three days. If the lease itself specifies a notice period, the landlord must still honor that contract term. The complaint must be in writing, verified, and served with a summons. Service is not a single event: the sheriff or other authorized server must make a minimum of two service attempts, at least one week apart, with both attempts falling within thirty days. On the second attempt the summons may be posted conspicuously on the property, delivered to a person residing there if one can be found, and sent by first class mail to the tenant at the property. The landlord may also publish the summons once in a legal newspaper on the same day as the first attempted service. The tenant's time to appear and plead is five days from service, or thirty days after publication, whichever occurs sooner; a continuance beyond fourteen days requires the tenant to post an undertaking with surety for accruing rent and costs. If the landlord prevails, the court awards possession, rents and profits or damages, and costs, and may tax reasonable attorney fees as costs to the prevailing party - either party - if that party is represented by a licensed attorney. An execution for possession may only be served during the daytime. No federal notice is a filing condition in South Dakota. Some states' court rules make the CARES Act 30-day notice to vacate a precondition to filing against a 'covered dwelling'; South Dakota's forcible entry and detainer procedure is statutory, and neither SDCL chapter 21-16 nor the Rules of Civil Procedure in SDCL chapter 15-6 imposes any such condition. A landlord whose property carries a federally backed mortgage or federal subsidy may still owe a CARES Act notice as a matter of federal law; it is simply not something a South Dakota court checks before accepting the filing.

title: Habitability & Repair Duty
bodyText: South Dakota landlords have a non-waivable duty to keep residential premises and common areas in reasonable repair, fit for human habitation, and in good and safe working order throughout the tenancy - including the electrical, plumbing, and heating systems - except where the disrepair is caused by the tenant's own negligent, willful, or malicious conduct. Landlord and tenant may agree that the tenant will perform specified repairs or maintenance in lieu of rent. If a landlord fails to repair a condition within a reasonable time after the tenant gives notice, the tenant may repair it and deduct the cost from rent (or otherwise recover it), or may vacate and be discharged from further rent and lease obligations. If the necessary repair cost exceeds one month's rent, the tenant may instead withhold rent and deposit it into a separate bank or savings-and-loan account (with written evidence of the deposit provided to the landlord) until the landlord makes the repairs or the tenant accumulates enough to have the repairs made.

title: Returned Check Fee Cap
bodyText: South Dakota does not give a landlord an automatic right to charge a returned-check fee. SDCL 57A-3-421 makes the issuer of a dishonored check liable for all reasonable costs and expenses of collection - reasonable only if they do not exceed sixty dollars plus any applicable sales tax - but the liability arises only where the payee is a merchant or place of business that has either conspicuously posted a notice on its premises, or regularly extends credit and prints a notice on its customer statements of such size and location as to be conspicuous, stating that a fee will be assessed against returned checks. Liability attaches only where the check was dishonored because the drawer's account is closed, has insufficient funds, or the drawer lacks sufficient credit. Whether a residential landlord is a merchant or place of business for this purpose, and how a landlord would satisfy a posting-or-customer-statement condition written for retail and credit businesses, are not settled. A landlord should not assume that stating a fee in the lease satisfies the statute, because a lease term is not one of the two mechanisms the statute names.

title: Fair Housing Protected Classes
bodyText: In addition to the federally protected classes, South Dakota's own fair housing law prohibits housing discrimination based on creed and ancestry. The full list under SDCL 20-13-20 is race, color, creed, religion, sex, ancestry, disability, familial status, and national origin. South Dakota has not extended source-of-income (housing voucher) protection, and has not added sexual orientation or gender identity at the state level. South Dakota's refusal-to-rent and discriminatory-terms prohibitions do not apply to rooms or units in a dwelling containing living quarters for no more than two families living independently of each other, if the owner maintains and occupies one of those living quarters as the owner's residence. Two points about that exemption matter in practice. First, it does not reach discriminatory advertising, which remains prohibited regardless of building size or owner-occupancy. Second, it is NARROWER than the federal Fair Housing Act's four-unit owner-occupied exemption - so an owner-occupied three- or four-unit building can fall outside the federal exemption while still being fully covered by South Dakota law. A landlord relying on an owner-occupied exemption in South Dakota should count to two, not to four.

title: Rent Control Preempted
bodyText: South Dakota state law preempts local rent control: no county, municipality, or other local government in South Dakota may enact, maintain, or enforce an ordinance or resolution that would control the amount of rent charged for leasing private residential property. This does not limit a local government's ability to manage rents on residential property it owns.

title: Right to Call Police / Emergency Assistance
bodyText: A South Dakota landlord may not penalize or take adverse action against a tenant for calling the police or other emergency assistance in response to domestic abuse, unlawful sexual behavior, or stalking. A tenant cannot waive this right, and any lease provision purporting to waive it is unenforceable.

title: Tenant Early-Termination Causes
bodyText: Besides the domestic abuse and stalking right, a South Dakota tenant may end the lease if you don't, within a reasonable time after the tenant's written request, put and keep them in quiet possession or put the property into good condition or repair it; or if the greater part of the property, or the part that was a material inducement to the lease as you had reason to know, is destroyed by any cause other than the tenant's ordinary negligence (SDCL 43-32-19(1), (2)).

title: Holdover Tenancy Mechanics
bodyText: South Dakota's holdover rules sit in two different chapters, and the damages are not in the landlord-tenant chapter. In chapter 43-32 the mechanic is renewal rather than damages: if a tenant remains in possession after the hiring expires and the landlord accepts rent, SDCL 43-32-14 presumes the parties renewed the hiring on the same terms and for the same time, not exceeding one year, and SDCL 43-32-15 then lets either party end an unspecified-term renewal on notice scaled to the length of the term, capped at one month. So accepting rent from a holdover tenant is itself a decision to renew. The damages measures are in chapter 21-3. SDCL 21-3-8 provides that for wilfully holding over after the end of the term, after a notice to quit has been duly given and a demand of possession made, the measure of damages is double the yearly value of the property for the time of withholding, in addition to compensation for the detriment occasioned - and SDCL 21-16-10 lets the court award those damages in the forcible entry and detainer judgment itself where they are claimed in the complaint. SDCL 21-3-7 separately gives double the rent the tenant ought otherwise to pay where the tenant gave notice of an intention to leave and then failed to give up the premises. Where neither applies, SDCL 21-3-5 measures the detriment from wrongful occupation as the value of the use of the property for the time of occupation, up to six years back, plus the costs of recovering possession. Two practical points. Each multiplier has conditions, and § 21-3-8's are easy to miss: wilfulness, the end of the term rather than an earlier termination, a notice to quit duly given, and a demand of possession. And South Dakota repealed its statutory notice-to-quit requirement in 2024, so a landlord may now file an eviction without one - but § 21-3-8 still conditions double damages on a notice to quit having been given and possession demanded, so a landlord who wants the double measure should still serve a notice to quit and demand possession even though filing no longer requires it.

title: Smoke and Carbon Monoxide Detector Requirements
bodyText: South Dakota has no single smoke-detector statute covering all rentals, but it does have three administrative rules, and one of them reaches ordinary rental housing. A multifamily residence housing six or more families must have at least one smoke detector in each family living unit, located on the ceiling or wall of the main room or a sleeping room; in new construction the detector must draw primary power from the building wiring with battery backup. A lodging establishment - a hotel, motel or similar - must have smoke detectors in each sleeping room. A manufactured home must have at least one operable smoke detector and one carbon monoxide detector on each floor, including basement and attic, located in common areas or hallways. What is NOT covered is the gap that matters: a single-family rental house, a duplex, or any multifamily building housing fewer than six families falls outside all three rules, and South Dakota imposes no detector requirement on it beyond the general habitability duty. Carbon monoxide detectors are required only in manufactured homes; no rule requires them in a conventional rental of any size. Enforcement of the multifamily rule is by written notice with thirty days to comply.

title: Unconscionable Lease Terms
bodyText: South Dakota has no dedicated landlord-tenant statute voiding unconscionable lease clauses. Four things fill that gap. First and most directly, SDCL 53-9-3 voids any contract term whose object is, directly or indirectly, to exempt anyone from responsibility for their own fraud, willful injury to the person or property of another, or violation of law whether willful or negligent. Second, and often overlooked, SDCL 53-9-4 provides that penalties imposed by contract for any nonperformance of it are void, and SDCL 53-9-5 voids a term fixing damages in anticipation of breach except where the parties agree on an amount presumed to be the damage in cases where it would be impracticable or extremely difficult to fix actual damage. Those two reach fee and liquidated-damages terms - a late fee, an early-termination fee, a flat charge for a violation - and they are the provisions to measure such a figure against: set it to approximate real loss, not to punish. Third, South Dakota's Deceptive Trade Practices and Consumer Protection Act can reach a deceptively presented term: SDCL 37-24-6(1) makes it a deceptive act to knowingly use any deceptive act, false promise or misrepresentation, or to conceal, suppress or omit any material fact, in connection with the sale or advertisement of merchandise, regardless of whether anyone was in fact misled, and SDCL 37-24-31 gives a person adversely affected a private action for actual damages. Whether a residential lease of real property is 'merchandise' for that chapter is not settled - the definitions reach goods and services 'purchased, leased, or rented' and an 'intangible', but the operative words are 'sale or advertisement' - so treat it as live for how a tenancy is advertised and presented, and unsettled for lease terms themselves. Fourth, common-law unconscionability remains a general backstop; South Dakota has struck a liability limitation as an unconscionable adhesion term where the bargaining disparity was severe.

title: No General Landlord Lien
bodyText: South Dakota does not give a residential landlord a general lien or security interest over a tenant's personal property to secure unpaid rent or other lease obligations. The only lien-like mechanism found in South Dakota's landlord-tenant statute is narrower and different in purpose: when handling higher-value abandoned property left behind by a tenant (see the abandoned-property provisions), a landlord has a lien limited to the reasonable costs of handling and storing that property - not a general security interest usable to collect unpaid rent from a tenant who is still in possession.

title: No Reservation-of-Rights Requirement for Late Rent
bodyText: South Dakota does not impose a statutory rule requiring a landlord to reserve its rights when accepting late rent in order to preserve a later right to terminate for that same late payment - unlike the reservation-of-rights requirements found in some neighboring states. This is architecturally consistent with South Dakota's broader 2024 shift away from a mandated notice-and-cure framework for nonpayment (see the eviction-procedure findings): because South Dakota does not require a landlord to give notice-and-an-opportunity-to-cure before pursuing eviction for nonpayment in the first place, there is correspondingly no waiver-by-acceptance doctrine tied to such a framework.

title: No Enumerated Prohibited-Terms List
bodyText: South Dakota's landlord-tenant chapter does not contain an enumerated list of prohibited lease provisions of the kind Kansas and Nebraska have - no specific statutory ban on a confession-of-judgment clause, and no enumerated ban on an exculpatory or liability-limitation/indemnification clause. South Dakota follows the North Dakota pattern. That absence is not the whole picture: a general contract statute, SDCL 53-9-3, independently voids any contract term whose object is to exempt a party from responsibility for its own fraud, willful injury to the person or property of another, or violation of law. Two further limits sit outside chapter 43-32: SDCL 43-32-8 makes the landlord's repair and habitability duty expressly non-waivable, and SDCL 15-17-39 voids attorney-fee-on-default provisions contained in an evidence of debt.

title: Lease Survival on Death or Incapacity
bodyText: If a South Dakota lease is terminable at the pleasure of either party (a true at-will arrangement), it terminates upon notice to the other party of that party's death or incapacity to contract. In every other case - including an ordinary fixed-term residential lease - the lease is NOT terminated by a party's death or incapacity; it survives and continues to bind the deceased or incapacitated party's estate or successor.

title: Criminal Penalty for Prohibiting a Service Animal in Housing
bodyText: South Dakota makes it a crime for a landlord to prohibit a service animal in residential housing. Under SDCL 20-13-23.4, no landlord may prohibit, by lease or otherwise, the keeping of a service animal by a person who is totally or partially physically disabled, totally or partially blind, or totally or partially deaf, in an apartment or other rented or leased residential property. A violation is a Class 2 misdemeanor. Note two things about the reach of this section. First, it is a direct restriction on lease content - a no-pets or no-animals clause that operates to bar a service animal for a covered tenant is prohibited by the statute itself, not merely unenforceable. Second, the disability categories it lists are narrower than those in South Dakota's public-accommodations service-animal provision, which also covers psychiatric and mental disability; a tenant whose qualifying disability is psychiatric or mental appears to fall outside this criminal provision, though the landlord's civil obligations under SDCL 43-32-33 through 43-32-36 and under federal fair housing law are unaffected and remain the primary source of duty. Separately, SDCL 20-13-23.7 requires good faith efforts to reasonably accommodate a disabled person in housing unless the accommodation would impose undue hardship.

title: Advance Rent Treated Separately From Security Deposit
bodyText: Whether money a South Dakota landlord collects up front is a 'security deposit' turns on what the money does, not what the lease calls it. SDCL 43-32-6.1 provides that any deposit of money whose function is to secure the performance of a residential rental agreement, or any part of it, is deemed to be a security deposit. So a payment labeled 'last month's rent' that is genuinely held and applied as rent for the final month is advance rent and does not count against the one-month deposit cap. But the same payment, if in fact held as security against damage, unpaid charges, or other nonperformance, is deemed a security deposit no matter what the lease calls it - and it then counts against the one-month cap and carries all the deposit rules, including the twenty-one-day return-or-written-statement deadline, the forty-five-day itemized accounting on request, forfeiture of all withholding rights for noncompliance, and exposure to punitive damages for bad-faith retention. Collecting both a full one-month deposit and a last month's rent payment is therefore safe only if the latter really is applied as rent.

title: Notice and Cure Is a Landlord Decision, Not a Lease Term
bodyText: South Dakota law gives a landlord broad discretion over whether, and how much, opportunity to cure a default a tenant receives before Landlord pursues eviction - there is no statutory requirement to offer one, for nonpayment or for an ordinary lease violation. Whether to give written notice and a set number of days to fix a curable problem before filing is therefore a case-by-case enforcement decision, not a fixed lease term. A real, in-use South Dakota lease reviewed for this project (South Dakota Achieve's residential lease) reflects this directly - its own default/eviction section states only that eviction will comply with SDCL Ch. 21-16, without building in any separate cure mechanism. Landlords who want to offer a cure opportunity consistently, rather than deciding fresh each time, should consider adopting - and following - a documented internal practice (for example, always giving written notice and a stated number of days before filing for an ordinary lease violation), since South Dakota law leaves this entirely to the landlord's own judgment and consistency at the point of enforcement.

title: Limits on Exculpatory and Indemnity Clauses
bodyText: South Dakota has no enumerated list of prohibited lease provisions, but a general contract statute limits how far an exculpatory, hold-harmless, or indemnification clause can reach. SDCL 53-9-3 provides that all contracts whose object is, directly or indirectly, to exempt anyone from responsibility for their own fraud, willful injury to the person or property of another, or violation of law whether willful or negligent, are against the policy of the law. In practice a clause releasing the landlord for ordinary negligence is generally enforceable if clear and unambiguous, but the same clause is void to the extent it reaches fraud, willful or wanton conduct, or a violation of law. A blanket release for any and all claims risks being read against the landlord. Separately, no exculpatory language can waive the landlord's repair and habitability duty, which SDCL 43-32-8 makes non-waivable.

title: Attorney Fee Clauses Are Restricted
bodyText: South Dakota follows a strict American Rule, and the limits on attorney fee clauses sit in the costs chapter rather than the landlord-tenant chapter. SDCL 15-17-38 leaves attorney compensation to the agreement of the parties but allows fees to be taxed as disbursements only where a specific statute permits it, and the disbursements SDCL 15-17-37 lists do not include attorney fees. SDCL 15-17-39 makes any provision in a note, bond, mortgage or other evidence of debt that provides for attorney fees on default or foreclosure against public policy and void, except as authorized by specific statute. Two separate uncertainties stack here, and a landlord should treat a fee-on-default clause as risky rather than reliable. First, whether a residential lease is an 'evidence of debt' has not been squarely decided. Second, SDCL 15-17-42 says the chapter 'applies to any civil action or special proceeding in which the State of South Dakota or any of its divisions, departments or political subdivisions is a party'. On one reading that scopes the whole chapter, including SDCL 15-17-39, to cases involving the State, which would mean it never reaches a private landlord-tenant dispute; on another it merely confirms the State is bound alongside everyone else, which is the reading that fits SDCL 15-17-37's plainly general language about 'the prevailing party in a civil action'. The general reading is the stronger one: SDCL 15-17-42 says the chapter 'applies to' such actions, not 'only' to them, and it came from the same 1992 act as the general sections. No case resolving that was located. Either way the practical answer is the same: do not rely on a lease fee clause. If chapter 15-17 reaches the lease, SDCL 15-17-39 may void the clause; if it does not, South Dakota's American Rule leaves no statutory basis to tax fees in an ordinary lease dispute anyway, and SDCL 53-9-4 separately voids penalties imposed by contract for nonperformance. Note where fees ARE available: SDCL 21-16-11 lets a court tax reasonable attorney fees to the prevailing party in an eviction, either party, if represented by a licensed attorney; and SDCL 43-32-28 lets a court award a prevailing tenant reasonable and customary fees in a retaliatory-conduct action. Both are the kind of specific statute SDCL 15-17-38 contemplates.

title: Termination Notice Scales to the Length of the Term
bodyText: Where a South Dakota tenancy runs for a term the parties never specified, the notice required to end it scales to the length of the term rather than being a fixed number of days. SDCL 43-32-15 provides that such a hiring is deemed renewed at the end of the term implied by law unless one of the parties gives the other notice of intent to terminate at least as long before expiration as the term of the hiring itself, not exceeding one month. The length of that term comes from SDCL 43-32-4: a hiring of lodgings for an unspecified term is presumed to run for whatever period the parties adopt to estimate the rent, so a weekly rent rate presumes a one-week term, and a hiring is presumed monthly only where no rent interval was agreed. A month-to-month tenancy therefore takes about a month's notice, a week-to-week tenancy takes about a week's, and the one-month ceiling means no unspecified-term tenancy ever requires more than a month. The rule runs both ways - either party may give the notice. This is separate from the modification-notice mechanics of SDCL 43-32-13 and from the fifteen-day rule for a tenancy at will under SDCL 43-8-8.

title: Tenant Belongings After an Eviction
bodyText: South Dakota imposes no post-writ inventory, storage, notice, or care-standard duty specific to eviction. The general abandoned-property rules govern instead, and they are triggered by the tenant having quit the premises rather than by service of a writ. Property with a total reasonable value of five hundred dollars or less, left for ten days after the tenant has quit, is presumed abandoned and may be disposed of. Property worth more than five hundred dollars must be stored, and Landlord has a lien on it to the extent of the costs of handling and storing the property; after storing it for thirty days or more, Landlord may treat it as abandoned and dispose of it. Because the trigger is the tenant quitting rather than the writ, the same timeline applies whether the tenant leaves voluntarily or is removed.

title: No Rules for Tenant Animals After an Eviction
bodyText: South Dakota law says nothing about what happens to a tenant's animals after an eviction. There is no animal-control notification route, no notice-posting requirement, no unattended-animal rule, and no duty assigned to Landlord or to the sheriff. The abandoned-property provisions are written for property and are a poor fit for a live animal, so a landlord facing this situation has no statutory procedure to follow and should contact local animal control.

title: Reasonable Accommodation of Disabled Tenants
bodyText: South Dakota imposes its own reasonable-accommodation duty in housing, separate from federal fair housing law. SDCL 20-13-23.7 provides that for purposes of employment, public accommodation, public service, and education or housing, good faith efforts shall be made to reasonably accommodate a disabled person unless the accommodation would impose undue hardship. The standard is framed as good faith efforts subject to an undue-hardship limit, and the statute does not define either term or set out a request-and-response procedure, so in practice a landlord should document what was requested, what was considered, and why any accommodation was or was not made. Two limits sitting in the same chapter qualify that duty and are easy to miss. SDCL 20-13-21.1 provides that nothing in chapter 20-13 requires a person selling, renting or leasing property, or anyone acting for the owner, to modify the property in any way, to incur any additional expense, or to exercise a higher degree of care for a person having a disability than for a person who does not have one. It further provides that the chapter does not relieve any person of the obligations generally imposed on all persons, regardless of disability, in a written lease or rental agreement, and does not forbid distinctions based on an inability to fulfil the terms and conditions of the lease, including its financial obligations. So South Dakota's own good-faith accommodation duty carries no state-law obligation to pay for or carry out physical modifications, and it does not excuse a tenant from rent. Federal fair housing law is a separate and generally more demanding source - it requires you to permit reasonable modifications made at the tenant's expense and to make reasonable accommodations in rules, policies, practices and services - and SDCL 20-13-21.1, which limits only what chapter 20-13 requires, does not cut it down. One more provision in the same chapter cuts the other way and should be read with SDCL 20-13-21.1, not instead of it. SDCL 20-13-20(4) makes it an unfair or discriminatory housing practice to refuse to permit, AT THE EXPENSE OF THE DISABLED PERSON, reasonable modifications of existing property that may be necessary to afford full enjoyment of the property - and it lets the landlord, where reasonable, condition permission on the renter agreeing to restore the premises to its prior condition, reasonable wear and tear excepted. So South Dakota does impose a state-law duty to PERMIT modifications; what SDCL 20-13-21.1 denies is any duty to PAY for them or to carry them out. The two fit together. Note also that the owner-occupied exemption in SDCL 20-13-20 reaches subdivision (4) as well as (1) and (2), so in a dwelling with living quarters for no more than two families where the owner occupies one of them, the modification duty does not apply either - though the advertising prohibition in subdivision (3) still does.

title: Towing From Private Property
bodyText:
South Dakota regulates towing from private property through its abandoned-vehicle chapter, and the duties fall on the tow company rather than on you. A vehicle counts as an abandoned motor vehicle on private property only if it was left there without the permission of the landowner or tenant (SDCL 32-36-2(1)). No removal agency may remove an abandoned motor vehicle from private property without the written permission of the landowner or tenant, and a violation is a Class 2 misdemeanor (SDCL 32-36-4.1); once it has that authorization the agency may enter the land to make the removal (SDCL 32-36-4). Removal agency includes an ordinary tow business, and motor vehicle reaches boats, house trailers, trailers, campers, snowmobiles and off-road vehicles as well as cars (SDCL 32-36-2(4), (5)). After a removal the agency must mail certified notice to the registered owner and to all readily identifiable lienholders within forty-five days on a form provided by the Department of Revenue, and if it does not mail that notice within ten days of the removal it may charge no storage beyond the ten-day period until the notice goes out (SDCL 32-36-8). The agency holds a possessory lien for the reasonable costs of taking custody and storage, but no more than five hundred dollars against the contents of the vehicle, and no lien at all against the tools a person keeps for their trade or business, or against clothing or food (SDCL 32-30-18).

Two consequences matter in practice. First, a tenant's own vehicle parked with your permission is not an abandoned motor vehicle, so this chapter gives you no authority to tow it for breaking a parking rule - that is a lease-compliance matter to take up with the tenant, not a towing matter. Second, South Dakota imposes no signage requirement for towing from private property; your written authorization is what makes the tow lawful. The statute does not say whether that authorization must be a per-tow order or may be a standing written contract, so it does not settle which form to use.

title: Removing Someone Who Is Not a Tenant
bodyText:
When someone who is not your tenant will not leave, South Dakota's criminal trespass statute is the usual tool and it moves faster than an eviction. Under SDCL 22-35-6 a person who enters or remains anywhere knowing they are not privileged to do so, where notice against trespass has been given by actual communication to that person, by posting in a manner reasonably likely to come to a trespasser's attention, or by a fence or other enclosure a reasonable person would recognise as designed to exclude trespassers, is guilty of a Class 2 misdemeanor. If that person then defies an order to leave communicated personally by the owner of the premises or by any other authorized person, the offence becomes criminal trespass, a Class 1 misdemeanor.

Two limits decide whether this is actually available to you. A tenant is privileged to be on the property under the lease, so trespass is never the route against a tenant - use the forcible entry and detainer process instead. And SDCL 22-35-7 makes it an affirmative defence that the person reasonably believed the owner, or another person permitted to license access, would have permitted them to enter or remain. Your tenant is such a person, so a guest your tenant still welcomes has that defence available. A guest who overstays with the tenant's blessing is therefore a lease-violation problem to take up with the tenant under the guest and default provisions, not a trespass problem. Where someone took possession by force, intimidation, fraud or stealth against your prior actual possession, or holds possession by force, threats or menacing conduct, forcible entry and detainer is independently available under SDCL 21-16-1(1) to (3) without regard to trespass.

title: Medical Cannabis Cardholders
bodyText:
South Dakota's medical cannabis law limits how you may treat a registered cardholder. Under SDCL 34-20G-19 a cardholder may not be refused a lease by a landlord, or otherwise be penalized by a landlord, solely for the person's status as a cardholder - unless failing to do so would violate federal law or regulations, or would cause you to lose a monetary or licensing-related benefit under federal law or regulation. That carve-out is what matters for federally subsidized housing. The same section then provides that it does not prevent a landlord from imposing reasonable restrictions on the medical use of cannabis by a cardholder who resides at the landlord's property.

Two things you may clearly do. SDCL 34-20G-27(3) provides that nothing in the chapter requires a landlord to allow the cultivation of cannabis on the rental property, so a cultivation ban is squarely permitted. SDCL 34-20G-27(2) provides that nothing requires a person in lawful possession of property to allow a guest, client, customer or other visitor to smoke or vape cannabis there. Read that second one carefully: it is written about visitors, not about your resident tenants, so it is not the authority for restricting a tenant's own use. The reasonable-restrictions sentence in 34-20G-19 is.

Steinoak's Smoking Policy clause prohibits smoking and vaping of any kind, including of marijuana, rather than prohibiting possession or non-combusted use, and it applies to every tenant rather than to cardholders as such. That is the shape most likely to qualify as a reasonable restriction: it leaves other methods of medical use available and it is not a penalty imposed for cardholder status. But reasonable is not defined anywhere in the chapter and no South Dakota decision applying it was located, so treat the margin as argued rather than settled. Do not screen out an applicant, raise their rent, refuse a renewal or threaten them because they hold a card, and note that the clause as written says nothing about cultivation even though South Dakota would let you prohibit it.

title: Selling the Property With a Tenant in Place
bodyText:
South Dakota has no statute moving security deposit liability to a buyer when a rented property is sold, and none releasing the selling landlord. Several states do: Kansas, Nebraska, North Dakota, Minnesota, California, Nevada, Texas, New Jersey, Florida and Arizona all have an express successor-liability or transfer-or-return provision. South Dakota does not, and nothing in chapter 43-32 - read in full - requires you to notify a tenant that the property is for sale or has been sold, or imposes a landlord-identity or identity-change disclosure duty.

So in South Dakota the question is answered by your purchase agreement and by ordinary property and contract law rather than by statute. A buyer takes the property subject to an existing lease as a general matter, but no South Dakota statute makes the buyer answerable for a deposit the seller is holding, and none discharges the seller's own obligation under SDCL 43-32-24 to account for that deposit. The practical consequence is that the deposit obligation stays with whoever took the money unless your sale documents move it. Transfer the deposit at closing against a written acknowledgment that the buyer has assumed the accounting duty, keep a copy of the accounting you would have owed, and tell the tenant in writing who now holds the deposit and where to send the mailing address or delivery instructions that start the twenty-one-day clock. If you sell without doing any of that, you remain the person the tenant can pursue.

title: An Uncashed Deposit Refund Is Unclaimed Property
bodyText:
A deposit refund your former tenant never cashes does not become yours. South Dakota's Uniform Unclaimed Property Act presumes all intangible property abandoned when it has remained unclaimed by the owner for more than three years after it became payable or distributable, less any lawful charges, and the owner's failure to make demand or to present the instrument does not stop that clock (SDCL 43-41B-2(a), (b)). Expiry of any limitation period does not prevent the property from being presumed abandoned or affect your duty to report it (SDCL 43-41B-18).

Before you file, you must communicate with the owner and exercise due diligence to find them, and for property worth fifty dollars or more you must mail notice to each person entitled to it - unless your records indicate the address is inaccurate - stating that you hold property that appears to be theirs and that it will escheat to the state (SDCL 43-41B-18). The report goes to the administrator, must be verified, and is due before November 1 each year as of the preceding June 30. It must give the owner's name and last known address for property worth ten dollars or more, the nature and amount of the property, the date it became payable, and the date of your last transaction with the apparent owner; items worth under ten dollars each may be reported in the aggregate. If you took over the property from a previous holder, or your own name has changed while you held it, the report must list every previous holder's name and address.

One practical point: reissuing a stale cheque does not restart the three years, because the period runs from when the refund first became payable rather than from the date of any replacement instrument. For a South Dakota deposit that is when your accounting was due under SDCL 43-32-24 - though the Act does not say so in those terms, so treat it as the better reading rather than a stated rule.

title: Winter Utility Disconnection
bodyText:
South Dakota does not impose a winter moratorium on utility disconnection, but it does lengthen the notice. Under ARSD 20:10:20:10, from November 1 through March 31 a utility may not disconnect residential service without adding thirty days to the time periods in ARSD 20:10:20:03(2), and it must notify the customer before the normal disconnection date that the customer has that additional thirty days. The underlying periods are a payment period of not less than twenty days from the billing transmittal date to the due date, plus a further notice period of not less than ten days during which the bill has been owing. So the runway before a nonpayment disconnection is roughly thirty days outside the winter window and roughly sixty days inside it.

The utility must also send written notice of its intent to disconnect, and it must postpone a residential disconnection for one 30-day period when a physician or a public health or social services official certifies that disconnection would aggravate a medical emergency of someone living there.

Scope matters more than the numbers here. These are Public Utilities Commission rules, and the commission's rule power reaches only public utilities as the statute defines them. That definition leaves out gas and electric utilities owned by a city, town or other public body and rural electric cooperatives (a cooperative that sells gas is still covered for its gas service), so these protections don't reach those utilities' customers; ask that utility what its own policy is. Water and sewer service is not covered by these rules at all. Two consequences for you. If the tenant is the customer of record, a winter shutoff takes considerably longer than you might assume, which changes how quickly an unpaid utility becomes a habitability or lease-compliance problem rather than a private matter between the tenant and the utility. If you are the customer of record - a master-metered building, or a lease where you pay a utility - the extension and the notice are yours, and the notice will come to you rather than to the tenant. Before disconnecting a landlord-customer's service where it knows a tenant lives there, a covered utility must offer the tenant the chance to take the service in the tenant's own name, if that is economically feasible, and it may not collect your unpaid bill from the tenant or make the tenant pay it to get service.

None of this touches SDCL 43-32-6. If you willfully diminish services by interrupting, or causing the interruption of, electric, gas, water or other essential service to the tenant, the tenant may sue for an injunction, recover possession or end the lease, and in any case recover two months' rent plus return of any advance rent and deposit. Willfully letting a utility you pay for be shut off can count, whatever your reason.

title: Service-Animal Misrepresentation Reaches Public Accommodations, Not Housing
bodyText:
South Dakota now has a criminal penalty for misrepresenting a service animal, and it does not reach housing. SDCL 22-35-9, added in 2026, makes it a Class 2 misdemeanor for an individual to misrepresent an animal in that individual's possession as a service animal, directly or indirectly through statements or conduct, intentionally and in any place of public accommodation, in order to obtain rights or privileges available to someone who qualifies for a service animal under state or federal law, knowing they are not entitled to them. For that section service animal means a dog trained to do work or perform tasks for the benefit of an individual with a disability as set out in 28 C.F.R. 36.104 (January 1, 2026), and the section states expressly that a dog's crime-deterrent effect and the provision of emotional support, well-being, comfort or companionship do not constitute work or tasks.

A leased dwelling is not a place of public accommodation, so do not expect this offence to cover a tenant or applicant who misrepresents a pet as a service or support animal, and do not threaten anyone with it. Your remedy in housing remains civil: SDCL 43-32-36 permits eviction and a damage fee of up to one thousand dollars where a tenant knowingly makes a false claim of disability requiring a service or assistance animal or knowingly supplies fraudulent documentation, which is what the Assistance Animal clause states.

One trap follows from this. South Dakota now carries three different service-animal standards in three places: the civil housing framework in SDCL 43-32-33 to 43-32-36; the criminal prohibition in SDCL 20-13-23.4 on a landlord barring a service animal, which covers only tenants who are totally or partially physically disabled, blind or deaf; and this public-accommodations definition, limited to dogs performing trained tasks and expressly excluding emotional support. Do not carry one section's definition into another, and in particular do not use this section's exclusion of emotional-support animals to deny an assistance-animal accommodation in housing, where federal fair housing law and the chapter 43-32 framework govern and both reach support animals.

title: Residential Rent Is Exempt From Sales Tax
bodyText:
Residential rent is not subject to South Dakota sales tax. The sales tax reaches sales of tangible personal property, listed services and room rentals to transient guests, and the law defines a taxable lease or rental as one of tangible personal property or electronically delivered products, so leasing a dwelling falls outside it. The Department of Revenue's Lease and Rental guidance says the same: the lease or rental of real property is exempt from sales and use tax. So you do not collect or remit state sales tax on rent under an ordinary residential lease, and you should not add a tax line to the rent or describe part of the rent as tax.

Two boundaries matter if you operate outside ordinary residential leasing. Sales tax applies to room rentals by a place held out to the public as furnishing sleeping accommodations to transient guests, meaning guests who stay less than 28 consecutive days; renting a sleeping accommodation for 10 or fewer days in a calendar year is exempt as casual or occasional. South Dakota's tourism tax and municipal gross receipts taxes on lodging can apply on top and were not researched here, so do not read this as covering a short-term or vacation rental. Second, a lease or rental of tangible personal property is a taxable retail sale, so a separately stated charge for renting furniture, appliances or equipment with the dwelling may be taxable, and how the state treats such charges, or charges for services, bundled with a dwelling was not researched. If you charge separately for anything other than the dwelling itself, get that specific question answered before deciding not to collect tax on it.

title: Domestic Abuse or Stalking: Tenant's Right to End the Lease
bodyText: If a South Dakota tenant or a household member is the victim of alleged domestic abuse, unlawful sexual behavior or stalking, the tenant may end the lease without an early-termination penalty, effective on a specified date, by giving you written notice that the termination is due to fear of imminent danger or injury, with one of these dated within the 30 days before the notice: a signed police report on the incident, a protection order issued in response to it, or documentation from a licensed health care provider who examined the person and has reasonable cause to believe they were a victim (SDCL 43-32-19(3), 43-32-19.1). The tenant owes no otherwise-applicable early-termination fee and no rent for the month after the month they move out.

title: Disclose Known Prior Meth Manufacturing
bodyText: If you actually know methamphetamine was previously manufactured on the property, you must tell the tenant before they become obligated under the lease. For a building of two or more units, the duty covers only the unit you know about (SDCL 43-32-30). The lease's optional clause records the disclosure.

title: No Just-Cause Eviction Requirement
bodyText: South Dakota has no just-cause or good-cause eviction statute. The end of the term ends the right to possession, and a landlord may decline to renew without giving a reason. SDCL 43-32-14 and 43-32-15 presume renewal where a lessee holds over and the lessor accepts rent, or where the term was never specified and neither party gives the scaling notice - so the way to end an unspecified-term tenancy is to give that notice, not to show cause. For a tenancy at will, SDCL 43-8-8 requires 15 days' written notice, or two months where the tenant or an immediate family member is on active military service. SDCL 43-32-27 is the one place a reason matters: a notice to vacate not based on a breach of the lease can support a retaliation claim if it follows a protected event, and the statute says expressly that failing to renew a written lease before or upon its expiration is not retaliation. No conversion-notice year, no rent-escrow filing bar, and no tenants'-association protection beyond SDCL 43-32-27's union-organising limb were found.

title: No Rule on Algorithmic Rent Setting
bodyText: South Dakota has no statute addressing algorithmic or software-assisted rent setting, revenue-management pricing, or the sharing of rent data among landlords. Nothing requires disclosure that software set the rent, and nothing prohibits using it. SDCL 43-32-6.1 caps the security deposit and SDCL 43-32-13 governs how a month-to-month rent change is noticed, but neither speaks to how the figure is arrived at, and South Dakota separately preempts local rent control. Federal and state antitrust law still applies to agreements among competitors, and that is a different question from the lease.

title: Whether Fees Count as Rent
bodyText: No South Dakota statute deems a non-rent charge to be rent, and none forbids a lease from defining rent to include other charges. Two places make the distinction matter anyway. SDCL 21-16-1(4) gives a forcible entry and detainer ground where a lessee 'fails to pay his rent for three days after the same shall be due' - that ground is written about RENT, so a lease that sweeps late fees, utilities and other charges into the defined term risks an eviction built on unpaid fees rather than unpaid rent, which is a weaker filing. SDCL 43-32-24 separately lets a landlord withhold from the security deposit both rent defaults and 'other funds due to the landlord pursuant to an agreement', so for deposit purposes the lease's own definition of what is owed does the work and no relabelling is needed. The practical course is to keep rent meaning the monthly payment for occupancy and to pursue other charges as other charges.

title: No Landlord Self-Cure and Bill-Back Right
bodyText: South Dakota gives a landlord no statutory right to perform a tenant's obligation, cure a tenant's breach, and bill the cost back as rent. The statutory traffic runs the other way: SDCL 43-32-9 lets the TENANT repair and deduct from rent when the landlord fails to repair within a reasonable time after notice, and SDCL 43-32-8 permits the parties to agree that the tenant performs specified repairs or maintenance in lieu of rent. SDCL 43-32-10 makes the tenant liable to repair deterioration or damage caused by the tenant's own negligent, willful or malicious conduct, which is a liability rule, not a self-help mechanism. So a landlord who wants to fix something the tenant should have fixed and recover the cost is relying on the lease and on ordinary damages, not on a statute, and should expect to prove the cost was reasonable and actually caused by the tenant.

title: No Lease-Completeness or Copy Requirement
bodyText: South Dakota imposes no statutory requirements about the physical completeness of a residential lease. There is no rule against leaving blank spaces to be filled in after signing, no requirement to give the tenant a copy of the signed lease, no deadline for delivering one, and no requirement that the lease identify the landlord or an agent for service. The lease also need not be in writing at all: SDCL 43-32-8 and 43-32-10 both apply to a hiring of residential premises 'whether in writing or parol'. None of that makes blanks or a missing copy a good idea - a landlord who cannot produce a complete signed lease has trouble proving the term, the rent and any lease-defined eviction ground under SDCL 21-16-1(7), which depends entirely on what the lease says.

title: Quiet Possession and Quiet Enjoyment
bodyText: South Dakota puts the covenant of quiet enjoyment in statute rather than leaving it to common law. SDCL 43-32-6 requires a lessor to deliver the leased premises to the lessee and to secure the lessee's quiet enjoyment against all lawful claimants. The same section supplies the remedy when the landlord is the one interfering: if the landlord unlawfully removes or excludes the tenant, or willfully diminishes services by interrupting electric, gas, water or other essential service, the tenant may sue for an injunction, recover possession by suit, or terminate the rental agreement, and in any case recover damages equal to two months' rent plus the return of any advance rent and deposit. SDCL 43-32-19(1) adds a termination right where the landlord does not, within a reasonable time after the tenant's WRITTEN request, put or keep the tenant in quiet possession. Two practical consequences: the duty runs against lawful claimants - a title or lien claim - rather than against every nuisance a neighbour creates; and because it is statutory and tied to SDCL 43-32-6's remedy, a lease cannot usefully disclaim it.

title: No Statutory Lease or Notice Forms
bodyText: South Dakota prescribes no form for a residential lease or for any landlord notice. There is no statutory lease form, no prescribed notice-to-quit or termination form, and no 'substantially the following form' language anywhere in the landlord-tenant statutes. What the statutes prescribe is content and service, not layout: SDCL 43-32-13 requires the month-to-month modification notice to be in writing and given 30 days before the end of the month; SDCL 43-8-9 requires a notice ending a tenancy at will to be in writing and served by delivery to the tenant or to a person of discretion residing on the premises, or, if neither can be found with reasonable diligence, by affixing it to a conspicuous part of the premises where it can conveniently be read; and SDCL 43-32-32 requires an entry notice to specify the date or dates of entry, a period during normal business hours, the purpose, and a means for the tenant to ask to reschedule. Meet those and the wording is yours.

title: No Rule on Tenant Security Cameras
bodyText: South Dakota has no statute about a tenant installing a security camera, video doorbell or other recording device at a rented home, and none about a landlord doing so. Nothing gives a tenant a right to install one over the landlord's objection, and nothing prohibits a landlord from allowing or refusing it. In practice the question is answered by the lease: a camera screwed to a door frame or wired into the building is an alteration, so the no-alterations clause governs, and a device a tenant can hang and remove without damage usually is not. Two outside limits are worth knowing. A camera a tenant aims at a neighbour's windows or a shared bathroom can reach South Dakota's criminal invasion-of-privacy provisions, which are not a landlord-tenant matter but are a reason to write the rule down. And a tenant whose disability makes a monitoring device necessary may be entitled to install one as a reasonable modification at the tenant's expense under SDCL 20-13-20(4).

title: Electronic Notices and Delivery
bodyText: South Dakota's landlord-tenant statutes say nothing about delivering notices electronically, so the rules come from the Uniform Electronic Transactions Act in SDCL chapter 53-12, and three of its provisions cannot be contracted around. First, the Act applies only between parties who have each agreed to conduct transactions by electronic means, judged from the context and the parties' conduct (SDCL 53-12-8) - a clause reciting consent helps, but conduct can establish or undercut it. Second, a party who agrees to one electronic transaction may refuse to conduct others, and SDCL 53-12-9 says that right 'may not be waived by agreement' - so a lease cannot bind a tenant to accept every future notice electronically. Third, where a law requires information in writing, an electronic record satisfies it only if the record is capable of retention by the recipient, and a record is not capable of retention if the sender or its system inhibits the recipient's ability to print or store it (SDCL 53-12-17); if the sender does inhibit that, the record 'is not enforceable against the recipient' (SDCL 53-12-19). SDCL 53-12-20 makes those requirements unvariable by agreement, with two narrow exceptions - where the other law's writing requirement is itself variable by agreement, and where the other law's first-class-mail requirement is variable. The Act also does not reach transactions under SDCL chapter 15-6 or other transactions involving the Unified Judicial System (SDCL 53-12-3), so court filings and service in an eviction action are outside it. Practical upshot: use a portal the tenant can download and print from, keep paper available for any notice that ends the tenancy, and do not treat a consent clause as permanent.

title: Abandonment: The Lease Survives, and Nothing Makes You Re-Rent
bodyText: South Dakota answers the two halves of this question differently, so treat them separately. On the property the tenant leaves behind, the statutes are detailed: anything worth five hundred dollars or less that sits on the premises for ten days after the tenant has quit is presumed abandoned and you may dispose of it, and anything worth more must be stored, with a lien for your handling and storage costs, and may be treated as abandoned only after thirty days or more. A separate chapter handles a mobile or manufactured home left on leased land. On your own money, the statutes say nothing. There is no South Dakota duty to mitigate your damages after a tenant walks out, and no provision requiring reasonable efforts to re-rent. The lease is not ended by the tenant leaving, by your notice, or by your filing: a lease ends when the term expires, when both sides agree, or when the tenant acquires better title, and terminating early for a breach is something you may do, not something that happens to you. So the tenant stays liable for rent as it falls due, and a possession action may be brought without giving up the money claim, since the eviction statute lets you join rents and damages or sue for them separately. Do not translate the absence of a mitigation duty into a clause reciting that you owe none, and do not accelerate the balance. South Dakota voids a contractual penalty for nonperformance and voids agreed damages except where fixing the real loss would be impracticable. The cautious course is to re-let promptly, credit what you collect, and claim the documented shortfall plus your costs of recovering possession.

title: No State ADU Law - It Is Entirely Your City’s Call
bodyText: South Dakota has no accessory dwelling unit statute. Nothing stops a city or county restricting or prohibiting an accessory unit, nothing authorizes one by right, nothing bars an owner-occupancy condition, and nothing addresses whether an accessory unit may be rented out. States that have legislated here typically do all four; South Dakota has done none of them, so the answer for any given property is whatever the local zoning ordinance says. Two state-level points are still worth knowing. Building standards are set by reference rather than by a statewide residential code: where a municipality adopts construction standards for a residential structure it does so by adopting the 2024 International Residential Code, and where no local ordinance exists the 2024 International Building Code supplies the design standard for buildings commenced after July 1, 2026, with residential structures, mobile and manufactured homes and farmsteads excluded. A municipality may not require a sprinkler system in a residential structure, which matters if the accessory unit is in a detached one- or two-family dwelling or a townhouse of not more than three stories. And once an accessory unit is let as a residence, the ordinary rules follow it - the non-waivable habitability duty, the deposit cap and timetable, the entry standard - regardless of how the zoning treats it. The cautious course is to confirm in writing with your city's planning or building official that the unit may lawfully be occupied and rented before you let it, and to keep that confirmation; an unpermitted unit is a rent-collection problem as well as a zoning one.

title: An Agreed Notice Channel Works Only Where the Statute Says So
bodyText: South Dakota has no general provision letting the parties add a way of giving notice where a statute requires it. Instead each notice statute names its own manner, and the pattern across them is consistent: where the legislature wanted the lease to be able to supply the channel, it said so, and where it did not, the manner is fixed. The entry statute is the clear example of the first kind. Twenty-four hours' written notice is presumed reasonable unless alternate methods of notification, or times for entry, are mutually agreed between you and the tenant in the lease, so a lease that names a text or email channel for entry notice does real work. The self-service storage lien statute does the same thing for a different relationship, allowing notice by email if the rental agreement provides for it. The termination notice for a tenancy at will is the other kind. It must be in writing and served by delivering it to the tenant or to some person of discretion residing on the premises, and only if neither can be found with reasonable diligence may it be posted conspicuously where it can be read. That list is the statute's, and a lease term adding email or text does not replace it. The cautious course is to write the agreed electronic channel into the lease as an additional, belt-and-braces method, used alongside and never instead of the statutory manner, and to keep proof of both. Where a court filing is involved, service runs on the eviction statute and the civil rules, not on anything the lease says.

title: No Duty to Notify Tenants of Proceedings Against the Property
bodyText: South Dakota imposes no duty on a residential landlord to tell tenants about a foreclosure, condemnation, code-enforcement action or other proceeding that could affect their tenancy, and South Dakota's foreclosure notice scheme does not reach them either. A foreclosing creditor must serve written notice of the sale at least twenty-one days before the sale date on the mortgagor and on any lien holder or encumbrancer whose interest would be affected - not on tenants or occupants. The published notice names the mortgagor, the mortgagee, any assignee, and persons claiming a recorded lien, encumbrance or other recorded ownership interest; an ordinary residential tenant holding an unrecorded lease appears nowhere in that list. The statutory duty in this area runs the other way: the tenant must immediately forward to you any notice of a proceeding to recover the property. The practical consequence is that your tenant may first learn of a foreclosure when a stranger appears claiming possession. The cautious course is to commit in the lease to give prompt written notice of any foreclosure, condemnation or code action affecting the property, and to honor it; the commitment costs you nothing while the property is sound, and it is the only notice your tenant will get. FEDERAL: after a foreclosure a bona fide tenant is entitled to ninety days' notice to vacate from the successor in interest under the Protecting Tenants at Foreclosure Act, a duty on the buyer rather than on you.

title: No Statutory Alarm-Tampering Fee - Charge Actual Cost Instead
bodyText: South Dakota has no statute letting you charge a set lease fee for removing or tampering with a smoke or carbon monoxide alarm. Some states fix a dollar figure you may put in the lease; South Dakota does not, and that absence matters because of how South Dakota treats contractual charges. A flat sum payable because the tenant broke a lease term is a penalty imposed by contract for nonperformance, and penalties of that kind are void. An agreed figure standing in for damages is enforceable only where actual damage would be impracticable or extremely difficult to fix - which is hard to argue about a detector whose replacement cost is a receipt. So the lawful route is the ordinary one: require that alarms be kept in place and operating, and charge the actual documented cost of replacing or reinstalling the device. That cost is recoverable as restoring the premises to their move-in condition beyond ordinary wear and tear, and may be withheld from the deposit if you meet the deposit deadlines - the deposit returned or a written statement of the specific reason for withholding within twenty-one days, and an itemized accounting within forty-five days if the tenant asks. Tampering can also be a crime in its own right where a fire alarm system is involved, which is a deterrent you can describe without turning it into a fee. Note also that South Dakota's detector rules reach only some buildings; a unit outside them has no alarm the rules require you to maintain.

title: No Duty to Rehouse a Tenant
bodyText: South Dakota imposes no duty to provide alternative or temporary housing, and no relocation assistance obligation, in any circumstance - not during a repair, not after a fire or flood, not on a condemnation or vacate order, and not on a conversion or sale. There is no tenant-request mechanism to trigger one and no payment schedule. The relocation provisions in South Dakota's statutes belong to public acquisition and urban renewal, where a government body displacing someone pays benefits; none of them reaches a private landlord. So if a unit becomes uninhabitable, you owe the tenant no accommodation. What the tenant has instead is an exit, and it is worth understanding because it is the mechanism that actually resolves these situations. After notice to you of conditions requiring repair and a reasonable time without repair, the tenant may vacate the premises and is then discharged from additional charges of rent and from performing the other lease conditions. A tenant may also terminate the lease where the greater part of the premises, or the part you had reason to believe was the material inducement to the tenant, is destroyed other than by the tenant's ordinary negligence. So the statutory answer to an uninhabitable unit is that the tenancy ends and the rent stops - not that you house the tenant elsewhere. The cautious course is to treat rehousing as a commercial decision rather than a legal one: offering another vacant unit often preserves a tenancy you would otherwise lose, but say in writing that it is offered as an accommodation and on what terms.

title: No Entry Right to Care for an Abandoned Animal
bodyText: South Dakota gives you no right to enter a rented dwelling to feed, water or remove an animal a tenant has left behind, and imposes no duty on you to do so. There is no provision covering an animal abandoned in a unit, none authorizing you to surrender it, and none protecting you from liability if you do. The general entry rule is all you have: except in an emergency or where it is impracticable, you owe the tenant reasonable notice of your intent to enter and must enter only at reasonable times. An animal in genuine distress is the clearest case for the emergency exception, but the exception excuses the notice, not everything that follows. Removing the animal is a separate act and South Dakota routes that through law enforcement rather than through you. An animal that is neglected, abandoned, mistreated or cruelly treated may be impounded, and that power sits with the authorities and animal care and control agencies, not with a landlord. Property the tenant leaves behind has its own statutory handling - presumed abandoned after ten days if worth five hundred dollars or less, stored thirty days with a lien if worth more - but an animal is not a thing you should be running through a storage-and-lien analysis. The cautious course is to call animal control or the sheriff, document the condition, the date and whom you contacted, and let the impoundment power be exercised by the people who hold it. Address pet abandonment in the lease too, requiring the tenant to remove any animal at the end of occupancy and making the tenant responsible for the cost you actually incur.

title: No Presumption About Appliances - but Some Cannot Be Excluded
bodyText: South Dakota has no provision presuming that appliances present in a unit are landlord-supplied unless the lease excludes them. If the lease says nothing, whether a stove left in the kitchen is part of what you let is a question of construction rather than a statutory presumption. That is a reason to be explicit, not a reason to be silent. Two statutory points bound what exclusion can achieve. The tenant's own duty treats appliances as part of the leased property: the tenant must preserve the premises, the appliances, the appurtenances and the other leased personal property, and repair deterioration caused by the tenant's own negligent, wilful or malicious conduct. So appliances you do supply come with a tenant obligation attached, which is useful to you. More importantly, you cannot exclude your way out of the systems the statute names. You must maintain all electrical, plumbing and heating systems of the premises in good and safe working order and condition, and that duty cannot be waived or modified - so a lease that purports to exclude the furnace, the water heater, the wiring or the plumbing from your responsibility does not work, whatever it says about appliances. The line to hold in drafting is between a system and a convenience: the heating system is yours by statute, a dishwasher is not. The cautious course is a schedule in the lease listing every appliance you supply and its condition, stating that anything not listed is the tenant's own and is not your responsibility to repair or replace, and confirming the statutory systems remain yours.

title: No Application-Fee Rule - but Watch What the Money Is For
bodyText: South Dakota does not regulate rental application fees. There is no cap, no annual adjustment, no refund right if you do not screen the applicant or if an earlier applicant takes the unit, no pre-application disclosure of estimated rent and fees, no exemption for a minor household member, and no unit-count threshold below which a different rule applies. Nothing bans the fee and nothing limits it. Two South Dakota rules nonetheless decide how to charge it safely. The first is the deposit statute's deeming sentence: any money whose function is to secure performance of a residential rental agreement, or any part of one, is a security deposit however it is denominated, and your ceiling for all of it together is one month's rent. An application fee that genuinely pays for screening work you do is a fee for a service and sits outside that; a sum you keep and later apply to rent or damage is deposit money whatever the receipt says. The second is that a fixed sum you keep because an applicant did not go ahead is a penalty for nonperformance and void. So charge the actual cost of screening, charge it only when you screen, and say in writing before you take it what it covers and that it is not refundable because it pays for work done. Keep the screening report. A fee collected for work never performed is also the clearest case of a deceptive practice in a consumer transaction, which is a separate and larger exposure than the fee itself.

title: No Asbestos Disclosure or Abatement Duty in a Lease
bodyText: South Dakota places no asbestos duty on a residential landlord. There is no disclosure requirement, no survey or inspection duty, no abatement trigger, no notice to tenants before disturbing material, and no operations-and-maintenance plan requirement. The asbestos provisions South Dakota does have are about something else entirely - they limit the liability of a corporate successor for asbestos claims, which is tort-reform legislation rather than a building rule. One adjacent point is worth knowing because it shows what South Dakota does ask, and of whom: the state's property condition disclosure statement, which a seller must give a buyer, asks about asbestos among many other conditions. That duty arises on a sale, not on a lease - but note that a lease with an option to purchase is a covered transfer, so adding a purchase option brings the asbestos question into your disclosure obligations. For a plain tenancy, the duty that applies is the general one: keep the premises fit for human habitation and in good and safe working order, non-waivably. Damaged, friable asbestos-containing material in an occupied unit is a condition within that; intact material that nobody disturbs generally is not. Federal law is where the real obligations sit for work that disturbs it, and those reach contractors and renovation work rather than the tenancy. The cautious course is to disclose in writing anything you know, never to let maintenance staff cut, sand or remove suspect material, and to use a licensed contractor for any work on it.

title: No Association Disclosure Duty in a Lease
bodyText: South Dakota does require an association disclosure, but it runs on sale and not on lease. A seller of residential real property governed by a homeowners' association must give the buyer, before the buyer makes a written offer, a disclosure that the property is governed by an association, a copy of the association's governing documents, a statement of whether there is an assessment and its amount, frequency and purpose, and a list of any special one-time assessments from the most recent three years, and must amend that in writing if a material fact changes before closing or possession. Nothing imposes any part of that on a landlord letting the same unit. A lease with an option to purchase is the exception to plan for: the section applies to all transfers, and the seller-disclosure chapter counts that lease as a transfer, so give the association disclosure before the tenant signs one.
