No statute requires a lease of a condominium or association-governed unit to disclose the association's obligations, to attach its documents, or to carry the owner's statement that the owner knows the governing documents, and nothing requires a copy to go to the board. Your exposure is therefore practical rather than statutory: your tenant can be fined or lose privileges under rules they were never shown, and they will come to you. The cautious course is to name the association in the lease, attach its current rules and regulations as a dated exhibit, and make the tenant's compliance duty run to the rules as attached rather than to rules the tenant has never seen. Where the association can assess you for a tenant's conduct, pass through the documented amount actually assessed, not a flat sum, because a separate statute voids contractual penalties for nonperformance. And the condominium chapter does not help: the particulars it requires in a master deed or lease are structural - each unit's number, area and location, the common areas, and the council of co-owners' insurance - with nothing about a tenant.

title: No Auto-Renewal Statute - but Two Renewal Presumptions Operate by Default
bodyText: South Dakota has no automatic-renewal statute for leases. No consumer-contract auto-renewal law reaches a lease, nothing requires bold-face terms or an affirmative opt-in, nothing conditions an auto-renewal clause on a separate reminder notice served in a window, and nothing limits how far before the end of a term you may require a tenant to decide about renewing. An auto-renewal clause is simply a lease term. What South Dakota supplies instead are two renewal presumptions that operate whether or not your lease says anything, and they are the ones to know because they can renew a tenancy you meant to end. If a tenant remains in possession after the hiring expires and you accept rent, the parties are presumed to have renewed the hiring on the same terms and for the same time, not exceeding one year - so a single accepted payment after a term ends can create another term. And a hiring of real property for a term the parties did not specify is deemed renewed at the end of the term implied by law unless one party gives notice of intention to terminate at least as long before expiry as the term of the hiring itself, not exceeding one month. Note that the first presumption works against a landlord who is careless about accepting money, and the second against one who is careless about notice. The cautious course is to decide before a term ends whether you want a renewal, give or get the notice in writing, and refuse or clearly characterise any payment you are not accepting as rent for a new term.

title: No Balcony or Deck Inspection Requirement
bodyText: South Dakota requires no periodic inspection of balconies, decks, stairs or other exterior elevated elements. There is no inspection interval, no qualified-inspector requirement, no reporting duty and no certification to file. States that have legislated here did so after structural collapses; South Dakota has not. The obligation that applies is the general one, and for this hazard it is the right frame anyway. You must keep the premises and all common areas in reasonable repair and fit for human habitation and in good and safe working order throughout the term, and you may not waive or modify that. A balcony is part of the premises and usually part of a common area, so its structural condition is squarely within the duty - and unlike a cosmetic defect, a failure here injures people, which puts it alongside your exposure to third parties that the habitability section expressly leaves unaltered. Construction standards come from the model codes the state adopts by reference rather than from an inspection statute: a municipality that adopts construction standards for a residential structure does so by adopting the 2024 International Residential Code, and where no local ordinance exists the 2024 International Building Code supplies the design standard for buildings commenced after July 1, 2026. Those govern how a balcony is built, not how often it is looked at. The cautious course is to inspect exterior elevated elements on a schedule you set yourself, in writing, paying attention to ledger connections, flashing and anything holding water, and to keep the records - the absence of a statutory interval means your own documented programme is what shows you acted reasonably.

title: No Pest Statute - Cooperation Has to Come From the Lease
bodyText: South Dakota has no bed bug or pest provision for residential rentals: no duty on a tenant to report an infestation, no duty to cooperate with treatment, no preparation obligations, no allocation of treatment cost, and no timetable for a landlord to respond. Everything here comes from your lease, and because treatment fails without tenant cooperation, a lease that says nothing about it leaves you paying for repeat visits you cannot compel anyone to prepare for. Three pieces of South Dakota law shape what the clause can do. Your own obligation is non-waivable: the premises must be kept fit for human habitation and in good and safe working order, so an infestation that is not the tenant's fault is yours to remedy whatever the lease says, and a term making the tenant responsible for all infestations regardless of cause does not work. Entry for inspection and treatment runs on the ordinary standard - reasonable notice, reasonable times, twenty-four hours' written notice presumed reasonable - but the statute lets the lease agree alternate methods or times, which is how a recurring treatment schedule becomes lawful rather than a series of separate notices. And cost recovery must be actual: where an infestation is the fault of the tenant, a household member or someone they let in, the tenant's statutory duty to preserve the premises and repair deterioration from their own conduct supports recovering the reasonable cost you actually pay, while a flat pest fee is a penalty and void. The cautious course is a cooperation clause requiring prompt written notice, access on the agreed schedule, compliance with the operator's written preparation instructions, and fault-based actual cost.

title: No Bed Bug Disclosure or Treatment Statute
bodyText: South Dakota has no bed bug statute at all. Nothing requires you to disclose a current or past infestation, nothing sets a treatment timeline, nothing allocates the cost of treatment between you and the tenant, and no administrative rule fills the gap. The subject is governed instead by the two general duties that run in opposite directions. You must keep a residential premises and its common areas in reasonable repair and fit for human habitation, and that duty cannot be waived or modified by the lease; a serious infestation in a multi-unit building is a condition you are obliged to address, and if you do not, the tenant may repair and deduct, or vacate and be discharged from further rent. The tenant in turn must preserve the premises and is answerable for deterioration caused by their own negligent, willful or malicious conduct. Because no statute allocates cost, allocation is whatever your lease says, limited by the non-waiver sentence in the habitability statute. The cautious course is a lease term that requires the tenant to report suspected bed bugs in writing promptly, gives you access to inspect and to treat, obliges the tenant to cooperate with preparation instructions, and charges the tenant the documented actual cost of treatment only where the infestation is traced to the tenant's conduct or to a failure to cooperate. Do not write a flat bed bug fee or a fixed charge for refusing preparation, because a separate statute voids contractual penalties for nonperformance. Disclose a known active infestation before signing even though no statute compels it: concealing it is exposure under the deceptive trade practices statute and in fraud.

title: Arbitration Clauses Are Enforceable - Keep Possession Out of Them
bodyText: Arbitration is the one route out of court that South Dakota expressly protects. A written agreement to submit an existing controversy to arbitration, or a provision in a written contract to arbitrate a controversy arising later, is valid, enforceable and irrevocable save on grounds that would revoke any contract. That matters because the general rule is the opposite: any provision restricting a party from enforcing rights by usual legal proceedings in ordinary tribunals, or limiting the time to do so, is void - and arbitration is carved out of that voiding rule rather than being an exception to a permissive regime. So a lease arbitration clause works in South Dakota, and a home-made pre-suit condition does not. Two limits are worth building in. South Dakota has no provision - unlike some states - telling you what must stay in court or preserving a tenant's right to counsel in an arbitration, so those protections are yours to include or omit, and a clause that reads as stripping them invites a challenge on ordinary contract grounds. More practically, keep possession out of the clause. Forcible entry and detainer is a summary statutory proceeding with a five-day appearance, a jury available on demand, and a continuance beyond fourteen days conditioned on the tenant giving security for accruing rent. Sending possession to arbitration trades all of that away for a slower private process, and you are the party who usually wants speed. The cautious course is to arbitrate money claims if you want arbitration at all, exclude possession expressly, and say which rules and who bears the fees. The library now offers an optional clause, `arbitration-agreement`, built on these limits: money claims only, with possession, small claims, security-deposit, injury and emergency claims kept in court, every remedy and the right to a lawyer kept, the arbitration fees above a court filing fee paid by you, a 30-day opt-out for the tenant, and separate initials from both of you.

title: No Carpet-Cleaning Statute - What You May Charge
bodyText: South Dakota has no statute about carpet cleaning. Nothing entitles you to require professional cleaning at move-out as a matter of law, and nothing limits carpet or paint deductions by a condition-and-age test the way some states do. The question is therefore governed entirely by the deposit statute and by South Dakota's rule against contractual penalties. From the deposit you may withhold only what is reasonably necessary to remedy rent defaults, to collect other funds due to you under an agreement, and to restore the premises to their condition at the start of the tenancy, with ordinary wear and tear excepted. Carpet that is merely worn from ordinary use is wear and tear and cannot be charged. Carpet that is soiled or damaged beyond that may be cleaned or replaced at the tenant's expense, at your documented actual cost. A lease term charging a flat professional-cleaning fee whatever the carpet's condition is the risk: a fixed sum payable regardless of actual damage reads as a penalty for nonperformance, and penalties of that kind are void. The cautious course is a conditional term - used only where the carpets were professionally cleaned immediately before the tenancy, charging the reasonable cost you actually pay - together with a signed move-in condition report, which is your evidence of the starting condition. Observe the deposit deadlines: return or a written statement of the specific reason for withholding within twenty-one days, and an itemized accounting within forty-five days if the tenant asks.

title: Casualty Termination Is Statutory - and Not Expressly Protected From Waiver
bodyText: South Dakota gives your tenant a statutory way out after a casualty and then, unusually, says nothing about whether your lease may take it away. The right is this: a tenant may terminate before the end of the term if the greater part of the premises, or the part that was and that you had reason to believe at the time of leasing was the material inducement to the tenant, is destroyed from any cause other than the tenant's ordinary negligence. The same section also lets the tenant terminate where you fail, within a reasonable time after written request, to put the premises in good condition or repair them. Note what the destruction limb turns on - not habitability, but whether the greater part or the material inducement is gone - so a fire destroying a detached garage the tenant rented the house for can trigger it. Now the waiver question. The habitability section carries an express sentence barring waiver or modification; this termination section carries none, and its words are permissive rather than mandatory. So a term allocating casualty risk, or requiring notice and an opportunity to rebuild before the tenant may terminate, meets no express prohibition. That is not the same as being safe. A clause stripping the termination right altogether would leave a tenant paying rent on premises that no longer exist, which is the kind of provision the general rule treats as contrary to the policy of express law, and the habitability duty behind it cannot be waived in any event. The cautious course is to shape the right rather than remove it: require prompt written notice, define rent abatement while the premises are unusable, and reserve a stated period to repair before termination bites.

title: No State Certificate of Occupancy or Rental Licence Disclosure
bodyText: South Dakota issues no state certificate of occupancy for residential rental property, licenses no landlords, registers no rental units, and therefore requires no disclosure about any of those things. There is no state statute making a lease void or rent uncollectable because the unit lacks an occupancy certificate, which is the mechanism several other states use. What South Dakota does instead is leave building regulation to cities and counties while dictating the code they must use. If your local government has adopted an ordinance prescribing standards for construction, alteration, use and occupancy, or demolition of a building other than a residential structure, that ordinance must comply with the 2024 edition of the International Building Code, and an ordinance prescribing standards for the maintenance of existing structures and premises must comply with the 2024 edition of the International Property Maintenance Code; the governing body may amend, modify or delete portions before enacting. A municipality may separately enact requirements for residential structures. So the occupancy certificate, the rental licence and the inspection that precedes them are real in South Dakota, but they are creatures of your city or county, and whether one exists where your property sits is a local question this answer does not resolve. The cautious course is to confirm with the local building or code office what permit, certificate or rental licence your property needs before you let it, hold the current one, and say in the lease that occupancy is subject to applicable local requirements. Do not warrant compliance in the lease in absolute terms. Letting a unit you know is barred from occupancy puts your delivery and quiet enjoyment duty at risk, and that remedy is heavy.

title: Familial Status Is Protected - and Defined Narrowly
bodyText: South Dakota protects families with children in housing, and the definition is worth knowing precisely because it is narrower than the phrase suggests. It is an unfair or discriminatory practice for an owner, or anyone acting for an owner, to refuse to rent or lease to a person, or to discriminate in the terms, conditions or privileges of a rental, because of familial status - alongside race, colour, creed, religion, sex, ancestry, disability and national origin. For this purpose a family is one or more individuals under the age of eighteen domiciled with a parent, legal custodian, or a person granted custody with the parent's or custodian's permission, and it includes a person who is pregnant or in the process of securing custody of someone under eighteen. The statute says expressly that familial-status discrimination applies to housing accommodations only. The exemptions are for genuine senior housing: residences publicized as specifically designated for older or disabled residents, where a state or federal programme has designated them for the elderly, or they are intended for and solely occupied by people sixty-two or older, or facilities and services are designed for the elderly and at least eighty percent of the units are occupied or intended for one or more people fifty-five or older. What South Dakota does not do is require your lease to address occupancy by children, or set a persons-per-bedroom standard. So an occupancy limit is yours to set, and the cautious course is to base it on the unit's size and any local code rather than on the number of children, and to apply it identically to every household.

title: No Cold-Weather Notice Before a Tenant Leaves
bodyText: South Dakota imposes no duty on a tenant to tell you before leaving the property empty in winter, and no duty on you to warn a tenant about freezing. The statutes that govern winter risk in a South Dakota rental are the ordinary ones. You must keep the premises in reasonable repair and fit for human habitation, and the tenant may repair and deduct, vacate and be discharged, or, after written notice, withhold rent into a separate account where the cost runs past a month's rent. The tenant for their part must preserve the premises, the appliances and the other leased property, and must repair deterioration caused by their own negligent, wilful or malicious conduct. Nothing in that scheme turns on the weather or on a notice before an absence. Because the duty does not exist in statute, the lease has to create it if you want it. The cautious course is a plain term requiring the tenant to keep the heat on at a stated minimum temperature through the heating season, to report any loss of heat at once, and to tell you before leaving the property unoccupied for more than a set number of consecutive days, with your right to enter and winterise at the tenant's cost if they do not. Set the consequence as the documented actual cost of the resulting damage or of your winterising, not as a fixed charge. South Dakota voids a contractual penalty for nonperformance, and voids agreed damages except where fixing the real loss would be impracticable, so a flat freeze-up fee is the one version of this clause likely to fail.

title: No Collection-Fee Statute - What You Can Actually Add to a Rent Debt
bodyText: South Dakota has no statute or regulation governing what may be added to a past-due rent debt. There is no rule requiring that a collection fee be expressly authorized by the lease before it can be charged, and no collection-agency provision barring an agency from adding its costs or unagreed attorney's fees unless a judgment awards them. The absence cuts both ways: nothing specifically permits a collection fee either, so the charge is governed by general contract law, which is unfriendly to it. A percentage or flat collection charge added because the tenant did not pay is a penalty imposed by contract for nonperformance and void. An agreed sum is enforceable only where actual damages would be impracticable or extremely difficult to fix - and if you pay an agency a stated percentage, your actual cost is precisely ascertainable, which is the opposite of that test. Attorney's fees deserve separate attention: a provision in a note, bond, mortgage or other evidence of debt providing for attorney's fees on default or foreclosure is against public policy and void except as authorized by specific statute, so a fee-shifting clause aimed at a rent default should not be relied on. What is left is real but narrower than most leases assume: unpaid rent itself, other sums the lease makes due as funds owed under the agreement, interest where the lease provides for it, and amounts a court awards. Practical consequence for the deposit: you may withhold for rent defaults and for other funds due under an agreement, so a collection fee that is void as a penalty is also not withholdable, and withholding it puts the whole deposit at risk, since failing to comply with the deposit section forfeits all rights to withhold any portion of it.

title: Common Areas Are Expressly Yours - Including the Lighting
bodyText: South Dakota puts common areas inside the habitability duty by name. You must keep the premises and all common areas in reasonable repair and fit for human habitation and in good and safe working order throughout the term, and you must maintain all electrical systems of the premises in good and safe working order and condition. Neither may be waived or modified. So lighting in a shared hallway, stairwell, entry or parking area is your responsibility as a matter of statute rather than of lease drafting, and a term making a tenant responsible for maintaining it does not work. There is no footcandle standard, no specific lighting requirement and no schedule in South Dakota law; the standard is the general one, and a dark stairwell is the obvious case where it is not met. On the question the topic asks - whether a lease may make a tenant pay for common-area lights wired to the tenant's own electric service - South Dakota has no provision permitting or forbidding it, so it is a matter for the lease, with one caveat worth taking seriously. Charging a tenant for electricity consumed in common areas is a charge for something outside what the tenant has rented, so it must be created by the lease to be collectible at all, and it should be stated plainly rather than buried. The cautious course is to put common-area lighting on your own meter. If a shared fixture is unavoidably on a tenant's service, disclose it in the lease, quantify it, and credit the tenant rather than leaving them to discover it from a bill.

title: No Government Approval Needed for a Private Lease
bodyText: No South Dakota statute makes a residential lease depend on a government officer's approval. There is no communal or native land tenure in state law, no approval or registration step before a lease is valid, no rule suspending rent or possession until an officer signs, and no approval requirement for a lease to a corporation such as employer-provided staff housing. Your lease is effective between you and the tenant on its own terms. Two things do bear on the question and should not be confused with it. Land held in trust for a tribe or allottee, and leasing on a reservation, are governed by federal and tribal law rather than by the statutes in this library, and a lease of trust land generally does require federal approval. That is outside the scope of these rows, and if the property is in Indian country you need advice directed at that, because state landlord-tenant law may not supply the rules at all. Separately, state school and public lands have their own leasing machinery administered by state officers, but that concerns the state as landlord, not a private lease of a dwelling. For the ordinary private tenancy the only formalities are the plain ones: a lease for longer than a year must be in writing and signed by the lessor, an agricultural lease cannot run beyond twenty years, and a municipal lot lease cannot run beyond ninety-nine years. The cautious course is to treat approval as a non-issue for private property and to get tribal-specific advice before letting anything in Indian country.

title: No Statutory Bar on Collecting Rent After a Vacate Order
bodyText: South Dakota has no provision barring a landlord from collecting rent after premises are condemned or a vacate order issues. There is no automatic abatement, no forfeiture of rent already paid, and no penalty for continuing to bill. That is not a licence to collect, because the rest of South Dakota's law makes the position untenable in practice. The habitability duty requires you to keep the premises fit for human habitation and in good and safe working order throughout the term, and it cannot be waived or modified - premises a public authority has ordered vacated are not that. Once you have had notice of conditions requiring repair and a reasonable time has passed, the tenant may vacate and is then discharged from additional charges of rent and from performing the other lease conditions, which ends the rent obligation without any statute about condemnation. The tenant may also terminate the lease outright where you fail within a reasonable time after written request to put the premises into good condition, or where the greater part of the premises is destroyed other than by the tenant's ordinary negligence. And demanding rent for a unit nobody may lawfully occupy is the kind of conduct the deceptive practices chapter reaches. The cautious course is to stop billing from the date of the order, refund any rent covering a period after it, help the tenant leave, and return the deposit on the statutory timetable - the twenty-one-day clock runs from termination and receipt of the tenant's address, and a condemnation does not pause it.

title: No Required Move-In Inventory - Why You Should Do One Anyway
bodyText: South Dakota requires no move-in inventory, no joint signed condition list, and no notice telling the tenant of a duty to sign or dissent from a damage list. Nothing obliges you to document condition at the start of the tenancy, and nothing penalizes a tenant who stays silent about it. That absence is the reason to do it anyway, because of where the burden lands at the end. From the deposit you may withhold only what is reasonably necessary to remedy rent defaults, to collect other funds due to you under an agreement, and to restore the premises to their condition at the commencement of the tenancy, with ordinary wear and tear excepted. Every one of those words is about a comparison - the condition now against the condition then - and with no statutory inventory, the only record of the starting condition is the one you made. Your deadlines are short and the penalty for getting a withholding wrong is total: return the deposit or furnish a written statement of the specific reason for withholding within twenty-one days, give an itemized accounting within forty-five days if the tenant asks, and a failure to comply forfeits all rights to withhold any portion of the deposit, with punitive damages on top for bad faith. The cautious course is a dated condition report signed by both of you at move-in, with photographs, and the same again at move-out. Give the tenant a copy. For a voucher tenancy, ask the housing agency what its own inspection and close-out rules require, because those are contractual and are not resolved here.

title: No Confessed-Judgment Ban in Terms - but the Clause Cannot Work
bodyText: South Dakota has no provision abolishing a confessed judgment or a cognovit clause in a residential lease, and no court rule doing it either. The one statute that mentions a confession of judgment is confined to door-to-door sales, where including one in the contract or receipt is a deceptive act or practice - it is not a lease provision and does not reach a tenancy. So the prohibition landlords expect is not there. It does not follow that such a clause is worth having, because two general rules leave it with nothing to do. A provision by which a tenant agrees in advance that judgment may be entered against them without suit restricts the tenant from enforcing their rights by usual legal proceedings in ordinary tribunals, and every provision of that kind is void. And possession in South Dakota is obtained through a statutory summary proceeding: the forcible entry and detainer grounds, a verified complaint, service, a five-day appearance, and a judgment that awards possession, rents and profits or damages, and costs. There is no mechanism by which a lease clause substitutes for that process, and no court will enter possession on your paperwork alone. The cautious course is to leave confession-of-judgment and cognovit language out of a South Dakota lease entirely. It gains you nothing enforceable, it is the kind of term that colours a judge's reading of the rest of your form, and the process it tries to shortcut is already among the fastest in the country.

title: Habitability: What South Dakota Does Not Have
bodyText: It is worth knowing the shape of South Dakota's habitability law, because most of what landlords expect from other states is missing and the little that exists is strong. What exists: a duty to keep the premises and all common areas in reasonable repair, fit for human habitation, and in good and safe working order throughout the term, including the electrical, plumbing and heating systems, excepting disrepair caused by the tenant's own negligent, willful or malicious conduct; a bar on waiving or modifying that duty; and three tenant remedies - repair and deduct, vacate and be discharged from further rent, or, where necessary repairs cost more than one month's rent, withhold rent into a separate account after written notice. What does not exist: no uniform residential landlord and tenant act, so no statutory list of prohibited lease provisions and no non-waivable-rights section; no itemized habitability code telling you what counts as fit, no minimum temperature, no required hot water temperature, no pest-control standard, no window-guard or balcony rule; no statutory notice-and-cure timetable before a tenant may act; no rent-escrow-through-the-court procedure; no materiality threshold defining which defects are serious enough to matter; and no inspection or certification regime for private rentals. The practical consequence is that the standard is general and a court applies it to your facts, so the written record of what you were told and when you responded is what decides a dispute. Local housing codes fill part of the gap and are not resolved here - a city ordinance on maintaining existing structures must follow the 2024 International Property Maintenance Code, so check your own city's.

title: A Short List of Things South Dakota Simply Does Not Regulate
bodyText: It helps to know where the law is silent, because silence is where a lease does its real work. South Dakota regulates residential tenancies lightly, and the following have no statute at all: house rules and their enforceability; a tenant's duties beyond three short provisions; pests, including bed bugs; rent payment method and receipts; late fees and their size; application fees and screening criteria; a tenant's right to organise, to display anything or to a religious or cultural object; home-based business; firearms in a lease; guest and occupancy limits; smoking, beyond the workplace ban; alternative housing or relocation after a casualty; disaster and emergency tenancy rules; seasonal tenancies; double-letting; energy data; translation and type size; a state rights guide; stigma disclosure; and community associations. In each of those areas your lease is not merely permitted to set the rule - it is the only thing that does, and a gap in the lease is a gap with no statutory filler behind it. Two cautions go with that freedom. The handful of provisions that do constrain terms apply across all of it: the habitability duty cannot be waived except by specified repairs in lieu of rent, a contractual penalty is void, a term restricting enforcement or shortening a limitation period is void, and the deposit cap captures any money securing performance however it is labelled. And the protected-class list, the retaliation provision and the right to call for emergency help limit how a rule may be applied even where no statute governs its subject. The cautious course is to draft fully and to assume no default will rescue an omission.

title: Three Absences Outside the Lease Chapter
bodyText: Three things landlords expect to find outside the lease chapter are not in South Dakota law at all, and each absence changes how you should operate. First, there is no squatter or unauthorised-occupant remedy. Someone occupying without any tenancy is dealt with as criminal trespass, which is a police matter and gives you no civil summary route of its own; your civil route is the ordinary eviction action, which means the person has to be brought within its grounds. The practical consequence is that you should never let an occupancy drift into ambiguity, because an occupant with any colour of permission is a tenant to be evicted rather than a trespasser to be removed. Second, there is no duty to give a receipt for rent, in cash or otherwise, and no record-keeping requirement attached to rent collection. Nothing stops you taking cash, but nothing protects you either, and in a nonpayment case the proof is yours to produce - so issue receipts as a matter of practice and keep a ledger, because the statute will not supply one. Third, there is no landlord or rental registration, licensing or inspection scheme, and so no landlord-tenant provision making registration a precondition to a possession judgment. But two general business statutes can stop you bringing the case. If you rent under a name that does not plainly show the true surname of each person interested in the business, you may not maintain any legal action in that name, or recover anything due from the business, until you file a fictitious name statement (SDCL 37-11-1 and 37-11-5). And an out-of-state limited liability company that owns income-producing property here may not maintain an action until it has a certificate of authority, and an out-of-state corporation transacting business here faces the same bar (SDCL 47-34A-1003, 47-34A-1008 and 47-1A-1502; see `edu-no-nonresident-owner-agent-rule-sd`). Neither failure voids the lease, and once you file you can sue. The cautious course is to document occupancy status and rent payment yourself, since in each of these three areas the law leaves the record entirely to you.

title: Liens for Work a Tenant Orders - Repairs Cannot Touch You, Improvements Can
bodyText: South Dakota draws a line that most states do not, and it is worth knowing exactly where it falls. The mechanics' and materialmen's lien chapter starts by deeming everyone with an interest in land to have authorised improvements made on it, which would expose your title to a contractor your tenant hired. Attached to that rule is a proviso that rescues you for one category of work: as against a lessor, no lien is given for repairs made by or at the instance of the lessee. So for repairs your tenant orders, you are protected by statute and need do nothing. Improvements that are not repairs are the exposure. There you are deemed to have authorised the work, and the way out is a specific instrument on a short clock: a person who has not authorised the improvement may protect their interest by serving written notice on the people doing the work that the improvement is not being made at that person's instance, within five days after learning of it, or by posting the same notice conspicuously on the premises and keeping it posted. Five days from knowledge is the whole window, so this is an operational matter rather than a drafting one. The lien itself is a first lien ahead of everything except government liens and encumbrances already of record or known to the claimant, so it is not a nuisance claim. The cautious course is to require written consent for any alteration, say in the consent that it is not an agreement to pay, require the tenant to notify every contractor in writing that the tenant is responsible, and the moment you learn of unauthorised work, serve or post the nonliability notice and diary the five days.

title: The Deceptive Practices Act and Whether It Reaches a Tenancy
bodyText: South Dakota's consumer statute is its Deceptive Trade Practices and Consumer Protection chapter, and it is worth understanding precisely because so much of South Dakota's landlord-tenant law is absent - it is often the only general restraint on how you deal with a tenant. Its core prohibition is broad: it is a deceptive act or practice knowingly to use any deceptive act or practice, fraud, false pretense, false promise or misrepresentation, or to conceal, suppress or omit any material fact, in connection with the sale or advertisement of any merchandise, whether or not anyone was in fact misled or damaged. Note that last phrase - no proof of actual deception is needed. Whether it reaches a residential tenancy is a question the text leaves open rather than answers. The definitions point toward coverage: goods or services means goods or services purchased, leased or rented, and merchandise is defined to include an object, wares, goods, a commodity, an intangible, instruction or a service. A lease is a rental, and a leasehold is an intangible, so the Act is plainly capable of applying. But its operative language speaks of a sale or advertisement of merchandise and much of the chapter is built around consumer sales, and no South Dakota decision applying it to a residential lease was found. The cautious course is to assume it applies. Treat your advertising, your condition representations, your fee descriptions and your deposit accounting as if a consumer statute governs them - which costs nothing if it does not and is a complete answer if it does.

title: The Only Change-of-Use Notice Is the Mobile-Home One
bodyText: South Dakota has exactly one conversion notice, and it is not the condominium kind. If you lease land to the owner of a mobile or manufactured home and the property is to be developed for an alternate use, you must give no less than ninety days' notice to vacate and remove the home from the land. That ninety days does not apply where the notice rests on a breach of the lease, so a change-of-use notice and a breach notice are different instruments and should not be mixed in one letter. Everything else in this family is absent. There is no condominium-conversion notice to sitting tenants, no tenant right of first refusal on a conversion, no extended notice or relocation payment for a converted building, and no statute forbidding the conversion of rental housing to hotel or other transient use or its demolition for that purpose. The condominium chapter is a developer-registration and purchaser-protection act about notices of intent to sell, inspections, public reports and escrowed deposits; it creates no tenant rights. There is also no statutory first clause, no required capitalised conversion statement, and no prescribed form of any kind, so nothing has to come first in your lease. Outside the mobile-home situation you end a tenancy to convert the same way you end it for any other reason, on the ordinary notice for its type. The cautious course where you own a mobile-home community is to calendar the ninety days from the date the notice is served rather than from a board decision, and to say in the notice that it is given because the property is being developed for an alternate use.

title: No Implied Crime-Free Term - Your Lease Has to Create It
bodyText: South Dakota implies no no-criminal-activity term into a residential lease, gives you no expedited eviction for drug or violent crime, and imposes no duty to evict. Your lease has to create the obligation - but once it does, the eviction statute carries it further than landlords usually expect. Seven grounds support a forcible entry and detainer action, and the last of them is a lessee who commits waste upon the leased premises, or does or fails to perform any act which, under the terms of the lease, operates to terminate it. So a crime-free covenant drafted so that a breach terminates the lease is itself a filing ground: you are not confined to terminating first and then suing as for a holdover, though that route remains available and is the safer one where the breach is arguable. A separate statute also lets you end a lease before the term ends where the tenant uses the property contrary to the lease agreement. One South Dakota provision turns this from prudent into necessary. Knowingly permitting a place you own, manage, supervise or control to be regularly used for prostitution, or failing to make reasonable effort to abate that use by ejecting the tenant, notifying law enforcement or using other legally available means, is a felony. Without a lease term letting you eject, you have no ready means to abate. Keep the victim carve-out: a tenant who is the victim of domestic abuse, unlawful sexual behaviour or stalking has a statutory right to terminate without penalty, and penalising a tenant for being a victim or for calling for help invites a claim rather than a judgment.

title: No Defective Drywall Disclosure Duty
bodyText: South Dakota never legislated on defective or corrosive imported drywall. The word does not appear in the Code at all, so there is no disclosure duty, no remediation standard, no notice form and no limitation period peculiar to it. The states that did legislate were mostly those hit hardest by the imported wallboard installed during the mid-2000s building boom, and South Dakota was not among them. Nor does the subject reach you indirectly: the state's one mandated residential property-condition disclosure statement runs on a sale rather than a letting, and its hazardous-conditions list does not name drywall even there. What governs instead is the general habitability duty. You must keep a residential premises and its common areas in reasonable repair and fit for human habitation, and that duty cannot be waived or modified by the lease. Corroding copper, failing air conditioning coils, a sulphur odour and blackened wiring are conditions you would have to address under that duty whatever their cause, and the tenant's remedies are to repair and deduct, to vacate and be discharged, or, after written notice, to withhold rent into a separate account where the repair exceeds one month's rent. The cautious course is to treat defective drywall as an ordinary latent defect rather than a special category: if you actually know the building contains suspect wallboard or has had a corrosion problem, disclose it in writing before signing and keep the signed acknowledgement, because concealing a material fact is exposure under the deceptive trade practices statute and in fraud even where no disclosure statute exists. Do not take a waiver of the habitability duty in exchange for the disclosure; that waiver is void.

title: No Authority for a Deposit Cost Schedule
bodyText: South Dakota's deposit statute sets no schedule of charges and authorizes none. It tells you what you may withhold and says nothing about fixing a price in advance: only the amounts reasonably necessary to remedy the tenant's default in rent, to collect other funds due to you under an agreement, and to restore the premises to their condition at the start of the tenancy, with ordinary wear and tear excepted. There is no provision letting the lease pre-set carpet-cleaning charges, no list of chargeable items, and no prescribed tenant notice that would make such a list enforceable. The states that allow a cost schedule do it by express authority. South Dakota gives none, so a schedule in your lease stands or falls on general contract law, and there it is in trouble. A fixed sum payable on a breach regardless of what the breach actually cost you is a penalty for nonperformance, and South Dakota voids those outright. An agreed-damages figure survives only where actual damage would be impracticable or extremely difficult to fix, which is rarely true of cleaning and repair work you can invoice. The cautious course is to charge documented actual cost rather than a schedule price. Keep the invoices, photograph the unit at move-in and move-out, and have the tenant sign a move-in condition report, because the statute measures your deduction against the condition at commencement and that report is your evidence of it. If you want certainty about a recurring item, price it into the rent instead of into a damages table. Then meet the deadlines: return or a written statement of the specific reason for withholding within twenty-one days, and an itemized accounting within forty-five days on request.

title: No Deposit Installment Right - and How to Offer One Safely
bodyText: South Dakota caps a residential security deposit at one month's rent and says nothing at all about when the tenant pays it, so the timing is yours to set. No statute gives a tenant the right to pay a deposit in instalments, no statute requires you to offer that option, and there is no unit-count threshold, no income test and no notice duty attached to the question. If you want the whole deposit before the keys change hands, you may require it. If you want to spread it, you may do that too, and nothing limits how many payments you divide it into. Two cautions matter if you spread it. First, the cap is on what you demand or receive in total, not on each payment, so an instalment plan that adds up to more than one month's rent breaks the cap unless special conditions genuinely pose a danger to maintenance of the premises and the larger amount is agreed. Watch the aggregate when you are also holding money called last month's rent. Second, do not write a forfeiture or penalty term for a missed instalment. A fixed sum payable because the tenant fell behind is a penalty for nonperformance, and South Dakota voids those. The cautious course is to state the full deposit amount, each instalment and its due date, and that any unpaid balance is a debt due to you under the lease, which is a category the deposit statute already recognizes when you come to account for the money. Treat a missed instalment as the breach of the lease it is, and pursue the balance as a debt rather than through a clause that prices the default in advance.

title: The Tenant's Address Starts the Clock, Not Your Notice
bodyText: In South Dakota the deposit clock does not start on the day the keys come back. It starts when the tenancy terminates and you receive the tenant's mailing address or delivery instructions, and it needs both. So it is the tenant's own notice to you, not any notice from you to the tenant, that sets the deadline running. Nothing obliges you to tell the tenant that. There is no required surrender notice, no duty to offer a pre-move-out inspection, no duty to notify the tenant of a right to be present when you inspect, and no statutory form for surrender at all. That cuts both ways. A tenant who never gives you an address has not started your clock, but you should not build a strategy on it, because the price of getting the timing wrong is losing every right to withhold any part of the deposit, and the record of what you did and when is what decides the argument. The cautious course is to ask for the address yourself. Put the request in the lease and again in your move-out paperwork, ask in writing for a mailing address or delivery instructions, date the request, and record the date the answer arrives, because that date is the one the statute keys to. If nothing comes, send the refund or the written statement of your specific reasons to the last address you hold and keep proof of sending. Do a documented walkthrough with photographs even though no statute requires one, and compare it against a signed move-in condition report. One restriction to respect: where a tenant terminating after domestic abuse, unlawful sexual behavior or stalking gives you a forwarding address, you may not pass it to anyone without the tenant's consent or a legal requirement.

title: No Required Designated Repairer or Posted Contact
bodyText: South Dakota does not require you to name a person responsible for repairs, to post or disclose a maintenance contact, or to designate an agent to receive repair notices. Nothing has to appear in the lease and nothing has to be posted at the building. Lodging establishments operate under their own licensing rules, but an ordinary residential rental has no such requirement. What the law does instead is point the tenant's notice at you. The repair duty sits on the lessor, and the tenant's remedies open up only after notice to the lessor of conditions requiring repair and the passage of a reasonable time without the repair being made. So the question that matters is not who you designate but who counts as having received the notice, and when the clock started. A tenant who tells a handyman, leaves a voicemail on a disconnected number, or mentions it to a neighbor has an argument that notice was given; you have an argument it was not; and the reasonable time runs from a date a court will have to find. The cautious course is to name a single contact for repair notices in the lease, with an address, a phone number and an email, and to require that notices go there in writing. That is not compliance with a statute - there is none - it is how you control when the clock starts and keep the evidence of what you did about it. Keep a dated log of every report and your response.

title: No Protection for Housing Someone After a Disaster
bodyText: South Dakota has nothing allowing a tenant to take in someone displaced by a disaster, and nothing protecting a tenant who does from a guest-limit or unauthorized-occupant clause. There is no temporary-occupancy right, no notice mechanism, no time limit after which the arrangement must end, and no provision suspending your occupancy rules during a declared emergency. The lease governs entirely. That cuts both ways, and the exposure is worth thinking about before a flood or a winter storm rather than during one. If your lease treats any guest staying beyond a stated period as an unauthorized occupant and a breach, then a tenant sheltering a displaced relative is in breach on its face, and enforcing it in those circumstances is both unattractive and, if you terminate, an invitation to a dispute about whether the breach was material. If your lease says nothing, you have no clear basis to object to an indefinite extra occupant. Nothing in South Dakota law resolves that for you. The cautious course is to write the flexibility in: a stated guest allowance, a written-consent route for a longer stay that you commit to considering promptly, and an express short-term exception for displacement by fire, flood or storm, with the tenant remaining responsible for the person's conduct and for any damage. Keep the consent and the dates in writing. If you later need to end the tenancy, do it on the statutory notice rather than treating the extra occupant as a ground you have not actually reserved.

title: No Disaster Provisions - the Tenancy Does Not End by Itself
bodyText: South Dakota has no landlord-tenant disaster provisions. A declared natural disaster does not end a tenancy, does not suspend rent, does not stay an eviction, does not create a duty to rehouse and does not trigger any notice. There is no emergency rent provision and no price-gouging cap on dwelling rents during or after a declaration. The disaster machinery in South Dakota's statutes is governmental - emergency services, county budgets, leave for Red Cross service, provisions for officials displaced by a disaster - and none of it reaches a lease. So the tenancy continues and rent remains due unless something in the lease chapter operates, which is where the analysis actually happens. Two provisions do the work. If the premises become unfit and you do not repair within a reasonable time after notice, the tenant may repair and deduct, or vacate and be discharged from additional rent and the other lease conditions. And the tenant may terminate outright where the greater part of the premises, or the part you had reason to believe was the material inducement, is destroyed other than by the tenant's ordinary negligence. Both are tenant elections: neither happens automatically, and until the tenant acts the tenancy stands. For a unit that is intact but inaccessible - a road closed, a utility out area-wide - South Dakota gives no answer at all, and the lease is the only place one can come from. The cautious course is a casualty clause stating what happens on destruction, on partial damage and on inaccessibility, with rent abatement defined and a repair period before termination bites.

title: No Double-Letting Prohibition or Remedy
bodyText: South Dakota has no provision prohibiting the letting of the same premises to two tenants at once, and no rent-abatement remedy for a tenant who finds the unit already occupied. Nothing addresses double-letting as such. What South Dakota supplies instead is an obligation that makes the question answerable without a special rule, and it is one of the oldest in the chapter: the lessor shall deliver the leased premises to the lessee and secure the lessee's quiet enjoyment against all lawful claimants. A landlord who has let the same premises twice cannot deliver to the second tenant and cannot secure quiet enjoyment, so that is a straightforward breach - and a tenant whose lease you cannot perform has the ordinary contract remedies, with the deposit and any advance rent recoverable. The tenant may also terminate a lease before the end of the term where the landlord does not, within a reasonable time after written request, fulfil obligations as to placing and securing the tenant in quiet possession of the premises. Note what South Dakota does not give: no statutory damages multiple, no abatement formula and no penalty, so the exposure is the tenant's actual loss plus whatever a court makes of the circumstances. The practical risk is administrative rather than legal, and it arises most often with overlapping move-out and move-in dates or an application taken after a lease is signed. The cautious course is a single authoritative record of which unit is committed to whom from which date, a rule that no second lease is signed until the first is terminated in writing, and a realistic turnover gap.

title: No Statutory Drug-Free Addendum - and None Authorised
bodyText: South Dakota has no drug-free housing addendum, no model text for one, and no statute authorising or requiring one. Nothing gives such an addendum special status, and nothing makes a violation of it an expedited eviction ground. The drug-free provisions South Dakota does have are a criminal sentencing feature - drug-free zones treated as a separate count in an indictment - and a workplace provision in the medical cannabis chapter permitting an employer's drug-free policy. Neither reaches a tenancy. So a drug-free addendum in South Dakota is simply a lease term, and it stands or falls on the same footing as any other covenant: a breach reaches eviction through the ground covering a lessee who does or fails to perform any act which, under the terms of the lease, operates to terminate it, or through a termination for use contrary to the lease agreement. Two drafting points specific to South Dakota. Medical cannabis complicates a blanket drug prohibition: a cardholder may not be refused a lease or otherwise penalised solely for cardholder status, though you may impose reasonable restrictions on the medical use of cannabis and need not allow cultivation on the rental property - so an addendum that treats lawful cardholder use as a default is a real risk, while one restricting smoking and cultivation is not. And keep the victim carve-out: a victim of domestic abuse, unlawful sexual behaviour or stalking has a statutory right to terminate without penalty, and penalising a tenant for conduct done to them is a poor case. The cautious course is one crime-free covenant with a medical-cannabis carve-out rather than a separate addendum.

title: After a Domestic-Abuse Termination the Deposit Clock Is the Ordinary One
bodyText: South Dakota gives a tenant who is a victim of domestic abuse, unlawful sexual behavior or stalking the right to end the lease early on written notice with supporting documentation, but it attaches no special deposit timetable to that termination. The ordinary clock applies: twenty-one days from the termination of the tenancy and your receipt of the tenant's mailing address or delivery instructions, with an itemized accounting within forty-five days if the tenant asks. Nothing waits for other occupants to deliver possession, nothing extends the period because the termination was mid-term, and nothing shortens it either. What does change is the arithmetic. A tenant who terminates this way owes no early-termination fee and no rent for the month following the month in which they vacate, so neither may be deducted from the deposit. Withholding for a charge the tenant does not owe is withholding for funds that are not due, and the penalty for getting the return wrong is losing every right to withhold any part of the deposit. The confidentiality duty also bites: if the tenant gives you a forwarding address or other contact information with the termination, you may not disclose it to anyone without the tenant's consent or a legal requirement, and that includes a remaining co-tenant, a new occupant and a collection agent. Where other tenants stay on under the same lease it is genuinely unsettled whether the tenancy has terminated for deposit purposes, so the cautious course is to settle with the departing tenant on the ordinary twenty-one-day clock anyway. There is no penalty for refunding early and a severe one for being late. Finally, you may not treat the call for help itself as a lease breach.

title: No DV Eviction Shield in State Law - Where the Protection Comes From Instead
bodyText: South Dakota has no statute barring the eviction of a domestic-violence victim, no provision stopping the acts of an abuser being counted against a victim tenant, and no rule exempting a victim from a nuisance or crime-free termination. The protection a victim has in South Dakota runs the other way: rather than a shield against being evicted, the statute gives the victim a way out. A tenant, or a tenant whose household member is the victim of alleged domestic abuse, unlawful sexual behavior or stalking, may terminate the lease and vacate without any early-termination penalty, on written notice that the termination is due to fear of imminent danger or injury, with a police report, a protection order, or a licensed health care provider's documentation from the preceding thirty days attached; the tenant is then not liable for an early-termination fee or for the rent for the month after the one in which the tenant vacates. For you that is useful to know in both directions - it is the route a victim will usually take, and it limits what you can collect when they do. Because there is no statutory shield, the restraint on a victim-related eviction comes from general law and from good practice. A termination aimed at a tenant because of what was done to them, rather than a breach of the lease, is a poor case to put before a judge, and federal law bars it outright in covered subsidized housing. Keep the victim carve-out in your crime-free clause, act against the person responsible rather than the household, and ask for the protection order when you need an occupant excluded.

title: No Statutory Lock-Change Right - and Why You Must Not Improvise One
bodyText: South Dakota gives a domestic-violence victim no statutory right to demand a lock change, voids no lease term to the contrary, and attaches no private action with statutory damages. The protection-order statute is the mechanism instead, and it belongs to the court: on notice and a hearing, if the court finds by a preponderance of the evidence that domestic abuse has taken place, it may exclude the abusing party from the dwelling the parties share or from the petitioner's residence, and may order other relief it deems necessary for protection, including directives to a sheriff. An order may not affect title to real estate, and a victim who leaves the home to avoid abuse does not lose the right to apply. What this means in practice is that the paper you should be asking for is the order, not the police report. Where a protection order excludes one occupant, changing the locks implements a court directive. Where there is no order and both adults are tenants, changing the locks to keep one of them out is you excluding a tenant from the premises, and South Dakota's exposure for that is severe: damages equal to two months' rent plus the return of all advance rent and deposit, and separately a measure of three times the compensatory sum for forcibly excluding a person from possession. A victim's request does not change who your tenants are. The workable policy is to change locks promptly on request at the tenant's cost, give keys only to tenants not excluded by an order, and ask for the order before removing anyone's access. Note the separate right that does exist: a victim of domestic abuse, unlawful sexual behavior or stalking may terminate the lease early without penalty on the statutory notice.

title: Protection Orders: The Chapter Has Not Moved, But There Is More Than One
bodyText:
South Dakota's domestic-abuse protection-order law sits where it has long sat, in a single chapter of the domestic-relations title, and it has not been renumbered, relocated or recodified. The chapter runs unbroken from its definitions through its arrest, bail and record-keeping provisions, and the traffic in section numbers has gone the other way: four sections were moved into it from the criminal-procedure title, and the Legislature was still adding new sections to it in the 2026 session, citing the chapter's existing petition and hearing sections by their existing numbers. If you hold a form, an addendum or a policy that cites that chapter, the citation is still good. Nothing in the Code records any section being transferred out of it.

The trap is not the number, it is the count. South Dakota issues civil protection orders under three separate chapters: one for domestic abuse, a second for stalking inside the criminal title, and a third for vulnerable adults. The early-termination right a victim tenant has against you accepts a protection order without naming any chapter. What it does require is that the order was issued in response to an alleged incident of domestic abuse, unlawful sexual behavior or stalking, and that it issued in the thirty days before the tenant's notice.

The cautious course is to read the order for what it responds to rather than for which chapter produced it. Accept a stalking order on the same footing as a domestic-abuse order. Do not reject a document because the heading is unfamiliar, and do not accept a vulnerable-adult order granted on a financial-exploitation finding, because that is not one of the three triggers.

title: The Three Documents a Domestic-Abuse Termination Must Carry - and What You May Not Add
bodyText:
South Dakota fixes by statute exactly what a victim tenant must attach to a notice ending the lease early, and the list is closed: a police report on an alleged incident, signed in the thirty days before the notice; a protection order issued in that same window in response to such an incident; or documentation signed by a licensed health care provider confirming an examination of the tenant or a household member in that window, within the provider's scope of practice, leaving the provider with reasonable cause to believe the person was a victim. The notice itself must separately say that the termination is because of fear of imminent danger or injury.

Read the window carefully, because it runs backwards from the date of the notice, not from the incident. An old assault can support a fresh termination if the paper is fresh: the report must be signed, the order issued, and the examination performed inside those thirty days. The statute attaches nothing else. You get no right to verify the document with its author, to demand a case number or a certified copy, to require your own form, to insist the order be final rather than temporary, or to require that the paper use a particular label. One of the three triggering terms appears nowhere else in the whole Code and is nowhere defined, so insisting on a document that recites it would be inventing a condition the law does not impose.

The cautious course is to accept any document that satisfies the statute on its face, date-stamp receipt, hold it apart from the ordinary tenant file, and release nothing about the tenant's whereabouts to anyone.

title: Reselling Electricity to Tenants - No Disclosure Rule, One Hard Cap
bodyText: South Dakota requires no electric submetering disclosure in a lease. There is no statute on submetering electricity, no disclosure form, no unit threshold, and no equivalent of the rules some states impose on a landlord who measures and bills electricity unit by unit. The question most landlords actually need answered is a different one: does reselling electricity to your tenants make you a regulated utility? In South Dakota that question is not answered by a definition carving landlords in or out, the way it is in some states. It is answered practically, by a penal cap that applies to any person. Knowingly charging a consumer of gas or electricity an amount greater than the utility actually billed is a civil fine of up to five hundred dollars, and electric vehicle charging is expressly excepted. Falsifying a meter reading is separately a misdemeanour. So you may recover what you were billed, and you may not profit on the resale; cost recovery rather than sale is the posture the statute leaves open to you. The cautious course is to bill only at documented actual cost, keep the utility's own bill for every period you charge, read submeters on a stated schedule and show the reading on the tenant's statement, and put the whole arrangement in a signed utility page of the lease even though nothing compels it. Do not add a service or administrative fee to the pass-through, and do not charge a flat late fee on it. The Public Utilities Commission's gas and electric rules (ARSD 20:10:15 to 20:10:20) add no submetering or resale rule for landlords. Its master-metering rules do limit how a building is metered. A regulated gas or electric utility must meter each unit separately in a multi-unit building begun after June 13, 1980 (ARSD 20:10:26:03). Exceptions include a two-unit owner-occupied building, an older master-metered building not substantially remodeled since June 13, 1980, and central heating, cooling or water heating (ARSD 20:10:26:04). Otherwise the owner needs a Commission variance.

title: No Emergency-Contact Rule, in Either Direction
bodyText:
South Dakota imposes no emergency-contact obligation on either side of a residential tenancy. No statute makes you collect a tenant's emergency contact or next of kin, none tells you when or to whom you may pass that information on, none requires you to post or give the tenant a twenty-four-hour number for emergency repairs, and none requires you to identify yourself or a managing agent in the lease at all. The word emergency appears in the leasing law only twice, and in neither place does it create a contact duty: it excuses you from the usual notice before entering, and it protects a tenant who calls emergency responders from a lease term purporting to authorise eviction for doing so.

That absence cuts both ways, and the second direction is the one landlords miss. Because nothing in state law authorises the disclosure of tenant contact information, you have no statutory cover when you hand it to anybody. One narrow rule runs the other way: where a tenant ends the lease under the domestic-abuse provision and gives you a forwarding address, you may not pass it on without the tenant's consent unless the law requires it.

The cautious course is to collect the emergency contact on the rental application rather than in the lease, say plainly on the form what you will use it for and that you will use it only for that, and get the tenant's signature on it. Keep the entry you make in your own records current by asking at renewal. Do not promise in the lease to call the contact, and do not attach a fee or a penalty to a tenant who declines to give one, because a contractual penalty for nonperformance is void in South Dakota.

title: When the Property Is Taken by Eminent Domain
bodyText: South Dakota has a full condemnation chapter but it says nothing about your lease. No statute ends a residential tenancy on a taking, none abates or reduces the rent, none apportions rent to the surrender date, and none lets the court cancel the lease as a handful of other states do. The chapter is about compensating interests in land: interpleader where claimants to the compensation disagree, compensation determined parcel by parcel, the vesting of title and the right to compensation, and the terms on which possession is surrendered after notice and a hearing. What happens between you and your tenant is left to the lease. That has a practical edge. Because the award is determined for the parcel rather than estate by estate, the division of it between you and your tenant is a question your lease should answer in advance, or you will be arguing about it inside the condemnation case. And because nothing abates the rent, a tenant who has lost the use of part of the property has no statutory reduction to point to; the obligation runs on unless your lease says otherwise. The cautious course is a condemnation term: end the lease when the whole, or so much that the rest cannot reasonably be lived in, is taken; prorate the rent to the date possession is given up and refund the rest; reduce the rent proportionately for a partial taking the tenant can live through; and assign the award, including the value of the leasehold, to yourself while expressly preserving any relocation or moving payment made to the tenant. Keep that carve-out even though no general relocation statute applies, because the highway and urban-renewal schemes and federal law each pay displaced occupants directly. Return the deposit under the deposit statute when the lease ends this way.

title: No Screening Rule for Your Staff - But Your Managers May Need a Licence
bodyText:
South Dakota requires no background check, criminal-history search, fingerprinting or registry check on the people you employ to manage, maintain or let residential property. The Code carries dozens of mandatory screening provisions and every one of them attaches to public employment or to a licensed occupation, not to a private landlord's staff. There is no work card, no registration, no clearance and no bar on hiring a person with a record.

What does attach to your staff is licensing. South Dakota defines both a property manager and a residential rental agent in its real estate licensing chapter and licenses them, with an exemption for operators of state and federally assisted housing units, and the licensing authority can run a criminal background check on an applicant or on a licensee it is investigating. Your own regular employees are exempt when the work is part of managing property you own or lease, and so is a custodian or employee who shows units and takes applications. So the real question for a new hire is not whether you must screen them but whether what you are asking them to do requires a licence they do not hold, which is your exposure as the employer, not theirs.

South Dakota's employment discrimination law also constrains how you screen. It covers the housing law's protected grounds except familial status and reaches application, hiring and training, and it expressly permits an employer to act on a professionally developed ability test only where the test is not designed, intended or used to discriminate.

The cautious course is to screen anyone who will hold keys or enter occupied units, because you have no statutory shield either way and a negligent-hiring claim is the live risk, to apply the same criteria to every candidate for the same role and write them down, and to confirm before hiring that a manager or letting agent holds the licence the work requires.

title: No Energy-Data Statute - Consent Has to Come From the Utility’s Own Form
bodyText: South Dakota has no energy-data provision of any kind. Nothing authorises a lease clause consenting to the release of a tenant's usage data, nothing requires a utility to honour one, nothing obliges you to benchmark a building, and nothing forbids you asking. If you want consumption history for a tenant-metered unit - for benchmarking, an energy audit, a rebate application or allocating a bill - the lease alone will not get it, because a utility is not a party to your lease and owes it nothing. The practical route is therefore to use the lease to create an obligation you can enforce against the tenant rather than a consent you cannot enforce against the utility: a covenant that the tenant will sign whatever release, authorisation or online consent the utility itself requires, within a stated number of days of your written request. That converts the problem into an ordinary lease obligation. Two limits are worth building in. Make withdrawal of the authorisation expressly non-breaching, so the term is not a penalty, and keep your own promises about use and disclosure narrow and explicit, since no statute supplies them here. The Public Utilities Commission's gas and electric rules (ARSD 20:10:15 to 20:10:20) say nothing about releasing customer usage data either, so each utility's own policy governs. The cautious course is to ask the utility what form it accepts before relying on any lease wording.

title: No Located Bar on a Non-Attorney Appearing for an Entity
bodyText: South Dakota has no statute barring a non-attorney from appearing in court for a corporate or other entity landlord, and no court rule imposing that bar was located in the procedural chapters held for this pass. So the question of whether a manager or officer may file and conduct an eviction for an LLC is not answered by a provision this research could point to, and you should not assume either answer. Two things are worth knowing while that stands open. Unauthorised practice of law is regulated in South Dakota outside the rules of civil procedure, and the restriction on representing another in court usually comes from that direction rather than from the eviction statute - so the absence of a bar in the eviction chapter is not permission. And the statute gives you a concrete financial reason to instruct a lawyer in any event: in a forcible entry and detainer case the court may tax reasonable attorney fees as part of the costs to the prevailing party, whether or not a trial is had, but only if the prevailing party is represented by a licensed attorney. An entity that appears through its own manager cannot recover fees under that provision even if it wins, and the fee-shifting is mutual, so a represented tenant who prevails can recover against you. The cautious course is to instruct a licensed attorney for an entity-owned property's eviction: it resolves the representation question, preserves the fee recovery the statute offers, and in a proceeding with a five-day appearance there is little time to discover you were not entitled to appear.

title: A Casualty Lets the Tenant Out, Not You
bodyText: South Dakota gives the tenant a casualty exit and gives you none. If the greater part of the leased premises is destroyed, or the part that was the material inducement to the lease and that you had reason to know was, is destroyed by any cause other than the tenant's ordinary negligence, the tenant may end the lease before the term runs out. There is no matching landlord right. Your statutory grounds for ending a lease early are use of the premises contrary to the lease agreement and failure to repair after request, and neither reaches a tornado, a flood, a wildfire or a declared emergency. Nothing in South Dakota law lets you terminate because the building is damaged, because a disaster has been declared, or because the property has become uneconomic to repair. A lease ends by expiry of its term, by mutual consent, or by the tenant acquiring better title, so without a lease term you are left holding a tenancy you cannot end and a building you may not want to rebuild. That makes this one of the clauses worth writing. The cautious course is an opt-in landlord termination right keyed to objective facts rather than to your judgment: damage that makes the premises unfit or untenantable, or that your contractor certifies will take more than a stated number of days to repair, with the lease ending on written notice and rent prorated to the date of the damage. Keep the tenant's own statutory exit expressly intact, and do not attach a fee or forfeiture to a casualty, because South Dakota voids contractual penalties for nonperformance.

title: No Rule on What Happens to a Charger at Move-Out
bodyText: South Dakota has no provision about an electric-vehicle charger at the end of a tenancy. Nothing says who owns an installed charger, nothing requires you to let a tenant remove one, nothing requires the tenant to restore the space, and nothing allocates the cost of removal or of making good. Because the statutes are silent, the question is answered by your lease and by two general rules - and if the lease is silent, you are arguing about fixtures. That is the risk worth naming. South Dakota has a fixtures chapter dealing with a tenant's right to remove things affixed to the land, so a hard-wired charger bolted to a wall is exactly the kind of installation that generates a dispute about whether it is the tenant's to take or yours to keep. Settle it in writing before the installation rather than at move-out. The two rules that then apply are familiar: the tenant must preserve the premises and repair deterioration caused by the tenant's own negligent, wilful or malicious conduct, which covers damage from a removal done badly; and anything you charge must be documented actual cost, because a fixed removal or restoration fee is a penalty for nonperformance and void. Recovery runs through the deposit only as restoring the premises to their move-in condition, with ordinary wear and tear excepted. The cautious course is a consent letter at installation stating who owns the equipment, whether removal is required, who pays, and what making good means - signed before anyone drills a hole.

title: EV Charging - No Tenant Right, and the One Place You May Bill Above Cost
bodyText: No South Dakota statute requires you to allow or install electric-vehicle charging, and none gives a tenant the right to install a charger over your objection. The decision is yours. Two provisions matter once you decide to offer it. First, operating a charger does not make you a utility: a person who owns or operates an electric-vehicle charging station to resell or provide electricity to the public exclusively for vehicle charging is not an electric utility, so long as the electricity was bought from an electric utility making retail sales in its assigned service area. Second, and more useful, charging is carved out of South Dakota's anti-markup rule. Knowingly charging a consumer of gas or electricity more than the utility actually billed exposes you to a civil fine of up to five hundred dollars - but that rule expressly does not apply to an electric-vehicle charging station selling electricity under the exemption above. Electric-vehicle charging is therefore the one place South Dakota lets a landlord price electricity above its own cost; ordinary utility rebilling stays capped at the amount the utility billed.
