South Dakota also has no registration, meter-accuracy or price-posting regime aimed at charging equipment, unlike states that have put vehicle-charging equipment under their weights-and-measures laws. The cautious course is to state the charging price and who pays for the equipment in the lease or a parking addendum, and to keep ordinary electricity rebilling separate and at cost.

title: No Rules for Chargers in Shared Parking
bodyText: South Dakota has no provision about electric-vehicle charging in a shared or common parking area. Nothing requires you to allocate a space for charging, nothing governs how a tenant may run a cable across common ground, nothing addresses cost allocation among tenants for a shared charger, and nothing requires an association or a landlord to approve an installation in a common area. Everything here is yours to set in the lease and your rules. Three South Dakota points shape how to set it. Common areas are expressly inside your habitability duty - you must keep the premises and all common areas in reasonable repair and in good and safe working order, non-waivably - so a trailing cable across a walkway or a damaged bollard is your exposure, not merely the tenant's. Operating a charger for tenants does not make you a utility, provided you bought the electricity from a utility making retail sales in its assigned service area. And a shared charger is the one metered service you may bill above your own cost, because the anti-markup rule carves out vehicle charging - so a per-session or per-kilowatt-hour price is lawful where the same markup on ordinary electricity would not be. The cautious course is to treat a shared charger as an amenity you control: assign or allocate access by written policy, price it in the lease or a posted schedule, prohibit cables across pedestrian routes and any connection to the building's wiring without consent, and keep the equipment on your own maintenance schedule.

title: No Tenant Right to EV Charging
bodyText: South Dakota gives a tenant no right of access to electric-vehicle charging and no right to install a charger. There is no right-to-charge statute, no obligation to permit an installation on reasonable conditions, no notice-and-approval process, and no portfolio-size threshold above which a landlord must accommodate one. Whether charging exists at your property is your commercial decision, and a lease prohibiting a tenant from installing equipment answers the question. Two points make the decision easier than it looks. Operating a charger does not turn you into a regulated utility, provided the electricity is bought from an electric utility making retail sales in its assigned service area - so you can install and run one without entering utility regulation. And charging is the one place South Dakota lets you bill above your own cost: the rule that fines a landlord for charging a gas or electricity consumer more than the utility actually billed expressly carves out electric-vehicle charging stations. So the economics are yours to set, unlike ordinary utility rebilling. If you refuse installations, say so in the lease rather than relying on a general alterations clause, because a charger involves electrical work on a system you must keep in good and safe working order and cannot waive that duty for. If you permit one, require written consent, a licensed electrician, permits where applicable, a load assessment, metering, who owns the equipment at the end, and restoration of the parking surface and wall. The cautious course is a short parking addendum rather than silence.

title: No Hardship Stay, but Do Not Count on Same-Day Execution
bodyText: South Dakota gives a tenant no hardship stay. There is no provision letting a court delay possession because the tenant is ill, has children, cannot find housing or needs time to move, and no statute pairs a stay with an eviction at all. What the eviction statute does give is a short and bounded continuance. The tenant must appear and plead within five days of service, or thirty days after publication, whichever comes sooner, and no adjournment or continuance may run more than fourteen days unless the tenant gives you an undertaking with good and sufficient surety, approved by the court, for the rent that may accrue plus costs if judgment goes against them. The case can then be set for trial on two days' notice once the issues are joined, and a jury may be demanded. Execution for possession may be served only in the daytime. One real uncertainty remains, and you should plan around it rather than ignore it. The civil rules carry an automatic thirty-day bar on execution after a judgment is entered, with exceptions for a default judgment and for a court order on good cause shown. The rules also except forcible entry and detainer, by name, from their own reach where they are inconsistent with the eviction statute, and nothing in South Dakota settles whether that exception displaces the thirty days. The cautious course is to assume the bar may apply where the tenant actually defended, ask the court at judgment for an order permitting immediate execution for good cause, and build the possibility of a further month into your turnover schedule.

title: No Statutory Ban on Eviction-Penalty Clauses - General Contract Law Does It
bodyText: South Dakota has no statute listing prohibited lease provisions and none specifically banning a clause that makes the tenant pay a penalty, liquidated sum or fee because an eviction was brought. The constraint comes from general contract law instead, and it is blunt. Penalties imposed by contract for any nonperformance are void. An agreed sum standing in for damages is enforceable only where the parties agree on an amount presumed to be the damage for a breach in a case where it would be impracticable or extremely difficult to fix the actual damage. An eviction is not that case: what an eviction costs is a filing fee, a service fee and, if the lease and the law allow, legal fees, each of them a number on a receipt. A clause imposing a flat eviction charge, an administrative fee for filing, or liquidated damages pegged to a termination is therefore the kind of term South Dakota voids, and including it risks more than losing the charge - a provision contrary to an express provision of law, or to the policy of express law, is unlawful. What you may recover is what you actually and reasonably spend, where the lease provides for it, pursued as damages. Two related points. Statutory costs in an eviction are taxed by the court, not set by your lease. And a separate provision makes any term in a note, bond, mortgage or other evidence of debt providing for attorney's fees on default or foreclosure against public policy and void except as authorized by specific statute - so do not assume a fee-shifting clause carries into a rent default.

title: No Eviction-Record Sealing, but a General Access Request You Can Answer
bodyText: South Dakota has no eviction-record sealing or expungement statute. No provision seals an eviction file, none expunges a dismissed case automatically, none drops an eviction from a public index after a period of years, and there is no eviction-specific sealing proceeding. The expungement machinery that does exist in South Dakota runs to criminal records, to a genetic-database record, and to a notice of pendency on real estate, and none of it reaches a possession judgment. So assume an eviction you file is public and stays public. The judgment itself will record possession, the rents and profits or damages you claimed, and costs, and reasonable attorney fees may be taxed to the prevailing party, either side, where that party had a licensed attorney. All of that is on the face of a public record. Access to court records in South Dakota is governed instead by the judiciary's own court-records rule, which has general sections on what is publicly available, on records excluded from public access, and on how a person asks a court to prohibit public access to information in a record. Under it any party, or the person a record names, may ask the court to restrict access; every party gets notice, the court hears objections, and it decides case by case using the least restrictive means. The cautious course is practical. Do not tell an applicant or a tenant that a record can or cannot be sealed, do not promise to have a filing removed as a settlement term, and if a motion about access to one of your cases is served on you, respond on time rather than assume it cannot affect you.

title: You Cannot Name Someone in the Lease to Take Court Papers
bodyText: South Dakota has no provision letting a lease designate a person to accept eviction court papers, and no address-confidentiality program whose participants are served through a state office. Service in a possession action is set by statute and is not something the lease can rearrange. The complaint must be in writing and verified by you or your agent, or signed by your attorney, and served with a summons. A sheriff, a constable of the county, or any person legally authorised to serve a summons under the civil rules must attempt service on the tenant, subtenant or party in possession at least twice, with the attempts at least a week apart and both within thirty days. On the second attempt the summons may be posted conspicuously on the property and handed to a person residing there if one can be found, and also sent by first class mail to the tenant at the property. You may in addition publish the summons once in a legal newspaper on the same day as the first attempt. The person who serves may be the sheriff, a constable, or any non-party who is an elector of any state. A separate rule governs who is served when the tenant is a business entity, a minor, or a person under guardianship. The cautious course is to use the lease for what it can do and not for what it cannot. Collect and keep a current forwarding address and emergency contact, require the tenant to pass on any legal paper about the property promptly, and name a party to receive lease notices. Then serve the court papers the statutory way whatever the lease says.

title: No Criminal Fast Track, Because Every Eviction Is Already Fast
bodyText: South Dakota has no expedited eviction for drug activity, violence, weapons or gang involvement. There is no shortened notice for a criminal ground, no priority setting, no nuisance-abatement route to possession, and no mechanism for a neighbour, a prosecutor or a city to petition for a tenant's removal. The reason the absence matters less here than elsewhere is that the ordinary possession action is already a summary one and runs at the same speed for every ground. The tenant must appear and plead within five days of service, the case may be set for trial on two days' notice once the issues are joined, and no continuance may exceed fourteen days unless the tenant posts surety for the accruing rent and costs. There is nothing faster to be given. What the eviction statute does give you is a ground you have to build yourself. Besides holding over and unpaid rent, it reaches a tenant who commits waste, or who does or fails to do any act which under the terms of the lease operates to terminate the lease. That subdivision is the pathway for criminal conduct: write the crime-free covenant so that a breach terminates the tenancy by its own terms, and you are in court on the statute rather than waiting out a notice period. A separate statute lets you end a lease early where the tenant uses the premises contrary to the lease agreement. Two limits are firm. Nothing authorises evicting a tenant merely because they or a household member is the victim of domestic abuse, unlawful sexual behaviour or stalking, and a lease may not include a term authorising eviction for calling law enforcement or emergency responders about such an incident.

title: One Deposit Clock, No Faster Track
bodyText: South Dakota runs a single residential deposit timetable and provides no accelerated one. You return the deposit or furnish a written statement of the specific reason for withholding within twenty-one days of the tenancy ending and your receipt of the tenant's mailing address or delivery instructions, and you provide an itemized accounting within forty-five days if the tenant asks. No statute lets a tenant demand the money sooner, and none shortens the period because the tenancy ended early, because the tenant terminated after domestic abuse, unlawful sexual behavior or stalking, because of a military transfer, because the property was sold or condemned, or because the unit became uninhabitable. There is no summary or expedited court route reserved for deposit claims either. The only variation the legislature has written runs in the opposite direction: commercial tenancies get sixty days to return or explain and ninety days for the accounting, so the residential clock is already the short one. Read the deadlines as outer limits rather than targets. Nothing stops you from paying earlier, and there is a strong reason to: a landlord who fails to comply forfeits all rights to withhold any portion of the deposit, and a landlord who has already refunded has nothing left to forfeit. The cautious course is to diary both trigger dates, the day the tenancy ended and the day the tenant's address reached you, and to finish inside the first week. Give the itemized accounting together with the written statement rather than waiting for the second deadline, since one document that does both closes the question. Do not promise a shorter period in the lease; you would be bound by it and gain nothing.

title: No Absence-Notice Duty - Put It in the Lease
bodyText: South Dakota has no statute requiring a tenant to tell you about an extended absence, and none requiring the rental agreement to contain an absence-notice term. States with a uniform landlord-tenant act typically impose that duty and set the notice period; South Dakota has no such act, so if you want the notice you must bargain for it. The surrounding law still puts some of the risk on the tenant. The tenant must preserve the premises, the appliances, the appurtenances and the other leased personal property, and must repair deterioration caused by the tenant's own negligent, willful or malicious conduct - so damage that follows from an unreported absence, a heating system left off in winter and the pipes that follow, can be the tenant's responsibility without any absence-notice clause at all. Property the tenant leaves behind is handled by the abandoned-property sections rather than by an absence rule. What an absence-notice clause buys you is earlier knowledge rather than a new remedy, and that is worth having: a lawful optional term requiring written notice of an absence beyond a stated number of days, with permission to enter to inspect and protect the property during it, is enforceable as an ordinary contract term. Do not attach a flat charge to a failure to give the notice; a sum payable simply because the tenant broke the term is a contractual penalty and void.

title: No Right to Run a Day Care in Your Rental
bodyText: South Dakota does not require you to let a tenant operate a family day care home in a rented dwelling. There is no statutory right of the kind some states give, and so no statutory conditions either - no mandated liability waiver, no insurance requirement you may impose, no notice procedure. Whether a tenant may run a day care from your property is a matter for your lease. Two pieces of South Dakota law shape the decision rather than the right. Registration reaches only publicly funded care: an application to operate a family day care home is made to the Department of Social Services, whose rules regulate homes providing services paid for directly or indirectly out of public funds, and those rules and the registration requirement expressly do not apply to a family day care home whose services are not publicly funded. So a tenant minding children for private fees may be operating with no state registration and no state inspection at all. Municipalities may regulate separately: any municipality may provide for the regulation of family day care homes and adopt standards of care, including personnel qualifications and requirements for safety, sanitation and the condition and maintenance of the physical plant - so a city ordinance may apply where state registration does not. One consequence to note if you do permit it: South Dakota's smoke-free law does not reach a private residence unless the residence is used for day care, so permitting a day care brings the unit within the statutory smoking prohibition. The cautious course is to address business use expressly in the lease, require written consent, and ask for proof of registration where applicable and of liability insurance naming you.

title: Your Tenant Can Give Hunting Permission - Reserve It or Lose It
bodyText: South Dakota has no statute allocating hunting or fishing rights between an owner and a tenant, so nothing says the sporting right stays with you when you let the land. What it does have is a trespass rule that makes the default run against you. Nobody may fish, hunt or trap on private land without permission from the owner or lessee of the land - and because a lessee can give that permission, a lease of land that says nothing about hunting leaves your tenant able to authorise it, and able to charge for it. A second provision deepens the point: a resident may hunt small game, game birds or fish in an open season on land owned or leased by the resident without first securing a licence, so a tenant of the land needs no licence for small game and the licensing system will not slow anything down. The rights-of-way provisions use the same owner-or-lessee pairing for written permission, so the pattern is consistent across the chapter. None of this is a grant to the tenant; it is simply the absence of a reservation to you. In a state where access for pheasant and deer season has real money attached, that absence is expensive. So treat the sporting right as a separate asset and deal with it expressly in any lease of land, including a farmhouse let with acres attached. The cautious course is to reserve hunting, fishing and trapping to yourself, bar the tenant from granting permission to anyone else, and make any exception a written one.

title: A Fee in Lieu of a Deposit Is Still a Deposit Here
bodyText: South Dakota has no deposit-alternative statute, and that matters less than the rule it leaves in charge, which actively defeats most of what is sold as one. Any money whose function is to secure performance of a residential rental agreement is deemed a security deposit however it is denominated. A recurring non-refundable fee you collect instead of a deposit, to stand behind unpaid rent or damage, is doing precisely that work. So in South Dakota it is a security deposit. It counts against the one-month cap, and because you collect it month after month it will exceed the cap quickly; it must be returned or explained on the deposit timetable; and it may be withheld only for rent defaults, other funds due to you under an agreement, and restoring the premises to their move-in condition with ordinary wear and tear excepted. Nothing authorizes a fee in lieu, nothing obliges you to offer a deposit alternative or to offer it to every applicant, and no state housing agency has been directed to write rules for one, because there is no statute for rules to implement. There is likewise no notice you must give before reporting a damage claim to a credit bureau or a collection agency. The cautious course is to take a conventional deposit inside the cap and follow the deposit rules. If a tenant would rather buy third-party coverage, have the tenant contract directly with the insurer or surety and stay out of the money chain yourself, because a policy the tenant purchases is not money you demanded or received, while a fee you collect and keep is. Do not let a vendor's product label settle a question the statute settles by function.

title: No All-In Pricing Law - the Lease Is What Makes a Fee Collectible
bodyText: South Dakota has no fee-transparency or all-in pricing law for rentals. There is no requirement that rent appear as a single figure including every mandatory fee, no first-page disclosure in statutory words, no itemisation duty, no junk-fee regulation covering dwelling units, no auto-renewal regulation reaching residential leases, no subsidy-format exemption, and no general landlord-fee prohibition sitting outside the landlord-tenant provisions. You may price however you like and advertise a base rent with fees stated separately. The discipline comes from a different direction, and it is practical rather than cosmetic. From the security deposit you may withhold only amounts reasonably necessary to remedy defaults in the payment of rent and of other funds due to you under an agreement, and to restore the premises. A fee that is not created by the lease is not funds due under an agreement, so it is not collectible from the deposit and, if you withhold it anyway, you have failed to comply with the deposit section - which forfeits all rights to withhold any portion of the deposit, not merely the disputed part. So transparency in South Dakota is enforced through your own recovery rights: an undisclosed fee is an uncollectible one. Separately, charging a fee that the rental agreement does not state is the kind of conduct the deceptive practices chapter reaches in a consumer transaction. The cautious course is to list every non-optional charge in the lease with its amount and purpose, show the realistic monthly total once, and add nothing later except by the statutory route for modifying a month-to-month tenancy.

title: Charging for a Service You Do Not Provide
bodyText: South Dakota has no provision specifically forbidding a fee for a service that is not provided, which is worth knowing mainly because it tells you where the exposure actually sits. Three general rules reach the practice, and together they are more dangerous than a dedicated prohibition would be. A charge the tenant pays for nothing is not a charge for a service at all; if you keep it because the tenant failed to do something, it is a penalty imposed by contract for nonperformance and void, and if you keep it in exchange for nothing it is money with no consideration behind it. Second, the deposit statute lets you withhold only amounts reasonably necessary to remedy rent defaults, to collect other funds due to you under an agreement, and to restore the premises - a fee for an unprovided service is none of those, and withholding it forfeits all rights to withhold any portion of the deposit, which converts a small overcharge into the loss of the whole deposit. Third, and most seriously, representing that a tenancy includes a service you do not supply, or billing a line item that corresponds to nothing, is the kind of knowing misrepresentation the deceptive practices chapter targets, and the Attorney General enforces it. Whether that chapter reaches a residential tenancy is unsettled, so plan as if it does. The cautious course is to charge only for services you actually deliver, bill them at or below cost, stop charging the moment the service stops, and refund proactively if it lapses - an unprompted credit is cheap and a deceptive-practices complaint is not.

title: Which Fire and Building Codes Apply
bodyText: South Dakota has no statewide residential building code of its own. Two separate regimes reach a rental, and they run on different editions. Fire safety is statewide by rule: the Department of Public Safety has adopted the International Building Code, International Fire Code and International Mechanical Code, 2015 editions, as its fire-safety rules, and those rules carry the smoke-detector and sprinkler requirements that apply to rental housing. Building design is local and runs on the 2024 editions: if your city or county adopts a construction ordinance for anything other than a residential structure it must comply with the 2024 International Building Code; where no local ordinance exists, buildings commenced after July 1, 2026 are designed to the 2024 International Building Code, except residential structures, mobile and manufactured homes, and farmsteads. A municipality may adopt the 2024 International Residential Code for residential structures, meaning detached one- and two-family dwellings and townhouses up to three stories. A local ordinance on maintaining existing structures must comply with the 2024 International Property Maintenance Code - that ordinance, where one exists, is the practical housing-code standard for an older rental. Both regimes adopt the model codes by reference and neither reprints them, so compliance means reading the adopted edition and your local ordinance. Check with your city building official and the State Fire Marshal; local requirements vary and are not resolved here.

title: When Sprinklers Are Required - and When a City May Not Require Them
bodyText: South Dakota answers this from both directions. A sprinkler system is required throughout any new hotel, motel, or multifamily residence housing six or more families, by Department of Public Safety rule, built to the sprinkler provisions of the 2015 International Building Code. That is a new-construction requirement; South Dakota imposes no retrofit duty on an existing building, whatever its size. At the other end, a city may not impose one on a small residential building at all: a municipality that adopts the International Residential Code for residential structures may not require the installation of a sprinkler system in a residential structure, and may not impose requirements more stringent than the 2024 edition of that code. Residential structure means a detached one- or two-family dwelling, and townhouses not more than three stories in height, with a separate means of egress. So a new six-plex needs sprinklers, a new duplex cannot be made to have them by local ordinance, and an existing building of any size faces no retrofit mandate from state law. Before you rely on the absence, confirm with the State Fire Marshal and your local building official: the requirement sits in rules that adopt a model code by reference, the occupancy classification of your building drives the answer, and a change of use or a substantial remodel can pull a building into the new-construction requirement.

title: A Lease Firearm Restriction Is Enforceable Here - the Preemption Binds Cities, Not You
bodyText: South Dakota is strongly pro-firearm, and landlords often assume that means a lease cannot restrict firearms. It does not. No statute protects a tenant's possession of a firearm against a private lease term, none makes a lease restriction unenforceable against a permit holder, and none bars a rule about firearms locked in a vehicle in your parking area. The preemption the state has enacted runs against other rule-makers, not against you. A county, a township and a municipality are each barred from regulating firearms by ordinance, with the attorney general empowered to act, and since 2024 a homeowners' association is barred too: it may not include or enforce a governing-document provision restricting the lawful possession, transportation or storing of a firearm, a part or ammunition, or lawful discharge. Note which way that cuts. The Legislature has now reached a private recorded instrument and still has not reached a lease - so if you let inside an association, the association cannot restrict firearms in the community and you still can in your own lease. A firearm restriction is therefore a contract term, enforceable like any other, and a breach reaches eviction through the ground covering an act which under the lease operates to terminate it. Whether to have one is a commercial judgment rather than a legal one, and the reasons for caution are unrelated to enforceability: a restriction is unpopular here, hard to detect without entering, and gives you knowledge you may prefer not to have. Nothing requires you to restrict firearms and nothing makes you liable for a tenant's lawful possession. The cautious course, if you do restrict, is to confine the rule to common areas and to unsafe storage or handling rather than possession inside a unit, and to state it plainly rather than bury it.

title: No Flood Disclosure Duty to a Tenant
bodyText: South Dakota asks about flooding, but it asks a seller and not a landlord. The state's mandated residential property-condition disclosure statement, which runs on a transfer to a buyer, requires the seller to say whether the property is in a flood plain, whether federally protected wetlands sit on any part of it, whether water has ever stood in the yard for more than forty-eight hours, and whether there has been past flood damage or an insurance claim for it. None of that attaches to a letting. No statute requires you to tell a tenant that the unit is in a flood plain or a special flood hazard area, there is no state model rider, no twelve-point type rule, no signature requirement, and no statutory termination right triggered by a flood disclosure or by a flood. The flood statutes that do exist are about flood control, drainage and water rights, and they bind government rather than landlords. What fills the gap is general law. You owe a habitability duty that cannot be waived, and a tenant may terminate if the greater part of the premises or the thing that materially induced the letting is destroyed otherwise than by the tenant's own ordinary negligence. The cautious course is to disclose a flood-plain location and any history of water intrusion in writing before signing, keep the signed acknowledgement, and tell the tenant plainly that your insurance does not cover their belongings so they should carry renter's insurance with flood coverage. Concealing known flooding is exposure under the deceptive trade practices statute and in fraud even with no disclosure statute on the books.

title: No Duty to Disclose a Foreclosure to an Incoming Tenant
bodyText: South Dakota imposes no duty on you to tell a prospective or incoming tenant that the property is in foreclosure or that you have been served with a foreclosure action. There is no pre-signing disclosure, no prescribed form, no shortened term for a lease signed after a complaint, and no tenant right to rescind or terminate on learning of it. The one place the subject surfaces is a sale: a seller's mandated property-condition disclosure statement asks whether the seller is aware of current or pending litigation or foreclosure affecting the property. That question is put to a buyer and does not reach a letting. Where South Dakota puts its energy instead is on the lien side, and the notice scheme there does not help your tenant: the foreclosing creditor serves the owner and the holders of affected interests, and the published notice names people with a recorded interest, so an ordinary residential tenant on an unrecorded lease is not a required recipient. The statutory duty in this area in fact runs toward you, since the tenant must immediately forward any notice of a proceeding to recover the property, and an attornment to a stranger is void. The cautious course is to disclose a pending foreclosure before signing even though no statute compels it, and not to take rent for a term you cannot deliver. Concealing it while collecting a deposit and advance rent is where real exposure lies, in fraud and under the deceptive trade practices statute, and your delivery and quiet enjoyment duty carries a two months' rent remedy. After a sale a bona fide tenant gets ninety days' notice to vacate from the buyer under federal law, not from you.

title: What Foreclosure Does to the Tenancy
bodyText: South Dakota gives a residential tenant no foreclosure protection of any kind. There is no state notice after a sale, no provision making the lease bind the buyer, no treatment of a tenant as a lienholder with a right to redeem, no protection for an omitted tenant in possession, and no equity-skimming statute aimed at a buyer who collects rents without applying them to the mortgage. South Dakota routes the question through title and possession instead. The eviction statute's grounds include a party who stays in possession after a sale under mortgage, execution, order or judicial process, once the time fixed by law for redemption has run and the deed has been executed and delivered. The purchaser's route against a tenant who remains is therefore the ordinary eviction action, and it opens only after redemption closes and title has passed. Two older provisions still bite: your tenant must immediately forward to you any notice of a proceeding to recover the property and is liable for damages for failing to, and a tenant's attornment to a stranger is void unless you consent or a court orders it, so the tenant cannot simply start paying someone claiming to have bought the place. The cautious course is to treat the tenant as unprotected and act accordingly. Tell the tenant in writing as soon as a foreclosure is filed, because no one else will. Do not collect advance rent or a new deposit for a term you may not be able to deliver. Transfer the deposit at closing against a written acknowledgment. If the loan is federally backed, the federal thirty-day notice to vacate applies, and after a sale federal law gives a bona fide tenant ninety days' notice from the buyer, not from you.

title: A 2026 Chapter Reaches Leases - but You Have No Duty to Ask
bodyText: South Dakota has two foreign-ownership chapters, and the newer one reaches residential leases. It defines a real property interest to include a lease, and it bars a prohibited entity from holding or obtaining any such interest in the state while a military installation exists here - which one does. A prohibited entity means an entity, government or person from one of six named countries, and the definitions treat a natural person who is not a United States citizen or a resident as a foreign person. So a twelve-month residential tenancy is squarely inside the chapter's reach, with no acreage limit and no short-lease carve-out. Then comes the provision that matters most to you, and it cuts decisively in your favour: a person who is not a prohibited entity has no duty to determine or inquire whether anyone else is one, and cannot be held liable for failing to find out. Enforcement is the attorney general's alone, by court action, and the remedy is a judgment declaring the interest void from the date of judgment with forfeiture or termination. There are broad exclusions, including anyone who is a lawful permanent resident or citizen, including a dual citizen, and an individual with lawful status. The older chapter is narrower: it is confined to agricultural land, and for non-prohibited foreign persons it expressly leaves leasing unrestricted while capping ownership. The cautious course is to run your ordinary screening and not to build nationality questions into it, because the law gives you no duty to ask and fair housing law makes asking hazardous.

title: Forfeiture, Reentry and the Absence of Any Right to Redeem
bodyText: South Dakota is unusually generous to a landlord who reserves a right of reentry, and gives the tenant nothing to set against it. If your lease reserves it, reentry may be made any time after the right has accrued on three days' previous written notice of intention to reenter, served as a notice to quit is. More striking still, an action for possession of property leased with a reserved right of reentry may be brought at any time after the right accrues without that notice at all. So a reserved reentry shortens your notice to three days, and suing on it requires none. Contrast the ordinary tenancy at will, where you must wait out the full statutory period first. The forfeiture itself is whatever your lease makes it. An eviction ground covers a tenant who does or fails to do any act which, under the lease, operates to terminate it: the lease defines the trigger and the statute enforces it. A separate provision lets you end the term early for use contrary to the lease agreement or for failure to repair after request. There is no statutory relief against forfeiture here, and no redemption: nothing lets a tenant reopen a forfeited lease by paying. That is power worth using carefully. The cautious course is to reserve the right of reentry expressly, state exactly which breaches operate to terminate, and still give a short written cure opportunity as a matter of practice, because a court asked to enforce a forfeiture will look at proportionality and at your own conduct. Do not attach a forfeiture penalty or fixed sum to the breach; a contract penalty for nonperformance is void, as is a damages figure that is not a genuine estimate. Never write a term shortening the tenant's time to sue.

title: South Dakota Freezes the Standards It Borrows - Check the Edition
bodyText: South Dakota regularly regulates by adopting an outside standard, and it almost always freezes the version. That matters to you because your obligation is the edition named in the statute or rule, not the current edition the publisher sells. Three examples carry most of the weight. Building design runs on the 2024 editions: a local construction ordinance for anything other than a residential structure must comply with the 2024 International Building Code, a municipality adopting residential standards does so by adopting the 2024 International Residential Code, and a local ordinance on maintaining existing structures must comply with the 2024 International Property Maintenance Code. Fire safety runs on older editions: the Department of Public Safety's rules adopt the International Building Code, International Fire Code and International Mechanical Code, 2015 editions, together with referenced standards except as modified in the rules - so the fire-safety requirements carrying the smoke-detector and sprinkler rules are a 2015 code while the design standards are a 2024 code. Pool standards for lodging run on a 1996 publication. Two practical consequences for you. When a contractor or an inspector cites a code provision, confirm which edition applies to the regime in question before you accept it, because the two can differ on the same subject. And none of these texts is reproduced in the statutes or rules - they are incorporated by reference, so complying means obtaining the named edition rather than reading the law. The cautious course is to record, for each property you hold, which codes and editions its local ordinance adopts, and to re-check that record whenever you are told a requirement has changed.

title: Furnished Lettings Are Unregulated - the Inventory Does the Work
bodyText: South Dakota has no rules about furnished lettings. Nothing requires an inventory, nothing presumes that furniture present is included, nothing sets a standard for the condition of furnishings, and nothing limits what you may charge for damage to them. A furnished unit is governed by exactly the same provisions as an unfurnished one. Two of those provisions carry the weight. The tenant's statutory duty is wider than most landlords realise: the tenant must preserve the premises, the appliances, the appurtenances and the other leased personal property, and must repair deterioration caused by the tenant's own negligent, wilful or malicious conduct or that of someone under the tenant's direction or control. The words other leased personal property are what bring furniture inside the duty, so damage to a sofa you supplied is recoverable on the same footing as damage to a door. And recovery runs through the deposit on the ordinary terms - you may withhold what is reasonably necessary to restore the premises to their condition at the commencement of the tenancy, with ordinary wear and tear excepted, which applies to furnishings too and means a worn item cannot be charged as damaged. Because nothing is presumed, the inventory is the whole of your evidence. The cautious course is a dated, signed schedule listing every item with its condition and, for anything valuable, a photograph; a note of which items the tenant may not remove or store; and a repeat of the exercise at move-out, charging documented actual cost rather than a fixed replacement fee, which would be void as a penalty.

title: Your Notice Must State a Period, Not a Reason
bodyText: South Dakota requires no cause for ending a tenancy and requires no statement of cause in the notice that ends it. What the notice to end a residential tenancy at will must contain is a period: it must be in writing and must tell the tenant to remove from the premises within a period, specified in the notice, of not less than fifteen days, and until that period has run you may neither reenter nor sue. The statute asks for nothing else. A lease ends on expiry of its agreed term, by mutual consent, or where the tenant acquires better title, and for unpaid rent the possession statute supplies its own trigger three days after rent is due, with no notice of any kind required before filing. There is no just-cause regime, no list of permitted reasons, no duty to offer a cure, and no obligation to explain yourself. Three exceptions run against you rather than for you. A notice to vacate that is not based on a breach of the lease can found a retaliation claim if it follows a tenant's good-faith code complaint, a written repair notice, or joining a tenant union, with a defence where the notice comes more than one hundred eighty days later, and a failure to renew a written lease at or before expiry is not retaliation. Nothing authorises eviction merely because a tenant is the victim of domestic abuse, unlawful sexual behaviour or stalking. And the two months notice owed where a tenant or an immediate family member is on active military service is cut short only on the grounds the statute itself names. The cautious course is a notice stating the period and nothing more, plus a separate dated file showing the real reason in case retaliation is raised.

title: No Rule on Passing Government Fees to Tenants - One Real Exposure
bodyText: South Dakota has no provision about recovering a government fee, charge or tax from a tenant. Nothing authorises a pass-through, nothing forbids one, nothing requires you to disclose it or to cap it, and nothing entitles you to reimbursement if a municipality imposes a new charge mid-tenancy. It is a matter for the lease, and if the lease is silent you absorb the cost until you can change the rent. There is one government charge that comes at you from the other direction and is worth more attention than the pass-through question. A delinquent solid-waste fee levied by a municipality, county or subdivision - other than a municipal garbage collection fee - may be certified to the county treasurer and must then be collected as a condition precedent to paying the real property tax on that very parcel. A delinquent municipal garbage collection fee is instead collected as a condition precedent to paying any water, sewer, utility or other charge the municipality collects. Either way the unpaid charge becomes your problem regardless of who incurred it, and South Dakota gives you no owner exemption and no affidavit to file. So the practical rule is the reverse of a pass-through: keep municipal service accounts in your own name, build the cost into rent, and if a tenant holds an account, verify it is clear before you return the deposit. If you do pass a government charge through, name it in the lease with its basis, because only a charge the lease creates is funds due to you under an agreement.

title: Passing a Government Fine to the Tenant Who Caused It
bodyText: South Dakota has no statute on this at all, in either direction. Nothing makes an occupant liable to the owner for a fine the owner paid or for the cost of abating a nuisance, as several other states do expressly, and nothing forbids you passing such a charge on either. There is no state rental registration, licensing or inspection fee scheme whose cost could be allocated, and no default rule a careless lease could give away. Reimbursement here is pure contract: you get it only if your lease creates it, and nothing if the lease is silent. The exposure that makes the clause worth having is real enough. The nuisance chapter provides for abatement on notice and for the taxing of the cost of abatement. County health boards may notify an owner of a nuisance, remove it if the owner does not, and charge the cost, subject to a hearing and an appeal. Failing to remove a public nuisance is itself a misdemeanour where no other punishment is prescribed. Those routes run at the owner, not the occupant, and they reach you whoever created the condition. The cautious course is to write a narrow reimbursement term and keep it honest. Confine it to a fine, penalty or abatement cost arising from a condition the tenant, a household member or a guest caused or permitted. Exclude anything that is your own responsibility in law or under the lease. Charge only the amount you actually paid, against a copy of the citation, order or bill, and never a flat or marked-up sum, because a contract penalty for nonperformance is void here and so is a damages figure that is not a genuine estimate. Because the obligation is contractual, the amount is also funds due to you under an agreement for deposit purposes.

title: No Guaranty Statute - the Guaranty Is Only as Wide as It Is Written
bodyText: South Dakota has no statute about lease guarantors. Nothing limits a guarantor's liability to the original term, nothing requires a separate guaranty to state a maximum amount or an end date, nothing requires the guaranty to be written on or to refer to the lease, and no cap on money collected at the start of a tenancy reaches a deposit or prepayment demanded from a guarantor. The guaranty is a contract and is construed as one, which puts all the weight on its drafting. Two points follow for a renewal, which is where guaranties usually fail. If the guaranty says nothing about renewals or extensions, a guarantor has a serious argument that the obligation ended with the original term, and you will be arguing construction at exactly the moment you need certainty. Say expressly whether the guaranty covers renewals, extensions and holdover periods, and whether it survives a change in the rent. And remember South Dakota's renewal presumptions operate by default: a holdover whose rent you accept is presumed to have renewed the hiring on the same terms for the same time, not exceeding one year, and a hiring for an unspecified term is deemed renewed unless notice is given - so a tenancy can roll forward without anyone signing anything, and whether the guaranty rolled with it depends only on its words. One deposit point: money you take from a guarantor to secure the tenant's performance is still money whose function is to secure performance of the rental agreement, so treat it as deposit money inside the one-month cap rather than as something outside the deposit rules.

title: No Statutory Guest Rights in a Residential Tenancy
bodyText: South Dakota gives a residential tenant's guests no statutory rights, and gives you no statutory limits on guest rules. There is no provision protecting a tenant's visitors or suppliers in buildings of any size, nothing making such a right non-waivable, and nothing barring a guest fee. Guest policy is therefore a matter for your lease and your rules. South Dakota's guest provisions sit in transient lodging instead, which is worth knowing so you do not read them as applying to a tenancy: a hotel, campground or RV park may eject a person without returning the rental payment for nonpayment, disorderly conduct or complaints from other guests, unlawful use, bringing an explosive or destructive device, not being a registered guest, exceeding the establishment's occupancy limits, obtaining the accommodation by false pretenses, being an unsupervised minor, or violating applicable law - and there are separate innkeeper provisions about guests' property. None of that reaches a residential lease. Two limits on how far a guest rule can go. A term that effectively excluded the tenant's own use of the premises would collide with the landlord's duty to secure the tenant's quiet enjoyment, and a flat charge imposed because a guest stayed too long is a penalty for nonperformance and void - the enforceable route is to define when a guest becomes an occupant and to treat unauthorized occupancy as a lease breach. The cautious course is a clear numerical limit on consecutive and cumulative guest nights, a written-consent route for longer stays, and the tenant's responsibility for guests' conduct and damage, which the tenant's own statutory preservation duty already supports.

title: No Materiality Threshold - Every Defect Is Measured Against One Standard
bodyText: South Dakota sets no materiality threshold for habitability. There is no provision saying a defect must substantially affect health and safety before the duty bites, no list of conditions deemed material, and no percentage or dollar test. The statute states one standard and leaves its application to the facts: reasonable repair, fit for human habitation, and good and safe working order, with electrical, plumbing and heating systems maintained in good and safe working order and condition. The one place a materiality-like phrase appears in South Dakota's landlord-tenant provisions is unrelated to repairs - it is in the notice rules for terminating a tenancy at will, where extended notice for a tenant on active military service is lost if the tenant has engaged in sustained disruptive, illegal, destructive or negligent conduct or a material breach of the implied lease conditions. Two consequences follow for you. Because there is no threshold, you cannot assume a minor defect is beneath the duty; a broken heating system in January and a dripping tap are both measured against the same words, and what differs is what a reasonable repair of each looks like and how quickly it is owed. And because the tenant's remedies turn on a reasonable time after notice rather than on a defect's severity, your response time is the variable you actually control. The cautious course is to triage by risk and document it: treat anything affecting heat, water, electrical safety or security as urgent, respond to everything in writing, and record what you did and when.

title: The Duty Cannot Be Modified, Not Even for a Property Without Utility Water
bodyText: South Dakota's habitability duty cannot be modified any more than it can be waived - the statute bars both in the same breath, saying the parties may not waive or modify its requirements. That matters here because some states allow a tailored reduction of the duty where the property's circumstances justify it, for instance letting the lease relieve the landlord of the water or hot-water supply duty where the premises have no well or utility service. South Dakota has no such provision, and no equivalent for heat, for seasonal properties, for rural properties or for anything else. The only permitted adjustment is the one the statute names: you may agree with the tenant that the tenant will perform specified repairs or maintenance in lieu of rent. Read those words closely, because they are narrower than they look. The repairs must be specified, so a general transfer of maintenance responsibility does not qualify. The consideration must be rent, so an agreement for a one-off payment or a reduced deposit is outside it. And it must be an agreement, not a recital buried in your standard form. What this means practically: if a property genuinely cannot meet part of the standard - no connection to utility water, a cabin without winter heat - you cannot fix that by drafting. Either the property is let in a condition that meets the duty, or you are exposed whatever the lease says, and the tenant's remedies remain available. The duty also stacks on any covenant imposed by law or ordinance, so a local code adds to it rather than replacing it.

title: No Presumption of Habitability - the Duty Is Imposed Directly
bodyText: South Dakota creates no presumption that premises are habitable, and none that they are not. There is no provision deeming a unit fit on delivery, none deeming it unfit after a code violation or a failed inspection, and no evidentiary presumption shifting the burden in a dispute about condition. The reason is structural rather than an oversight: South Dakota imposes the duty directly, in every hiring of residential premises whether written or oral, so there is nothing for a presumption to do. A tenant alleging a breach proves the condition and the notice; you answer on what you did and when. South Dakota's lease chapter does contain presumptions, and it is worth knowing they are about something else entirely, so you are not misled by finding them. A hiring of real property other than lodgings is presumed to be for one year unless the hiring says otherwise. A hiring of lodgings for an unspecified term is presumed to run for whatever period the parties used to set the rent - weekly rent, a weekly hiring - and monthly if there is no agreement about that either. A tenant who holds over and whose rent you accept is presumed to have renewed on the same terms for the same time, not exceeding one year. Those are term-length and holdover presumptions, not condition presumptions. The practical point: with no presumption either way, condition disputes are decided on evidence, which again puts the weight on your move-in record, your written responses to repair reports and your dated repair invoices.

title: The Lease Need Not Promise Habitability - It Is Implied Regardless
bodyText: South Dakota does not require your lease to state that you will deliver the unit fit for habitation, or to recite the habitability duty at all. Some states require exactly that sentence in the written lease; South Dakota requires no lease content on the subject, and a lease that says nothing about condition carries the duty anyway. The duty attaches to the hiring of residential premises, in writing or oral, so it reaches a handshake tenancy as surely as your standard form. Two things follow that are worth getting right. First, omitting the duty from the lease gains you nothing - it is implied, it cannot be waived or modified, and silence does not narrow it. Second, and more useful, including a statement of it costs you nothing either, and a short accurate sentence is better than the alternative that often appears in its place: an as-is clause, an acknowledgment that the tenant has inspected and accepts the premises in their present condition, or a recital that the tenant agrees the unit is habitable. Those are attempts to modify a duty the statute makes unmodifiable, and a court reading one of them learns that your form tried to contract out of a protected obligation. The cautious course is to state the duty plainly if you address condition at all, to pair it with a signed move-in condition report recording what the condition actually was, and to keep the one lawful reallocation separate and explicit: an agreement that the tenant performs specified repairs or maintenance in lieu of rent.

title: The Habitability Duty Cannot Be Waived or Modified
bodyText: South Dakota answers this in the statute itself, in one sentence: the parties to a lease or hiring of residential premises may not waive or modify the requirements imposed by the habitability section. That is a bar on both waiver and modification, and it is the only express non-waiver sentence in South Dakota's lease chapter. What it protects is the whole of that section's duties: keeping the premises and all common areas in reasonable repair, fit for human habitation, and in good and safe working order throughout the term, and maintaining all electrical, plumbing and heating systems in good and safe working order and condition. The duty already carries its own exception for disrepair caused by the negligent, willful or malicious conduct of the tenant or someone under the tenant's direction or control, so you do not need a lease term to achieve that result, and a term purporting to go further is unenforceable. One reallocation is expressly permitted, and it is narrow: you may agree with the tenant that the tenant will perform specified repairs or maintenance in lieu of rent. Note the three limits in those words - specified repairs, not a general transfer of the duty; in lieu of rent, so there must be rent consideration; and an agreement, not a lease recital. A clause that simply makes the tenant responsible for maintaining the heating system, or has the tenant accept the premises as-is, is a modification of the duty and void. The duty is also additional to any covenant imposed by law, ordinance or the lease, so a local housing code stacks on top of it rather than substituting for it.

title: Contamination - No Lease Disclosure Duty, but a Covenant Can Bind Your Tenant
bodyText: South Dakota requires no contamination disclosure in a residential lease. Nothing obliges you to tell a tenant that the site is a brownfield, that it has been through a cleanup, or that a recorded restriction limits how the land may be used, and there is no statute requiring a recorded environmental limitation to be copied into or attached to a lease. Two things matter more than that absence. First, South Dakota has adopted the uniform environmental covenants act, so a recorded environmental covenant on a remediated site is a real interest in the land that restricts its use, and the chapter deals expressly with the subordination of other interests and with the covenant's effect on other instruments. A tenant taking possession of land under such a covenant can be bound by use restrictions regardless of whether your lease mentions them, and your lease can put the tenant in breach of the covenant without either of you intending it. Second, the state does mandate one contamination-type disclosure on a letting, and only one: if you actually know methamphetamine was previously manufactured on the premises, you must tell the tenant, and in a building of two or more units the duty covers only the unit you know about. The cautious course is to run a title search before letting a property with any industrial or agricultural-chemical history, read any recorded environmental covenant, and then attach its use restrictions to the lease as an exhibit with a tenant covenant to comply. Disclose known contamination in writing even where no statute compels it. A recorded environmental covenant does reach your tenancy: it runs with the land as an interest in real property and stays valid even though it imposes a negative burden. The one exception is an interest that already had priority when the covenant was created, such as a lease signed before it: that interest is not affected unless its owner agreed to subordinate it.

title: No Health-District Rental Rules to Hand Over
bodyText: South Dakota imposes no duty to give a tenant a health district's rental regulations on request, and no duty to refer a complaining tenant to a health authority. There is no state health-district rental code for private housing at all. Public-health machinery exists but is aimed elsewhere: a city board of health has powers and duties over sanitation and health measures, counties and districts have boards of health, and there are nuisance and health-hazard provisions - none of which creates a residential rental code or a landlord disclosure duty. State health regulation of accommodation is instead concentrated on lodging, food service and campgrounds, which is licensing of transient establishments rather than anything that reaches an apartment. So a tenant with a habitability complaint in South Dakota has no health-district route the statutes create for them; they have the remedies the lease chapter gives directly. Those are the ones to keep in view, because they do not depend on any agency acting. After notice to you of conditions requiring repair and a reasonable time without repair, the tenant may repair and deduct, vacate and be discharged from further rent, or withhold rent into a separate account where the repairs would cost more than one month's rent. A tenant may also terminate the lease where you fail to repair after written request. The cautious course is to treat a tenant's written complaint as the start of your reasonable time rather than as something an agency might take off your hands, and to respond in writing with dates.

title: Heat Is Named in the Statute - and Cannot Be Shifted to the Tenant
bodyText: Heating is one of the few systems South Dakota names expressly, and the duty is among the strongest in the state's landlord-tenant law. You must maintain in good and safe working order and condition all electrical, plumbing and heating systems of the premises, and keep the premises fit for human habitation and in good and safe working order throughout the term. The parties may not waive or modify any of that. So a lease term making the tenant responsible for the heating system, or accepting the premises without working heat, is unenforceable - and the only reallocation South Dakota permits is an agreement that the tenant perform specified repairs or maintenance in lieu of rent, which is narrow and must be about particular work exchanged for rent rather than a transfer of the system. There is no minimum temperature and no heating season in South Dakota law. The standard is the statute's own - good and safe working order - applied to a climate where a failure in January is a serious matter, so treat heat as the most urgent category of repair and respond to a report of no heat immediately. Note what follows if you do not. After notice and a reasonable time the tenant may repair and deduct the cost, vacate and be discharged from further rent, or, where repairs would cost more than one month's rent, withhold rent into a separate account. A tenant who pays for emergency heating work and deducts it is exercising a statutory right, not breaching the lease. Paying the fuel bill is a different question and may be the tenant's by agreement; keeping the system working is not.

title: No Association Leasing Statute - the Governing Documents Are All There Is
bodyText: South Dakota's only statute limiting what an association's governing documents may contain is about firearms, not renting: since 2024 an association may not include or enforce a governing-document provision restricting the lawful possession, transportation or storing of a firearm or ammunition, or lawful discharge. On renting there is nothing. The Condominium Act contains no lease-approval provision, no rental restriction, no cap on an association's approval fee, no provision for an association to hold a tenant deposit, no power for an association to demand rent from your tenant when you are behind on assessments, and no mechanism for a court to order rent paid into court for the association. There is no act of the kind that in other states lets an association intercept rent, nor one limiting what tenant information an association may require. What binds you is the declaration, covenants and bylaws of the association itself, as a matter of contract and recorded covenant - so if the documents require the association to approve a lease or a tenant, that requirement is real even though no statute mentions it, and if they say nothing, the association cannot invent an approval step. Two consequences are worth planning for. Because an association has no statutory right to your rent, a tenant who pays an association instead of you has not discharged the rent, and you can treat that as nonpayment - though the better course is to tell the tenant in writing before it happens. And because no statute caps the association's fees or segregates its deposit, any money the association takes from the tenant should be kept outside your lease, since money securing performance of your lease counts toward the one-month deposit cap. The cautious course is to attach the governing documents and make approval an express condition of the lease.

title: Money Taken to Hold a Unit Before Signing
bodyText: South Dakota has no holding-deposit or earnest-money statute for residential rentals. Nothing authorizes you to take money to hold a unit before a lease is signed, nothing caps that money separately, nothing sets a deadline for returning it, and nothing makes you pay it back doubled if you are the one who walks away. The deposit statute still reaches it, because any money whose function is to secure performance of a residential rental agreement is deemed a security deposit however it is denominated, and your ceiling is one month's rent. So money you take to hold a unit and then keep or apply when the tenant moves in counts toward that ceiling along with everything else you are holding. Before any agreement exists the function test is harder to apply, and the rule that decides the practical question is a different one: a fixed sum you keep because an applicant did not sign is a penalty for nonperformance, and South Dakota voids those. An agreed-damages figure survives only where actual damage would be impracticable or extremely difficult to fix, and a week of lost availability on one unit is usually neither. The cautious course is a short signed writing that says what the money is, that it will be applied to the first month's rent or to the deposit on signing, and that if the applicant does not sign you refund it less your documented actual holding costs. Keep the total of everything you hold within one month's rent. Charge any application or screening fee separately, price it at what the screening actually costs you, and never treat it as a stake on whether the lease gets signed.

title: No Home-Business Right - and a Specified-Purpose Lease Gives You Teeth
bodyText: South Dakota has no statute making a home-based business a permitted use of a residential dwelling, and none limiting a lease restriction on one. There is no home-occupation provision, no protected category of business, and no requirement that you permit any trade from a rented unit. Whether a tenant may run a business is yours to decide, and South Dakota gives you an unusually useful tool for enforcing the decision - but only if the lease is drafted to use it. Where premises are leased for a particular and specified purpose, the tenant must not use them for another purpose; and if the tenant does, you may either hold the tenant responsible for the safety of the premises during that use, at all events, or treat the contract as rescinded. The first limb is the valuable one: it shifts the risk of the unauthorised use onto the tenant without proof of fault for anything that happens while it continues, which is exactly the exposure a business in a dwelling creates. But it works only where the lease specified the purpose, so a lease reciting that the premises are let solely for use as a private residence by the named occupants is doing real work, while one silent on use is not. You may also terminate before the end of the term where the tenant uses the property contrary to the lease agreement, and a breach of a use covenant that operates to terminate the lease is itself an eviction ground. Zoning is a separate question and is local, so a permitted business under your lease may still breach a city ordinance. The cautious course is a specified-purpose clause plus a written-consent route.

title: A Homestead Waiver in a Lease Does Nothing Here
bodyText: A homestead waiver is a stock lease clause that has no work to do in a South Dakota residential tenancy, and some reason to be left out. South Dakota's homestead exemption protects an owner, not a tenant: the homestead of every family resident in the state, so long as it keeps the character of a homestead, is exempt from judicial sale, from judgment lien, and from all mesne or final process, to the extent provided by statute. A tenant has no homestead in the leased premises to give up, so a clause waiving homestead rights in the property you are renting out is empty. Read as a waiver of the tenant's exemption in property the tenant owns elsewhere, it runs into the structure of the exemption rather than any single prohibition. The exemption is statutory and attaches to the homestead itself; a conveyance or encumbrance of a homestead by a married owner is valid only if both spouses concur and sign, so a signature by one tenant on your lease could not reach a family homestead; and in the collection statutes the absolute exemptions are not waived even by a failure to claim them. There is no South Dakota statute validating a contractual homestead waiver, and none stating the waiver in statutory words the way some states do. The cautious course is to leave the clause out. It gains you nothing against a tenant, it is the kind of provision a court reads against the drafter, and a term that purports to strip a statutory family protection is a poor thing to have in a lease you may need a judge to enforce.

title: Immigration Status Is Not a Protected Class - But Asking Is Still a Live Risk
bodyText:
South Dakota's fair housing list is closed and immigration status is not on it. The statute names race, colour, creed, religion, sex, ancestry, disability, familial status and national origin, and nothing else. There is no immigrant tenant protection act, no bar on asking an applicant about citizenship or status, no bar on reporting a tenant, and equally no statute making it unlawful to rent to a person unlawfully present, no verification duty, no federal work-authorisation analogue for tenancies, and no harbouring offence that reaches letting a dwelling. The only place in the whole Code where a noncitizen is excluded from a tenancy is a county and municipal housing commission provision governing public housing projects, which does not reach your private units.

Do not read that silence as permission. Two of the nine protected grounds are national origin and ancestry, and a question about papers, accent, visa type or birthplace is the classic proxy for both. South Dakota also has a separate prohibition, broader than the list itself, that reaches any person who uses a form of application, a record or an inquiry of any kind to bring about or facilitate discrimination. An immigration question that in practice sorts applicants by where they are from can be unlawful under existing state law without immigration status ever being added to the list, and federal fair housing law covers national origin independently.

The cautious course is to ask every applicant the same identity and income questions, document the standard, and not ask about status, birthplace or visa category at all. Where you need to verify who someone is and that they can pay, ask for identification and proof of income without specifying a document only a citizen could produce.

title: Illness or Entering Care Does Not End a South Dakota Lease
bodyText: South Dakota gives no one a lease exit on grounds of age, illness, infirmity or a move into care. A tenant who can no longer live independently has no statutory right to terminate, a family member or guardian has no right to terminate on their behalf, and you have no right to terminate because a tenant has become unable to manage the premises. The single provision in this area cuts the other way. If a lease is terminable at the pleasure of one of the parties, it is terminated by notice to the other of that party's death or incapacity to contract; in every other case it is not terminated by death or incapacity. So an ordinary fixed-term lease survives, and the obligation runs on against the tenant's estate or successor. The tenant's real statutory exits are elsewhere and are narrow: your failure after a written request to give quiet possession or to put the premises in good condition or repair them, destruction of the greater part or of the part that was the material inducement, and the domestic abuse, unlawful sexual behaviour and stalking right. None of those is a health ground. The exposure you should actually plan for is the accommodation duty, which can require you to release or transfer a tenant with a disability even though no termination statute does. The cautious course is a conditional term you offer rather than one the tenant has to argue for: termination on sixty days' written notice supported by dated documentation from a licensed health care provider, with the tenant liable for rent to the termination date and for your documented actual re-letting cost. Do not set a flat fee, because a contractual penalty for nonperformance is void in South Dakota.

title: A Pre-Suit Step Is Risky Here - Arbitration Is the Exception
bodyText: South Dakota is an unusually unfriendly place for a clause requiring the parties to try something before going to court. The governing rule is blunt: every provision in a contract restricting a party from enforcing his rights under it by usual legal proceedings in ordinary tribunals, or limiting his time to do so, is void. A term making a tenant complete a mediation or internal complaint process, or wait out a period, before filing is a restriction on enforcing rights by the usual proceedings, so it is at serious risk of being struck - and the risk runs both ways, since the clause would bind you too when you want possession. The one carved-out route is arbitration. A written agreement to submit an existing controversy to arbitration, or a provision in a written contract to arbitrate a future one, is valid, enforceable and irrevocable save on grounds that would revoke any contract. So if you want a non-court forum, use an arbitration agreement rather than a home-made pre-suit condition. Even then, keep possession out of it: an eviction is a statutory summary proceeding with its own short timetable and a jury available on demand, and nothing is gained by sending possession to arbitration. The cautious course is to invite informal resolution without requiring it - say that either party may raise a concern in writing and that you will respond within a stated number of days, as a commitment rather than a condition - and to leave every statutory remedy and every limitation period untouched.

title: No Duty to Disclose Inspection or Condemnation Orders
bodyText: South Dakota requires no disclosure to a tenant of an outstanding inspection order, code violation notice, abatement order or condemnation proceeding. There is no statute making rent uncollectable while an order is outstanding, no statute voiding a lease signed after one, and no state housing inspectorate for rental dwellings to issue such an order in the first place. Condemnation in the state statutes means eminent domain, not a code officer declaring a building unfit; the single statutory condemnation power over buildings is a municipal one over fire-damaged structures within fire limits. The real mechanism is local. Where a city or county has adopted an ordinance prescribing standards for the maintenance of existing structures and premises, that ordinance must comply with the 2024 edition of the International Property Maintenance Code, and that code is where the inspection, the notice of violation, the unfit-for-occupancy placard and the vacate order actually live. Whether your city has adopted it, and what it then requires you to tell a tenant, is a local question this answer does not resolve. Two state rules shape how you handle one. Your habitability duty cannot be waived, and a tenant facing conditions you will not fix may repair and deduct or vacate and be discharged. Separately, a tenant who complains in good faith to a code enforcement body is protected against retaliation. The cautious course is to disclose an outstanding order in writing before signing, give the tenant a copy, say what you are doing about it and by when, and never treat the complaint that produced it as a ground to refuse renewal in a way that looks like reprisal.

title: Nothing Penalises a Missing Inspection Notice, and the Entry Notice Carries No Penalty Either
bodyText: The only residential inspections South Dakota penalises belong to the state fire marshal, and the penalty runs on ignoring an order rather than on skipping a notice. The marshal may inspect periodically, must get the occupant's consent or an inspection warrant except in an emergency, and on finding a violation must issue a written notice setting a compliance deadline matched to the hazard; it is then a misdemeanour for an owner or occupant to maintain the condition or disobey the order. Nothing in that machinery touches you as a private landlord taking a unit back. There is no rental registration, no occupancy certificate and no private-rental inspection regime in the state at all. So there is no move-in walk-through duty, no move-out inspection duty, no notice telling the tenant that either is available, and consequently no penalty for leaving one out. South Dakota has no counterpart to the states that make a missed inspection notice cost you the withheld deposit twice over or forfeit your right to withhold for damage. Notice that the entry statute is the same way. It tells you what an entry notice must say and presumes twenty-four hours in writing to be reasonable, but it attaches no damages, fine or forfeiture to entering without one. Your exposure for that is the general one: unlawful exclusion and interference with quiet enjoyment, and ordinary trespass. Where the real penalty sits is the deposit return, and it is strict rather than fault-based. The cautious course is therefore to run joint written condition reports with dated photographs at both ends even though no statute asks for them, and to calendar the deposit deadlines, because that is the failure that actually costs money.

title: Jury Waiver - Untested in South Dakota, and the Jury Is Real in Evictions
bodyText: Start with the question that decides whether a jury waiver is worth anything: is a jury available in a South Dakota eviction? It is. In a forcible entry and detainer action, if a jury trial is demanded and no jury is in attendance on the day the case is noticed for trial, the court must issue a special venire, impanel a jury and try the action as in other civil cases. So a jury is available on demand, which means a waiver clause would do real work - it would stop the tenant demanding one. Whether it would be enforced is the problem, and South Dakota has not answered it. The state constitution says the right of trial by jury shall remain inviolate and extends to all cases at law without regard to the amount in controversy. A general contract statute voids every provision restricting a party from enforcing his rights by usual legal proceedings in ordinary tribunals, or limiting the time to do so, with arbitration under the Uniform Arbitration Act expressly excepted. Neither provision names jury waivers. A waiver does not stop a tenant going to court, which is what that statute is aimed at, so there is a real argument it survives; but it does give up a right the constitution calls inviolate, and no South Dakota decision settling the point was found. The cautious course, and our recommendation: do not rely on a jury waiver in a South Dakota residential lease.
