Treat it as likely to be challenged and possibly struck, keep the rest of the lease standing on its own if it falls, and do not let it become the reason your default provisions are not drafted to survive a jury.

title: No Key-Control or Staff-Screening Mandate
bodyText: South Dakota imposes no key-control requirements on residential landlords and no background-check duty for employees with access to occupied units, whatever the size of the building. There is no master-key logging rule, no rekeying-between-tenancies requirement, no limit on who may hold a key and no statutory standard for a large complex. Two general rules are the ones that actually constrain you. Entry by anyone using your keys is your entry: except in an emergency or where it is impracticable, reasonable notice of the intent to enter is owed and entry must be at reasonable times, so a maintenance employee letting himself in is measured by the same standard you are. And negligence exposure is the reason to have a policy anyway - the duty to keep the premises and common areas in reasonable repair and in good and safe working order runs to the security hardware on the doors as much as to the plumbing, and the statute's provisions are expressly additional to any covenant imposed by law, ordinance or the lease. There is no statutory bar to your charging for keys, but mind the form: a flat key fee payable because the tenant lost something is a penalty for nonperformance and void, while the cost you actually pay to rekey is recoverable, and is deductible from the deposit as restoring the premises to their move-in condition. The cautious course is a written policy you can produce: rekey between tenancies, log who holds what, require keys back at move-out, and charge documented actual cost.

title: No Penalty for Knowingly Using an Unenforceable Term
bodyText: South Dakota has no penalty for putting an unenforceable term in a lease, however deliberately you do it. There is no list of prohibited provisions to offend against in the first place, no damages award for including one, no actual-damages-plus-a-month remedy of the kind uniform-act states use, and no attorney's fee award attached to the attempt. A term that is contrary to an express provision of law, or to the policy of express law, is simply unlawful, and the ordinary consequence is that it does not work. The clause fails; you are not fined for having written it. That is a weaker sanction than most states apply, but it is not nothing, and two things can convert a bad term into a real liability. The first is the deceptive trade practices statute, which makes it a deceptive act to knowingly use a deceptive act or practice, a false promise or misrepresentation, or to conceal, suppress or omit a material fact. A tenant adversely affected by that may sue for actual damages. Note the structure carefully, because it cuts your way: the presumption that such conduct was knowing and intentional is given only to the attorney general and state's attorneys, and is expressly withheld from a private action, so a tenant must prove your knowledge. Those actions run out after four years. The second is the deposit statute, where failing to comply forfeits all rights to withhold any portion, and bad faith carries a small punitive award. The cautious course is not to rely on the absence. Take unenforceable terms out rather than leaving them in to deter a tenant who will not know the difference, keep a severability clause, and never present a void term as though it bound the tenant, because presentation is where the deceptive exposure begins.

title: What a Tenant Can Recover When You Breach
bodyText: South Dakota puts the tenant's remedies in statute, and the money ones are sharper than landlords expect. Break the delivery and quiet enjoyment duty by unlawfully removing or excluding the tenant, or willfully cutting off electricity, gas, water or another essential service, and the tenant may seek an injunction, recover possession, or terminate, and in any case recover damages equal to two months' rent plus return of all advance rent and the deposit. That is a fixed sum you cannot argue down by showing the tenant's loss was smaller. Forcible exclusion from possession exposes you to treble damages under a separate statute. The repair and habitability duty cannot be waived or modified, bar one narrow exception for an agreement that the tenant do specified repairs or maintenance in lieu of rent. If you do not repair, the tenant may repair and deduct, or vacate and be discharged; and where the cost of necessary repairs exceeds one month's rent the tenant may, after written notice stating the specific reason, withhold the rent in a separate bank account kept only for the repairs. The tenant may also terminate if you fail to act within a reasonable time after a written request. Missing the deposit deadlines forfeits all rights to withhold anything, and bad-faith retention adds a small punitive award. Retaliating for a good-faith code complaint or a repair notice is its own cause of action, with the same two-months remedy and a possible attorney's fee award. The cautious course is to treat the fixed remedies as the real exposure and manage the triggers. Never resort to a lockout or utility shutoff, whatever the arrears; that one decision converts a rent dispute into a two-months-plus-deposit judgment. Answer written repair requests in writing and on a date. Do not disclaim any of this, and never shorten the tenant's time to sue; such terms are void.

title: No Insurance Mandate and No Registration Scheme
bodyText: South Dakota does not require a residential landlord to carry liability insurance, and has no rental registration scheme that conditions letting on proof of coverage. There is no minimum limit, no certificate to file, no inspection tied to insurance and no penalty for going without. Nothing requires you to name a tenant as an additional insured or to carry coverage for a tenant's property. That means your coverage decision is commercial rather than regulatory - but note what it does not change. The habitability duty is not waivable or modifiable, and your liability to third parties is expressly untouched by the habitability section, so being uninsured removes a backstop without reducing an obligation. If you have a mortgage, your lender's requirements are contractual and are usually stricter than anything the state would impose. And if a property is in a homeowners or condominium association, the association's governing documents commonly require coverage and name limits, which is also contractual. Two cautions on what a lease can and cannot do about insurance. You may require the tenant to carry a renter's policy, which is a lawful lease term, but a flat charge imposed because the tenant let it lapse is a penalty for nonperformance and void - the enforceable route is to treat the lapse as a breach. And you may not use the lease to transfer responsibility for your own violation of law or willful injury, because a provision exempting anyone from that is void. The cautious course is to carry coverage, require a renter's policy, and ask for a certificate at move-in and renewal.

title: No Landlord Registration or Rental Licence
bodyText: South Dakota has no landlord registration, no rental licence and no occupancy precondition tied to either. There is no owner registration with the county assessor, no tenant termination right for an unregistered owner, no requirement that an out-of-state owner employ an in-state licensed broker or appoint an in-state contact for tenant communications, and no general business-licence law reaching residential rentals. Letting a property in your own name requires nothing of you at state level, but two general business filings can apply. If your rental business uses a name that does not plainly show the true surname of each person interested in it, and is not a name already on file with the Secretary of State, you must file a fictitious name statement, renewed every five years, and until you do you may not maintain any legal action in that name or recover anything due from the business (SDCL 37-11-1 and 37-11-5). And an out-of-state limited liability company that owns income-producing property here must obtain a certificate of authority, naming an in-state agent for service of process, before it can sue (see `edu-no-nonresident-owner-agent-rule-sd`). Two qualifications. Municipal ordinances are the real source of rental registration and licensing in South Dakota, and they are not resolved here - some cities do operate registration or inspection programmes, often tied to occupancy limits in low-density districts, and the consequences of non-registration are whatever the ordinance says. Check your city before assuming the absence helps you. And if you engage someone to manage the property for you, the licensing question shifts to them rather than to you: a property manager is a person who for consideration negotiates or attempts to negotiate a rental or lease, lists rentals or leases, or collects or attempts to collect rents, and a residential rental agent is a person associated with a broker or property manager who does those things. Collecting rent for someone else is a licensed activity; letting your own property is not. There is an exemption for a person contracting with the South Dakota Housing Development Authority or the United States to operate housing units. The cautious course is to confirm your city's position in writing once and keep it.

title: Possession and Money, Together or Separately
bodyText: South Dakota lets you pursue possession and money without choosing between them, and lets you sue for the money before the tenancy ends. The possession action may not be joined with any claim except rents and profits or damages, which you may also sue for separately. A judgment for you delivers possession and awards what you claimed, with costs, and the court may tax reasonable attorney fees to the prevailing party - either side - if represented by a licensed attorney. The damages come from a different chapter. The residual measure is the value of the use of the property for the time of occupation, up to six years, plus your costs of recovering possession. Double the rent applies where the tenant gave notice of an intention to leave and then stayed, and double the yearly value for wilfully holding over after the term where a notice to quit was duly given and possession demanded - which is the reason to serve both even though neither is needed to file. Your early-termination grounds are use of the premises contrary to the lease agreement and failure to repair after request. Do not accelerate the remaining rent: a contractual penalty for nonperformance is void here, and claiming the documented shortfall is the safe route. South Dakota also gives you a second route for one kind of breach, and it is unusually strong. Where a tenant for years commits waste, the person entitled to the reversion may sue for treble damages, forfeiture of the estate and eviction - the last two only where the injury is adjudged equal to the value of the unexpired term, or malicious. For serious deliberate damage that beats an ordinary damages claim, and waste is separately a filing ground in its own right.

title: No Late-Fee Cap - but the Figure Still Has to Be Defensible
bodyText: South Dakota sets no cap on a late fee. There is no percentage limit, no dollar ceiling, no mandatory grace period and no rule about when a fee may first be charged. That freedom is more qualified than it looks, because South Dakota voids contractual penalties outright: a penalty imposed by contract for any nonperformance is void, and a sum agreed in advance as damages is enforceable only where the parties fix an amount presumed to be the damage for breach in a case where it would be impracticable or extremely difficult to fix the actual damage. A late fee is exactly the provision that test was written for. A figure that plausibly represents what late payment costs you - the administrative work, the lost use of the money, the cost of chasing it - is a permitted estimate. A figure set to punish, or one that compounds daily without limit into something far beyond any conceivable loss, is a penalty and unenforceable, and the larger it is the more obviously so. Two practical consequences. Choose a modest flat amount or a low percentage with a stated cap, apply it consistently, and be able to explain how you arrived at it; the explanation is what makes it an estimate rather than a penalty. And remember a late fee is not rent: the eviction ground is written about a lessee who fails to pay rent for three days after it is due, so an eviction resting on unpaid fees rather than unpaid rent is a weaker filing.

title: No Duty to Cooperate With Police - and One Duty to Act
bodyText:
South Dakota imposes no cooperation duty on a landlord. No statute aimed at landlords requires you to report tenant conduct to police, to answer a request for tenant information, to hand over a lease or a rent ledger, to run a crime-free addendum, to attend a nuisance-property meeting, or to evict on a police referral. There is no crime-free lease statute and no chronic-nuisance property scheme in state law. The one place the leasing chapter mentions law enforcement is a prohibition aimed at you: a residential lease may not contain any term authorising the eviction of a tenant who calls or seeks help from law enforcement or other emergency responders over domestic abuse, unlawful sexual behaviour or stalking.

Against that, one real duty runs the other way, and it is criminal. Knowingly permitting a place you own, manage, supervise or control to be regularly used for prostitution, or failing to make reasonable effort to abate that use by ejecting the tenant, notifying law enforcement or using other legally available means, is a felony. That is a duty to act on what you know, not a duty to cooperate with a request. A second duty binds you as it binds anyone: a person who has knowledge, not privileged, that a felony has been committed and conceals it, or does not immediately disclose it to the proper authorities with the perpetrator's name if known and the other relevant known facts, commits misprision of a felony, a Class 1 misdemeanor; there is no misprision of a misdemeanor or petty offence, or of drug use by ingestion (SDCL 22-11-12). So if you or your staff know, not merely suspect, that a felony was committed at the property, report it. The child-abuse and elder-abuse reporting duties bind listed professionals and care staff, not landlords as such, though anyone may report (SDCL 26-8A-3, 22-46-9 and 22-46-10). And if a tenant dies in an unnatural or unexplained way, don't move the body from the scene without the coroner's permission; doing so is a Class 2 misdemeanor (SDCL 23-14-18 and 23-14-19). Separately, the general nuisance law lets a prosecutor or a neighbour move against a property, and municipalities hold their own abatement powers, so a local crime-free or nuisance ordinance may bind you where the state does not.

The cautious course is to answer legal compulsion and only legal compulsion: a subpoena, a warrant or a court order gets the documents, a request over the phone does not. Where a tenant ended the lease under the domestic-abuse provision, you may not give out their forwarding address to anyone without their consent unless the law requires it, and a police request is not by itself that requirement.

title: No State Lead-Safe Certificate to Attach
bodyText: South Dakota has no lead statute of any kind. There is no state lead-safe or lead-free certificate, no state inspection or clearance programme, no registry of certified units, and therefore nothing for you to obtain and nothing to attach to a lease as an exhibit. The states that require a certificate as a lease attachment built a state licensing and clearance apparatus behind it, and South Dakota built none. The word appears in the Code only in a highway description and a battery-recycling provision. The one place lead surfaces in South Dakota law is the seller's mandated property-condition disclosure statement, whose hazardous-conditions table asks a seller whether lead paint exists and whether a test has been performed, and that form runs on a transfer to a buyer rather than on a letting. FEDERAL: the real obligation on you is federal and it is not a certificate. For target housing built before 1978 you must give the lessee the lead hazard information pamphlet, disclose the presence of any known lead-based paint or lead-based paint hazards or state that you have no knowledge, list any available records and reports or state there are none, include the verbatim lead warning statement and the signed acknowledgements in the lease, and retain the records for three years. Renovation for compensation in such housing must be done by a certified firm following lead-safe work practices. The cautious course is to treat the federal disclosure as the complete obligation, use the library's lead-based paint clause rather than invent a certificate, and keep any inspection or risk-assessment report you do hold, because once it exists you must list it.

title: The Federal Package Is the Whole Lead Package
bodyText: South Dakota adds nothing to the federal lead disclosure. There is no state lead-paint notice, no state pamphlet or packet to hand over with the lease, no state-prescribed lease addendum or rider, no notice to repeat at renewal, no tenant notification when work disturbs paint, no registry to enrol in and no reporting duty on you if a child in your building is found to have an elevated blood lead level. The word lead does not appear in the landlord and tenant law, and there is no lead article in the state administrative code either. So for a pre-1978 rental your obligation is the federal one and only the federal one: the lead hazard information pamphlet, the written disclosure of known lead-based paint and hazards or a statement that you have none, the list of available records and reports or a statement that there are none, the prescribed warning statement, and the signed acknowledgements attached to the lease and kept for three years. Renovation for compensation in that housing has its own federal certified-firm and work-practice rules. Resist the instinct to dress the federal package up as a state one. A notice that tells a South Dakota tenant the state requires something it does not is a misstatement you gain nothing from, and it invites the argument that you promised more than the law asks. The cautious course is to use the library's federal lead clause unchanged, attach the federal pamphlet, keep the signed acknowledgement with the lease file for three years, and treat deteriorated paint as what it is under state law in any building of any age, a condition requiring repair under the habitability duty you cannot waive.

title: Nothing Has to Appear in the Lease, Anywhere
bodyText: South Dakota prescribes no lease content and no layout. Nothing must appear on the first page, the start and end dates need not be displayed anywhere in particular, there is no required caption or section structure, no mandatory font or type size, and no attachment or cover sheet. The only requirement touching the document at all is the writing rule for longer tenancies: an agreement to lease for more than one year must be in writing, or evidenced by a note or memorandum, signed by the lessor or an agent authorised in writing. Beyond that the form is entirely yours. Because nothing is mandated, the lease is purely an instrument of your own protection, and the items worth putting in it are the ones the statutes leave to agreement rather than the ones a statute would have forced. Four stand out. The amount and timing of rent, because the statutory default is rent payable in arrears unless the lease says otherwise. Every non-optional charge with its amount and purpose, because a charge the lease does not create is not funds due to you under an agreement and is not recoverable from the deposit. The permitted use, stated specifically, because that is what unlocks the risk-shifting and rescission remedies for an unauthorised use. And any entry arrangement you want to differ from the default, because the statute lets the lease agree alternate methods of notification or times for entry. The cautious course is a lease organised by headings with those four settled explicitly, and a copy given to the tenant even though nothing requires it.

title: No Duty to Give the Tenant a Copy - Do It Anyway
bodyText: No South Dakota statute requires you to give the tenant a copy of the signed lease, and no South Dakota statute makes a failure to do so a defense to enforcing it. Nor does the duty arrive through the licensing laws: South Dakota's real estate licensing chapter, which defines both property managers and residential rental agents and sets out what a licensee owes a customer, imposes no obligation to deliver a copy of a lease to a tenant. A transaction broker must perform the written agreement, exercise reasonable skill and care, present offers in a timely manner, account for money and property, comply with fair housing and civil rights law, and disclose adverse material facts known to the licensee - a list that does not include handing over the document. What South Dakota does require is a writing in the first place for the longer tenancies: an agreement to lease real property for more than one year is invalid unless it, or a note or memorandum of it, is in writing and signed by the lessor or an agent authorized in writing. Note where that cuts - the signature the statute demands is the lessor's. Give the tenant a copy regardless, and keep proof that you did. Nothing is gained by withholding it, and a tenant who cannot produce the lease is a tenant whose understanding of the terms will be decided on testimony rather than on the document you drafted.

title: Nothing Must Be Initialled, and Typeface Will Not Save a Bad Term
bodyText: South Dakota's formality rules for a residential lease are thinner than you probably expect. A letting for longer than a year has to be in writing, and the signature the statute asks for is yours as lessor, or that of an agent you authorised in writing. Your tenant's signature is not a statutory requirement at all, and nothing anywhere requires a tenant to initial a clause, to sign a particular term separately, or to acknowledge a disclosure in a prescribed box. There is no minimum type size, no boldface requirement, no capitals requirement and no prescribed heading for any residential lease provision. The state does prescribe type size, but for other transactions altogether, chiefly door-to-door consumer sales and residential roofing contracts. This matters because initials and bold print do less work here than they do elsewhere. What decides whether your term stands is its substance. A provision contrary to an express provision of law, or to the policy of express law, is unlawful; a penalty fixed by contract for a breach is void; and a term stopping a party from enforcing its rights by the usual legal proceedings, or shortening the time to do so, is void. None of those turn on how you typeset the clause, so no amount of initialling rescues a void term and no amount of small print defeats a lawful one. The cautious course is still to have every adult occupant sign, to have the tenant initial each page and separately initial anything unusual or rights-limiting - a fee, an optional service, an animal term, a waiver - and to keep the signed copy. Treat those initials as evidence the tenant saw the term, never as the thing that makes it enforceable.

title: No Duty to Record a Residential Lease
bodyText: South Dakota requires no registration or recording of a residential lease with any registry, and recording changes no statutory right between you and your tenant. A lease is valid and fully enforceable unrecorded, subject only to the writing requirement for terms longer than one year. Recording is permissive and matters for a different purpose: priority against third parties. That is the point worth knowing, and it cuts against tenants rather than landlords. South Dakota's foreclosure notice scheme reaches persons with a recorded interest - the published notice of sale names those claiming a recorded lien, encumbrance or other recorded ownership interest, and written notice of the sale goes to the mortgagor and to lien holders and encumbrancers whose interest would be affected. A residential tenant holding an unrecorded lease is neither named nor served, which is why a tenant can first learn of a foreclosure when a stranger appears claiming possession. So the practical consequence of South Dakota's silence is that an ordinary tenancy is invisible to the land records. For most residential lettings that is fine and recording would be an unnecessary expense. For a long lease, a lease with an option to purchase, or one where a tenant has invested in the property, recording protects the tenant against a later purchaser or mortgagee, and a tenant may ask for it. The cautious course is to say in the lease whether recording is permitted and who bears the cost, so the question is settled rather than argued.

title: Term Caps Exist - but Not for Ordinary Housing
bodyText: South Dakota does cap lease terms, though not the ones most landlords deal with. No lease or grant of agricultural land for longer than twenty years, reserving any rent or service, is valid; and no lease or grant of a municipal lot for longer than ninety-nine years, reserving rent or service, is valid. Both are property-policy limits against perpetual tenures rather than housing rules, and neither touches an ordinary residential lease of a house or apartment, for which South Dakota sets no maximum term. Formalities are light. A lease for more than one year must be in writing, or evidenced by a note or memorandum, signed by the lessor or an agent authorised in writing - and note what that requires and what it does not: the lessor's signature, not a seal, not an acknowledgment before a notary, not the tenant's signature, and no spousal consent. South Dakota requires no particular execution formality for a long residential lease and no co-signature from a married owner's spouse for a lease, although a conveyance or encumbrance of a homestead does need both spouses, which is a different transaction. Two practical points follow. A lease for a term of years that is not in writing signed by you is not a valid agreement for that term, which means a tenant occupying under it is holding on some shorter periodic basis - and the renewal presumptions then decide what that is. And because there is no residential cap, a long lease is enforceable; if you grant one, deal expressly with rent review, assignment and what happens on a sale.

title: No Parity Rule Between Lease Types
bodyText: South Dakota has no provision requiring parity between tenancy types. Nothing bars terms that are more burdensome for a month-to-month tenant than for a fixed-term tenant or the reverse, nothing caps the rent difference between them, and nothing requires you to offer a fixed term at all. You may price and draft the two differently, and charging a premium for month-to-month flexibility is lawful. What South Dakota does instead is give the two types genuinely different mechanics, and the differences are yours to use rather than to equalise. A month-to-month tenancy is the only one you can change unilaterally: you may modify the terms, rent included, on written notice given at least thirty days before the end of the month, and the tenant's counterweight is a right to terminate effective the first of the next month by notifying you within fifteen days of receipt. A fixed term cannot be changed that way - the rent is what the lease says until the term ends. Ending them differs too: a tenancy at will ends on not less than fifteen days' written notice, while a fixed term simply expires, with no nonrenewal notice required. And the renewal presumptions bite on both: accepting rent from a holdover presumes a renewal on the same terms for up to a year. The cautious course is to be deliberate about which type you are granting and to make sure the lease's notice and termination provisions match it, because a form written for one and used for the other is where disputes start.

title: No Minimum Type Size for a Lease
bodyText: South Dakota sets no minimum type size for a residential lease, and attaches no evidentiary sanction to small print. There is no point-size floor for the whole document, none for particular clauses, no bold-face or conspicuous-type requirement for any term, and no rule making an unreadably printed agreement inadmissible or unenforceable. Some states do exactly that - excluding from evidence a printed contract set in type below a stated size - and South Dakota has nothing comparable. Nor does it require captions, section divisions or a particular layout. So the format of your lease is unregulated, and no clause needs to be dressed up to be effective. Two reasons to use readable type anyway. South Dakota's deceptive practices chapter reaches the concealment, suppression or omission of a material fact in connection with a consumer transaction, whether or not anyone was actually misled, and a material term rendered in type nobody would read is nearer to concealment than the same term set plainly - which is a risk created by the formatting rather than cured by it. And unconscionability remains available to a tenant as a general contract doctrine, where the manner of presentation is part of what a court looks at. The cautious course is ordinary readable type throughout, with the terms a tenant would most want to know - the rent and when it is due, every other charge, the entry rules, the termination notice and what can be deducted from the deposit - set out plainly rather than compressed.

title: Six Years to Sue - and You Cannot Shorten It by Lease
bodyText: South Dakota gives you six years to sue on a lease. Except where a different limitation is prescribed, an action upon a contract, obligation or liability, express or implied, must be commenced within six years after the cause of action accrued - which covers a claim for unpaid rent, for damage beyond ordinary wear and tear, and for any other breach of the lease. A judgment, once you have one, lasts far longer: an action upon a judgment of a South Dakota court runs for twenty years. The limitation is not self-executing; the objection that an action was not commenced in time can only be taken by answer or other responsive pleading, so a tenant who does not plead it waives it. Now the part that matters for drafting, and it is unusual. You cannot shorten the period in the lease. Every provision in a contract restricting a party from enforcing their rights by usual legal proceedings in ordinary tribunals, or limiting the time to do so, is void - and a clause requiring a tenant to bring any claim within one year, or to give notice of a claim within thirty days as a condition of suing, is precisely a limitation on the time to do so. Those clauses are common in leases drafted for other states and they do not survive here. South Dakota has no statute saying whether a partial payment restarts the period for a rent claim, so do not rely on one; the cautious course is to date your claim from the earliest unpaid instalment and sue well inside six years.

title: Liquidated Damages Survive Only on a Narrow Test
bodyText: South Dakota is hostile to agreed-damages clauses and the test is narrow. Penalties imposed by contract for any nonperformance are void. A term fixing damages in advance is void too, except that the parties may agree on an amount presumed to be the damage for breach in cases where it would be impracticable or extremely difficult to fix the actual damage. So the clause survives only where two things are true: the sum is a genuine pre-estimate of loss, and the loss is one that would be impracticable or extremely difficult to quantify after the event. Most lease charges fail the second limb rather than the first, because what a breach actually costs a landlord is usually a receipt - a cleaning invoice, a re-letting advertisement, a locksmith, the rent for the days a unit sat empty. Where the number is ascertainable, an agreed figure is a penalty however reasonable it looks. There is no consumer regulation here expressly permitting retention of an agreed sum for a tenant's breach, so nothing softens that. One useful point of relief: a penalty clause does not poison the lease. The penalty statute voids the penal clause, not the obligation it is attached to - the offending clause fails, the agreement stands. The cautious course is to charge documented actual cost for everything you can measure, and to reserve an agreed figure for the rare item that is genuinely hard to value, with the lease explaining why.

title: No Opt-In Lockout - Locking Out Is the Most Expensive Mistake Available
bodyText: A few states let a landlord lock out a delinquent tenant if the lease opts in, with advance notice and a right to a key on request. South Dakota has nothing of the kind, and the absence is emphatic rather than accidental. If a lessor of residential property unlawfully removes or excludes the tenant from the premises, or wilfully diminishes services by interrupting electric, gas, water or other essential service, the tenant may sue for an injunction, recover possession by suit, or terminate the rental agreement - and in any case recover damages equal to two months' rent plus the return of all advance rent and deposit paid. A second statute makes it worse: for forcibly ejecting or excluding a person from possession of real property, the measure of damages is three times the sum that would compensate for the harm caused. Whether a tenant can recover under both is unsettled, so plan on the larger exposure. None of that depends on whether the tenant owed rent, and no lease term can authorise it, because a provision contrary to the policy of express law is unlawful and one exempting you from responsibility for a violation of law is void. The lawful route is the only route: once rent has been unpaid for three days the eviction ground exists and you may file. South Dakota's procedure is quick by design - the appearance is five days from service - so the legal route is rarely slower than the unlawful one and never costs two months' rent.

title: One Way to Shift Repairs - and It Has to Buy Rent
bodyText: South Dakota lets you move repair and maintenance work onto a tenant in exactly one way, and a lease that tries any other way does not work. The habitability section cannot be waived or modified by agreement. Attached to that bar is a single exception: you may agree with the tenant that the tenant will perform specified repairs or maintenance in lieu of rent. Read the exception's words closely, because each one is a condition. The work must be specified, so a clause saying the tenant is responsible for repairs, or for everything under a dollar figure, is not inside the exception and is void. It must be in lieu of rent, so a rent credit is not a nicety but the consideration that makes the arrangement lawful - swapping repairs for anything else, or for nothing, falls outside. And since nothing else in the section may be touched, you keep the duty to keep the premises and all common areas in reasonable repair, fit for human habitation and in good and safe working order, and to maintain the electrical, plumbing and heating systems. There is no general permission to shift a listed condition on a precondition, and no provision letting a shift ride on consideration plus a conspicuous writing. In practice this suits the arrangements landlords actually want - yard work, snow clearing, filter changes - and rules out the arrangement they often draft, which is a blanket transfer of repair responsibility. The cautious course is to list each task, state a monthly rent reduction for it, keep the licensed trades and the systems yourself, and treat non-performance as rent falling due rather than as a repair debt.

title: Repairs or Maintenance in Lieu of Rent
bodyText: [Optional. This is the only way South Dakota permits any part of Landlord's repair and habitability duty to be performed by Tenant. Do not use a term that simply makes Tenant responsible for repairs - it is void. List each item of work specifically, and give a rent credit for it.] Repairs or Maintenance in Lieu of Rent: Landlord and Tenant agree that Tenant will perform the following specified repairs or maintenance, and that Tenant's performance of them is in lieu of rent: [list each item of work specifically, for example: mowing and trimming the yard between April 1 and October 31; clearing snow from the walks and drive within 24 hours of a snowfall; replacing furnace filters quarterly with filters Landlord supplies]. For each month in which Tenant performs the work described above, the Rent otherwise payable is reduced by [amount] per month. If Tenant does not perform the work in a month, the full Rent for that month is due and Landlord may, after giving Tenant written notice and a reasonable time to perform, perform the work or have it performed and charge Tenant the reasonable cost actually incurred. Tenant will perform the work in a workmanlike manner and will not be required to do any work that requires a licensed trade. Landlord keeps every other obligation to maintain the premises and the common areas, including all electrical, plumbing and heating systems, and this Section does not waive or modify any of them.

title: No Conservation Charge or Submetered-Water Rules
bodyText: South Dakota has no energy-efficiency conservation charge for rentals, and no notice duty or rent-deduction remedy attached to one. It also has no submetered-water regime: nothing exempts a landlord who furnishes water from utility regulation on condition of charging the city or district rate, nothing bars a surcharge for the meter itself, and nothing requires a monthly statement showing both meter readings. States that regulate this do all of it; South Dakota does none. What constrains you is the single cap that runs through every utility question here. Knowingly charging a consumer of gas or electricity more than the amount the utility actually billed exposes you to a civil fine of up to five hundred dollars, with electric-vehicle charging the only express exception. Note the limit of that cap: it is written about gas and electricity, so water is not within its terms, and a water surcharge is therefore governed by the lease and by general law rather than by it. That does not make a water markup safe, because a charge the lease does not create is not funds due to you under an agreement and so is not collectible from the deposit, and a charge representing a service you did not provide is a deceptive-practice risk. The cautious course is to bill any metered utility at the amount billed to you, show the readings and the arithmetic on the statement, and keep a conservation or efficiency charge out of the lease unless it pays for something the tenant actually receives.

title: No Military Air Zone Disclosure - but a Military Tenant Gets Longer Notice
bodyText: South Dakota requires no military air installation disclosure in a lease. There is no noise zone or accident potential zone disclosure, no disclosure keyed to a set distance from a named installation, no military impact district disclosure, and no thirty-day termination right triggered by one. The state does regulate land around airfields, but it does so through zoning rather than disclosure: local airport layout plans and zoning regulations govern permitted land uses and runway protection zones, and an airport hazard is treated as a public nuisance. Those rules may restrict what can be built near a field; none of them obliges you to tell a tenant that the unit sits under a flight path. What South Dakota does for military households is quite different and worth knowing, because it cuts against you. On a residential tenancy at will your notice to terminate is normally not less than fifteen days, but it extends to two months where the tenant or an immediate family member is on active military service, unless the tenancy ends for sustained disruptive, illegal, destructive or negligent conduct or material breach, or you have sold the property or it has passed to your estate. The cautious course on the zone question is to disclose aircraft noise in writing before signing where the property is genuinely affected, and to say plainly in the lease that aircraft noise is not a condition you control and not a ground for abatement, because an undisclosed unlivable noise level invites a habitability argument you do not want. Separately, confirm the tenant's military status at signing so you apply the right notice period later.

title: A Minor Cannot Make a Lease in South Dakota
bodyText: This is one of the places South Dakota differs sharply from most states, and getting it wrong costs you the lease. A minor in South Dakota is a person under eighteen. In most states a minor's contract is valid but voidable, so a lease signed by a seventeen-year-old binds you and binds the tenant until the tenant disaffirms it. South Dakota does not put a residential lease in that category at all: no minor may make a contract relating to real property, or any interest therein. A lease is a contract relating to an interest in real property, so there is no lease to disaffirm - there is no valid lease. Everything else a minor signs is treated differently, which is why this is easy to miss: a minor may make any other contract subject only to a power of disaffirmance, exercisable before majority or within a year afterwards, and with the consideration restored where the minor was sixteen or older when contracting. A minor also cannot disaffirm a contract to pay the reasonable value of things necessary for support, which is what gives you a claim for the reasonable value of shelter actually provided even where there is no enforceable lease - but that is a restitution claim, not your lease terms, and it does not carry your late fees, your deposit terms or your remedies. The practical rule is simple: do not accept a tenant under eighteen as a signing party. Put an adult on the lease as the tenant, or take an adult guarantor who signs in their own right, and verify age before signing.

title: No Mold Disclosure or Remediation Standard
bodyText: South Dakota has no mold statute. Nothing requires you to disclose mold or a mold history to a tenant, no state agency sets a permissible level or a clearance standard, no rule prescribes remediation methods or who pays, and there is no mold addendum the state obliges you to use. Mold does appear in one South Dakota form, and knowing which one matters: the mandated seller's property-condition disclosure statement asks a seller whether mold exists on the property and whether a test has been performed. That form runs on a transfer to a buyer and has nothing to say to an ordinary letting. A lease with an option to purchase is a transfer under that chapter, so it does need the form. So the whole subject falls to the habitability duty. You must keep a residential premises and its common areas in reasonable repair and fit for human habitation, and that duty cannot be waived or modified by the lease, which means a mold addendum purporting to shift responsibility for a leaking roof or a failed bathroom fan onto the tenant will not hold. The tenant's side is real too: the tenant must preserve the premises and answers for deterioration caused by their own negligent, willful or malicious conduct, so condensation from never running the fan or blocked vents is fairly the tenant's. The cautious course is a mold clause that does the work the statute will support: require prompt written notice of visible mold or water intrusion, oblige the tenant to ventilate and to keep the unit reasonably heated, give yourself access to inspect and remediate, and charge the tenant the documented actual cost only where the cause is traced to the tenant's conduct. Never a flat mold fee, because contractual penalties for nonperformance are void. Disclose a known active problem before signing.

title: Unpaid Municipal Solid-Waste Fees Can Reach Your Property Tax
bodyText: This is the South Dakota exposure most landlords do not know about. A municipality, county or subdivision may levy solid-waste fees, charges and licences under a published fee schedule, and if such a fee becomes delinquent - other than a municipal garbage collection fee - the delinquency may be certified to the county treasurer and must be collected by the treasurer the following year as a condition precedent to payment of the real property tax on the very lot or parcel the fee was levied on. In practice that means you cannot pay the property tax without clearing the charge, whoever ran it up. A delinquent municipal garbage collection fee is handled differently but is no less yours: the municipality's chief fiscal officer must collect it as a condition precedent to the payment of any water, sewer, utility or other charge collected by the municipality. So the unpaid fee blocks your other municipal accounts instead of the tax. South Dakota gives you no statutory escape. There is no owner-exemption provision, no affidavit you can file with the utility to disclaim a tenant's bill, and no notice you are entitled to before the charge is certified - all of which some states provide. Water and sewer charges themselves are set by ordinance and sewer charges are commonly collected with water rentals, so the same practical risk runs through the municipal account. The cautious course is to keep the municipal solid-waste and water accounts in your own name and build the cost into rent, or, if the tenant holds them, require proof of payment before returning the deposit and check the municipal account before each move-out.

title: There Is No Pay-or-Quit Notice in South Dakota
bodyText: This is the single biggest difference between South Dakota and almost every other state, and it cuts in the landlord's favour. There is no statutory pay-or-quit notice for unpaid rent. No verbatim wording, no three-day or five-day demand, no state-agency form, no proof-of-delivery requirement, no mediation precondition, no move-in acknowledgment, and no once-a-year tender defence. The former notice section was repealed outright in 2024. The eviction ground stands on its own: a forcible entry and detainer action lies where a lessee holds over after the termination of the lease or expiration of the term, or fails to pay rent for three days after it is due. Those three days are not a notice period you must serve - they are simply when the ground matures. You may file once rent has been unpaid for three days. Two qualifications matter more here than the statute does. If your own lease promises a notice or a cure period before you act, that promise binds you as a contract term even though the statute does not require it, so read your lease before filing - a landlord in breach of its own notice clause is a landlord with a weaker case. And a tenancy at will is different: ending one requires written notice to remove within not less than fifteen days, served on the tenant or a person of discretion residing on the premises, or posted conspicuously. The cautious course is to decide deliberately whether you want a notice clause at all; if you do not need one, do not write one in.

title: Calling a Deposit Nonrefundable Does Not Make It So
bodyText: South Dakota has no statute requiring you to give notice that a deposit is nonrefundable, for the straightforward reason that South Dakota does not recognize a nonrefundable residential deposit at all. Any money you take to secure the tenant's performance is a security deposit whatever the lease calls it - a nonrefundable cleaning deposit, a redecorating fee, an administrative deposit - and once it is a security deposit it carries every deposit rule with it. It counts against the one-month cap, it must be returned or accounted for on the statutory timetable, and it may be withheld only for rent defaults, other funds due to you under an agreement, and restoring the premises to their move-in condition with ordinary wear and tear excepted. A label does not change any of that, and the penalty for getting it wrong is severe: a lessor who fails to comply forfeits all rights to withhold any portion of the deposit, and bad-faith retention exposes you to punitive damages. If you want money you can keep regardless of condition, charge it as rent or as a stated non-deposit fee for a service you actually provide, price it into the rent, and do not call it a deposit. If you want to be able to deduct for cleaning or damage, take a deposit and follow the deposit rules.

title: No Separate Signed Notice - and None Would Help
bodyText: South Dakota requires no separate document for any term of a residential lease, and nothing at all for a charge you want to call nonrefundable. No statute obliges you to set such a charge out in its own writing, to have it separately signed or initialled, to place it above the signature line, to use a particular type size, or to hand it over as a standalone notice before signing. The chapter governing leases of real property carries exactly one writing formality, that a lease for more than a year be in writing signed by the lessor, and says nothing about how individual terms are presented. The consequence is the one landlords tend to get backwards. In the states that require a separate signed notice, that signature is the thing that makes a nonrefundable charge enforceable. South Dakota has no such mechanism, so there is no ritual available that would validate the charge. A separately signed page in which the tenant agrees a deposit is nonrefundable changes nothing, because function controls: money taken to secure the tenant's performance is a security deposit whatever the paper says and however many times the tenant signs it. The cautious course is to stop looking for a signature that cures the problem and fix the structure instead. If you want money you may keep regardless of condition, charge it as rent or as the stated price of a service you actually supply, and do not call it a deposit or describe it as nonrefundable. If you want to deduct for cleaning or damage, take a deposit inside the cap and follow the return rules. Separate initials are still worth collecting as evidence the tenant read a term, but treat them as proof of notice and never as a cure.

title: Out-of-State Owners: No Lease Agent Rule, but Entities Must Register
bodyText: South Dakota does not require a non-resident individual owner of residential rental property to name an in-state agent, in the lease or anywhere else. An out-of-state limited liability company is different: owning income-producing real property in South Dakota counts as transacting business here, so it must obtain a certificate of authority from the Secretary of State, naming an agent for service of process in this state, and until it has one it may not maintain an eviction or any other action in a South Dakota court; its leases stay valid, and while it is unregistered it is treated as having appointed the Secretary of State as its agent for service of process (SDCL 47-34A-1002, 47-34A-1003 and 47-34A-1008). An out-of-state corporation transacting business here without a certificate of authority faces the same bar on suing, but owning property 'without more' is not transacting business for a corporation, so whether renting it out is more than that is a question to take advice on (SDCL 47-1A-1501 and 47-1A-1502). If you rent under a name that does not plainly show your true surname, you must file a fictitious name statement before you can sue in that name (see `edu-confirmed-absences-outside-title-sd`). And anyone who owns property in South Dakota can be sued here on a claim arising from it, wherever they live (SDCL 15-7-2). There is also no withholding on rent paid to a non-resident owner, for the simple reason that South Dakota levies no personal income tax - so the withholding regimes some states operate, with their exemptions for small portfolios and for a tenant's own home, have nothing to attach to here. Nor is an agent-designation requirement hidden in a receivership or code-enforcement chapter: no such scheme exists. Two things still make an in-state contact worth having. Service of a notice is the first. A notice terminating a tenancy at will must be served on the tenant or on a person of discretion residing on the premises, or posted conspicuously if neither can be found with reasonable diligence - that is service on the tenant, but it has to be done by someone, and an out-of-state owner without a local contact tends to discover that late. The second is that the tenant's repair remedies run from notice to the lessor, so where the tenant sends a repair notice, and whether it reaches you promptly, decides when your reasonable time starts and whether a tenant can lawfully repair and deduct. The cautious course is to name a single local contact for notices in the lease with an address, phone and email, and - if that person collects rent for you - to confirm they hold the licence that activity requires.

title: No Authorized Notice-Service Fee - Charge Nothing, or Charge Actual Cost
bodyText: No South Dakota statute authorizes a fee for preparing, posting, serving or delivering a notice to the tenant, and none sets an amount for one. Where a state permits such a charge it names it and caps it; South Dakota does neither, which leaves the charge standing or falling on general contract law. It mostly falls. A flat sum the tenant owes because you had to serve a notice is a penalty imposed by contract for nonperformance, and those are void; an agreed figure substituting for damages is enforceable only where actual damage would be impracticable or extremely difficult to fix, which is not true of a notice you prepared yourself or paid someone a known amount to serve. There is also little to charge for. A termination notice may be served by delivering it to the tenant or to a person of discretion residing on the premises, and if neither can be found with reasonable diligence by affixing it to a conspicuous part of the premises where it may be conveniently read - none of which requires a process server. The cautious course is to leave notice fees out of the lease. If you use a process server or a sheriff in an eviction, the cost of service is a disbursement in the action and is taxed by the court, which is the right place for it, rather than a lease charge you would have to defend. And remember what a notice fee buys you in risk terms: it is a small sum that gives a tenant a concrete reason to contest the whole accounting, including your deposit withholding, where the penalty for getting it wrong is forfeiting the right to withhold anything.

title: Notice Periods You Can Shorten, and One You Cannot Skip
bodyText: South Dakota has no provision forbidding a lease from shortening or waiving a termination notice, and it has no single notice to quit to waive. What it has is several routes to possession with different notice attached, and the lease decides which one you can use. A residential tenancy at will ends on written notice to remove within a period of not less than fifteen days, served on the tenant or a person of discretion residing on the premises, or posted conspicuously if neither can be found with reasonable diligence; you may not reenter or sue until that period has run. Where the lease reserves a right of reentry, the notice is three days' previous written notice of intention to reenter - and an action for possession on a reserved right of reentry may be brought without even that notice. So the practical way to shorten the notice is not a waiver clause but a reservation: a lease that reserves reentry gives you the shorter route, and a lease that is silent leaves you with the fifteen-day one. For unpaid rent the eviction statute supplies its own trigger, a lessee who fails to pay rent for three days after it is due, which does not depend on a notice to quit at all. Two things a lease cannot do. It cannot shorten the two months' notice owed where the tenant or an immediate family member is on active military service, except on the grounds the statute itself names. And a notice that is in substance a response to a tenant's code complaint, repair notice or tenant-union activity invites a retaliation claim whatever the lease says.

title: A Pending Notice to Vacate Suspends None of Your Duties
bodyText: A notice to vacate changes nothing about the tenancy until the period in it runs out. You may not reenter or go to court for possession before then, and until then every duty you had you still have. That is the answer to the question other states handle with an express ban on making a unit unlivable while a notice is pending. South Dakota has no such prohibition, but it gets there through remedies, and they are expensive. The repair duty runs for the term and you cannot waive or modify it, so starting demolition or letting a condition slide while the clock runs creates a condition requiring repair, with the tenant free to fix it and deduct, to vacate and be discharged from further rent and from the other lease conditions, or to withhold rent into a separate account if the work would cost more than a month's rent. Shutting off electricity, gas, water or another essential service is worse: that costs two months' rent plus the return of all advance rent and deposit, and lets the tenant sue for an injunction, recover possession, or end the tenancy. Watch the retaliation statute as well. A notice to vacate that is not based on a breach of the lease, given within one hundred eighty days after the tenant complained in good faith to a code authority, gave you written notice of a condition requiring repair, or joined a tenant organisation, is a cause of action in itself, and so is cutting electric, gas, water or sewer service. The cautious course is to keep services running and repairs moving, to schedule any renovation for after the unit is empty, to leave rent and terms alone while the notice runs, and to record the lease breach if there is one.

title: Nuisance Exposure and What It Does Not Do to Your Lease
bodyText: South Dakota has a full civil nuisance chapter, and the first thing to grasp is what it omits. Nothing in it voids or cancels a lease, nothing puts a receiver over your building or diverts the rents to repairs, nothing gives anyone a lien ahead of your mortgage, and nothing escrows rent or suspends a subsidy. There is no drug-nuisance statute here at all, so the familiar package of drug-related abatement suits by tenants or neighbours, with its rent escrows and sealing orders, does not exist here. No statute makes you a necessary defendant when a third party's conduct supports abatement, and none requires your lease to summarise a criminal provision. What the chapter provides is a definition of nuisance, a division between public and private nuisance, an enumeration of remedies, and abatement on notice with the cost taxed. It makes successive owners liable for a continuing nuisance, the limb that should worry a buyer, and identifies who may bring a civil action for an injunction and damages. For one category, a house of ill fame, it goes further: a state's attorney or a citizen may sue, and an order of abatement can have property removed and sold and the building closed, with release to the owner only on paying costs and filing a bond. Separately, failing to remove a public nuisance is a misdemeanour where nothing else is prescribed, and a county health board may notify you, remove the nuisance and charge you. The cautious course is to build your own exit. Make conduct amounting to a nuisance, and any unlawful use, an express breach that terminates the lease, because the eviction statute enforces whatever your lease says operates to terminate it and you otherwise have no means to abate. Act on complaints in writing and keep the record.

title: What an Optional Clause Can and Cannot Do Here
bodyText: South Dakota has no list of optional lease terms, no authorisation of particular clauses and no prohibited-provisions section - so the question is not which optional terms are permitted but what the general law does to them. Three rules decide nearly every case, and they are worth knowing as a set before you add anything to a South Dakota lease. First, a provision contrary to an express provision of law, or contrary to the policy of express law, is unlawful, and a provision exempting anyone from responsibility for their own fraud, wilful injury, or violation of law whether wilful or negligent, is void. That disposes of as-is clauses against the habitability duty, authorisations to lock out or cut off services, and indemnities reaching your own violations. Second, penalties imposed by contract for nonperformance are void, and an agreed damages figure survives only where the loss would be impracticable or extremely difficult to quantify - which is why almost every optional charge should be documented actual cost rather than a fixed fee. Third, any provision restricting a party from enforcing their rights by usual legal proceedings in ordinary tribunals, or limiting the time to do so, is void, with arbitration the only carve-out - which disposes of shortened limitation periods, notice-of-claim conditions and pre-suit hurdles, and leaves a jury waiver of uncertain standing. What is left is a wide field: optional terms about use, guests, pets, parking, smoking, alterations, keys, maintenance allocation by agreement in lieu of rent, and entry arrangements all work. The cautious course is to test every optional clause against those three rules before adding it.

title: No Ordnance, Demolition or Shared-Meter Disclosure Duties
bodyText: None of the three disclosures bundled under this heading exists in South Dakota. There is no military ordnance or former-range disclosure; the word appears in the Code only in firearms and ammunition provisions. There is no duty to tell a tenant that the building is scheduled for demolition or that you have applied for a demolition permit, and no statutory relocation payment or extended notice tied to one. There is no shared-meter disclosure, because the state has no submetering or master-metering statute at all. Each absence leaves a different thing in its place. Demolition notice does exist in South Dakota, but it runs to historic preservation rather than to occupants: an owner must give notice before demolishing or altering a designated historic property, with a waiting period for negotiation, and the mandated seller's disclosure statement now asks a seller whether the property is a designated historic property or sits in a historic district. Demolition standards themselves are local, and for a building other than a one- or two-family home or a townhouse, a local ordinance prescribing them must comply with the 2024 International Building Code. On metering, the operative rule is a cap on the amount rather than a disclosure: you may not knowingly charge a gas or electricity consumer more than the utility actually billed. The cautious course is to supply all three disclosures voluntarily. If you know the building is coming down, say so before signing and match the lease term to what you can actually deliver, because you owe delivery and quiet enjoyment and the remedy for breaking that is two months' rent plus return of all advance rent and deposit. If a meter is shared, write the allocation into a signed utility page.

title: Facilities You Supply Fall Under One General Duty
bodyText: South Dakota has no product-safety or consumer-protection provision imposing a specific duty on a landlord for a particular building facility - no automatic garage door opener rule, no elevator provision aimed at landlords, no laundry-room or playground standard. There is no itemised list of facilities and no standard for any of them. What there is instead is a single duty broad enough to cover all of them, and it is worth reading closely because its wording is wider than most landlords assume. You must keep the premises and all common areas in reasonable repair and fit for human habitation and in good and safe working order during the term, and maintain all electrical, plumbing and heating systems in good and safe working order and condition. Neither sentence may be waived or modified. The phrase and all common areas is what brings a shared laundry, a garage, a lift, a stairwell, a parking area, a mailroom and a playground inside the duty, and good and safe working order is the standard each is measured against. Two riders. The duty is expressly additional to any covenant imposed by law or ordinance or by the lease, so a local code stacks on top rather than replacing it; and nothing in the section alters your liability to third parties, so a guest injured by a defective facility is not confined to the tenant's remedies. The cautious course is to inventory every facility you supply, set your own inspection and service interval for each, and keep the records - with no statutory standard to comply with, your documented programme is what demonstrates reasonable repair.

title: No Day-One Owner or Manager Identity Disclosure
bodyText: South Dakota has no day-one landlord identity disclosure. Nothing requires you to give the tenant the owner's name and address, the name and address of a person authorised to manage the premises, or an agent for receiving notices and service of process, either in the lease or on request. There is no rental registration, no licensing of landlords, and no statutory consequence for staying anonymous. In particular, no disclosure failure bars an eviction here: the grounds for a forcible entry and detainer action are set out by statute and a landlord's non-disclosure is not among the defences, so the mechanism some states use to make identity disclosure self-enforcing does not exist. What does touch the subject is indirect but useful. A lease for more than one year must be in writing signed by the lessor or by an agent authorised in writing, so a long lease forces the owner or a properly authorised agent onto the page. If you manage for an owner for compensation you are likely to need a property manager or residential rental agent licence, and that licensing chapter carries its own agency duties. And every notice regime you depend on assumes the tenant knows where to write, including the thirty-day modification notice for a month-to-month tenancy and the deposit statement owed within twenty-one days. The cautious course is to disclose anyway: name the owner of record and a management agent in the lease, give one physical address in South Dakota for notices plus an email if you accept them, and update the tenant in writing when either changes. Anonymity gains you nothing and costs you the ability to prove notice.

title: No Owner-Use Recovery Ground - End the Tenancy Instead
bodyText: South Dakota gives you no owner-use, remodeling or sale ground for recovering possession, and so sets no minimum holding period that a lease could lengthen. States that let a landlord evict to move in, renovate or sell usually pair that right with a period the owner must then hold the unit; South Dakota has neither the right nor the period, because it does not need them. You recover possession by ending the tenancy rather than by proving a reason. A residential tenancy at will, however created, ends on written notice to remove within a period of not less than fifteen days, served on the tenant or on a person of discretion residing on the premises, or posted conspicuously if neither can be found with reasonable diligence; after that period expires, and not before, you may reenter or proceed to recover possession. A tenancy for a fixed term ends when the term ends. A month-to-month tenancy that is simply allowed to run out ends the same way. Two cautions. Where a tenant or an immediate family member is on active military service the notice period is two months, unless the tenant has engaged in sustained disruptive, illegal, destructive or negligent conduct or a material breach, or you have sold the property or it has passed to your estate. And a lease term reciting an owner-use right adds nothing to your remedies, since the right you actually use is the right to end the tenancy; what the lease should do instead is reserve a right of reentry, which is only yours if the lease gives it to you.

title: Parking Rules Are Pure Lease Terms, So the Modification Route Is the Only Lever
bodyText: South Dakota has no rules-adoption statute, which means your parking and towing rules are nothing but lease terms and they rise and fall as terms. Nothing requires you to deliver them before signing, to head them in prescribed words, to limit what vehicle information you ask for, or to make a permit expire with the tenancy. Equally, nothing lets you impose a new rule on a tenant who has not agreed to it. That makes one statutory route decisive. On a month-to-month letting you may modify the terms, including a parking rule, by written notice given at least thirty days before the month ends; the notice itself becomes part of the lease if the tenant stays on, and the tenant may answer by terminating effective the first of the next month on notice given within fifteen days of receiving yours. On a fixed term there is no such route, so a mid-term change needs the tenant's signature. Enforcement is where landlords go wrong. A flat parking-violation fee is a penalty fixed by contract for a breach, and those are void in South Dakota, so charge documented actual cost instead. Towing is not an enforcement tool either: a vehicle the tenant parked with your permission is not an abandoned vehicle, and the abandoned-vehicle chapter is the only route onto private property. The cautious course is to attach the parking rules to the lease and reference them in it so they are part of the bargain from day one, to change them only through the monthly modification route or a signed addendum, to collect no more vehicle data than make, model and plate, to say in the lease that any permit or decal ends with the tenancy, and to check the municipal code, which may add its own parking and towing requirements.

title: What Cannot Be Waived - a Short List, Not a Scheme
bodyText: States with a uniform residential landlord and tenant act usually have one section listing the rights a lease may not waive. South Dakota has no such act and no such list. What you get instead is one express non-waiver sentence, a few provisions whose own wording defeats evasion, and a general contract rule doing the rest of the work. The express one is in the habitability section: you and your tenant may not waive or modify its requirements, with a narrow exception for an agreement that the tenant perform specified repairs or maintenance in lieu of rent. The anti-evasion ones operate by definition rather than prohibition. Any money whose function is to secure performance of a residential rental agreement is deemed a security deposit however you denominate it, so a label cannot take it outside the deposit rules; and if you fail to comply with the deposit-return section you forfeit all rights to withhold any part of the deposit. The general rule is the one to keep in mind when drafting anything else: a contract provision contrary to an express provision of law, or to the policy of express law, is unlawful, and a provision purporting to exempt anyone from responsibility for a violation of law, whether willful or negligent, is void. Note the asymmetry that follows from having no scheme. The habitability duty is expressly protected, but your tenant's remedies for your breach of it - repair and deduct, vacate and be discharged, withhold into a separate account where repairs exceed a month's rent - carry no non-waiver sentence of their own. Whether those remedies can be given up by agreement is unsettled, and the cautious course is to assume they cannot.

title: Scheduled-Service Entry Works Only If the Lease Agrees It
bodyText: South Dakota lets you put regularly scheduled services on a different entry footing from one-off visits, but only by agreement in the lease. The default is that, except in an emergency or where it is impracticable, you must give reasonable notice of your intent to enter and enter only at reasonable times, with twenty-four hours' written notice presumed reasonable; and the notice must state the date or dates of entry, a window during normal business hours, the purpose, and a way for the tenant to ask to reschedule. The variation sits in the same sentence as that presumption: it applies unless alternate methods of notification or times for entry are mutually agreed upon between you and the tenant in the lease. A recurring pest-control treatment, a quarterly filter change, a scheduled lawn or snow service or a periodic smoke-detector check can therefore run on an agreed schedule set out in the lease rather than on fresh notice each time - which is exactly the pattern of the statute's reference to times for entry. Note the limits. The agreement must be mutual and in the lease, so a schedule you circulate later is not an agreement. What the lease displaces is the twenty-four-hour presumption, not the underlying standard of reasonable notice at reasonable times, so the schedule itself has to be reasonable. And a standing right of entry is not a right to enter for other purposes. The cautious course is to set the schedule out specifically - what service, how often, in what window - and to give ordinary notice for anything outside it.

title: No Pest Statute, So Infestation Is a Habitability Matter and Treatment Is an Entry Matter
bodyText: South Dakota has no pest-control provision for residential rentals at all. Nothing requires you to disclose a past or current infestation, to notify a tenant before a treatment, to publish a treatment schedule, to give a pesticide fact sheet, or to respond within a set number of days. Two existing duties carry the subject instead. The duty to deal with an infestation is the habitability duty. You must keep the premises and all common areas in reasonable repair, fit for human habitation and in good and safe working order for the whole term, and you may not waive or modify that by lease. An infestation is therefore a condition requiring repair, which means notice from the tenant starts a reasonable time for you to act, after which the tenant may treat it and deduct the cost, vacate and be discharged from further rent, or, where the cost would exceed one month's rent, withhold rent into a separate account. Getting in to treat is governed by the entry statute. Reasonable notice at reasonable times is the standard, twenty-four hours in writing is presumed reasonable, and the notice must state the dates, a window in normal business hours, the purpose and a way to ask to reschedule. The presumption gives way where alternate methods of notification or times for entry are mutually agreed in the lease, and that is how a recurring treatment schedule is lawfully set. The cautious course is to write the schedule into the lease specifically, to give written notice naming the product and the date for anything unscheduled, to ask your applicator what notice its own licence obliges it to give the occupant, and to charge documented actual cost rather than a flat pest fee, because a penalty fixed by contract for a breach is void.

title: No Pet Fact Sheet, and the One Animal-and-Eviction Rule Runs the Other Way
bodyText: South Dakota connects an animal to an eviction in exactly one place, and it works in your favour rather than the tenant's. Where a person is found to have knowingly made a false claim of a disability requiring a service or assistance animal, or knowingly supplied fraudulent supporting documentation, the lessor may evict, and may recover a damage fee capped at a thousand dollars from a lessee who produced fraudulent disability documentation. That is the whole of the statutory intersection. Nothing requires you to give a tenant a state fact sheet, packet, pamphlet or brochure about pets and eviction, and nothing triggers such a duty because you know the tenant keeps a dog or a cat. There is no such document to give: no South Dakota agency publishes a tenant fact sheet on any subject that is delivered with a lease, and there is no pet disclosure, no pet-deposit notice and no required warning that keeping an unapproved animal can end a tenancy. The law is also silent on what happens to the animal itself. The abandoned-property provisions are written for property and fit a live animal badly, and no statute tells you, the sheriff or anyone else what to do with a pet left behind. The cautious course is to fill that gap in the lease. Say what happens to an animal on termination or abandonment, who must remove it and by when, and that you will contact local animal control if nobody does, because no statute will answer it for you. Keep your pet application wholly separate from the service and assistance animal documentation route, so a disability request is never processed, or refused, as a pet request.

title: A Pet Deposit Is Deposit Money - Pet Rent Is Not
bodyText: South Dakota has no pet-fee statute, so the answer comes entirely from the deposit statute, and it is clear. Any money whose function is to secure performance of the rental agreement, or any part of it, is deemed a security deposit however it is denominated - and a pet deposit is money held against pet damage, which is performance of the agreement. So a pet deposit is security deposit money. It counts inside the one-month-rent ceiling together with everything else you hold, it must be returned or accounted for on the statutory timetable, and it may be withheld only for rent defaults, other funds due to you under an agreement, and restoring the premises to their move-in condition with ordinary wear and tear excepted. Calling it nonrefundable does not take it out of that; there is no pet-deposit exclusion in South Dakota's definition and no separate pet ceiling. Pet rent is a different thing and is the cleaner instrument: a recurring charge for the privilege of keeping the animal is rent or a sum due under the agreement, not money held as security, so it does not touch the deposit cap at all. The cautious course is therefore to price the pet through pet rent rather than through a large pet deposit, to keep any pet deposit inside your one-month total, and to charge pet damage at documented actual cost against the deposit. One exception to remember: a service or assistance animal is not a pet, and you may not charge a pet deposit or pet rent for one.

title: No Plain-Language or Consumer-Statement Requirement
bodyText: South Dakota has no plain-language statute for residential leases. There is no readability test your lease must pass, no requirement to attach a statement of consumer restrictions listing every right the lease waives, no optional preapproval route through the Attorney General, and no dollar threshold excluding larger transactions. Your lease may be as long and as technical as you choose to make it. Two South Dakota rules nonetheless reward plain drafting.
