The first is the one that disposes of unreadable boilerplate: a provision contrary to an express provision of law, or contrary to the policy of express law, is unlawful, and the clauses most likely to fall into that are exactly the ones buried in dense paragraphs - a waiver of the habitability duty, a penalty for breach, a term restricting the tenant from going to court. Length conceals those from you, not just from the tenant. The second is the deceptive practices chapter, which reaches misleading conduct in connection with a consumer transaction, so a lease whose plain words say one thing and whose fine print says another is a risk rather than a protection. There is also a straightforward drafting reason: the remedies that matter in a dispute are statutory, and a court reading a lease against the drafter will not strain to rescue a clause nobody could follow. The cautious course is short sentences, a heading for every section, the figures the tenant actually needs stated once and consistently, and a signed copy given to the tenant even though no statute requires you to hand one over.

title: No Plain-Language Law Reaches a South Dakota Lease
bodyText: South Dakota has no plain-language or consumer-contract statute that reaches a residential lease. There is no readability standard, no requirement to divide and caption a lease by sections, no front-page statement listing the landlord-protective terms, and no dollar threshold above or below which a different rule applies. Nothing about the way your lease reads is regulated. The nearest thing South Dakota has is its deceptive practices chapter, and it works on substance rather than style: knowingly using a deceptive act or practice, a false promise or a misrepresentation, or concealing, suppressing or omitting a material fact in connection with the sale or advertisement of merchandise, is prohibited whether or not anyone was actually misled. Its definitions expressly reach goods or services leased or rented, so the chapter is capable of applying to a tenancy, although its application to residential leases is not settled. Note the practical overlap with readability. A material fact buried in dense boilerplate is closer to concealment than a material fact stated plainly, and a lease whose headings promise one thing while the fine print does another is where an omission argument starts. So plain drafting is a defence to the statute that does exist rather than compliance with one that does not. The cautious course is short sentences, a heading for every section, each figure stated once and consistently, and the terms a tenant would care about - fees, entry, termination, deposit deductions - visible rather than buried.

title: No Canvasser or Political-Access Right
bodyText: South Dakota gives candidates, canvassers, petition circulators and tenant organizers no right of access to a residential rental property, and gives tenants no statutory right to receive them. There is no provision requiring you to admit a canvasser to a multi-unit building, none protecting a tenant's political signs or displays, and none limiting a no-solicitation rule. Access to private property remains yours to control. One related South Dakota rule runs the other way and is worth knowing: a registered sex offender is prohibited from circulating petitions, with narrow exceptions, so a canvasser's status is something the law does address even though access is not. Two general limits bound a no-solicitation policy. Tenants are entitled to quiet enjoyment of what they rent, so a rule may regulate common areas and the exterior without reaching what a tenant does inside the unit, and that includes receiving whomever the tenant chooses to admit. And retaliation is a defined risk where tenant organizing is involved: a cause of action arises against a landlord who raises rent above fair market value, cuts electric, gas, water or sewer service, or gives a notice to vacate not based on a breach of the lease, after the tenant has organized or become a member of a tenants' union or organization - with a defence where the notice to vacate came more than one hundred eighty days after the event. So a no-solicitation rule is lawful; applying it selectively against organizing is the thing that creates liability. The cautious course is one written, content-neutral rule applied consistently, and no response to organizing that touches rent, services or possession.

title: No Residential Pool Rules - the Pool Rules Are for Hotels
bodyText: South Dakota imposes no pool-safety duty on a residential landlord. There is no barrier or fence requirement, no safety-notice duty at lease signing, no lifeguard or shut-off requirement, and no classification of an apartment complex pool as a regulated facility. South Dakota does have pool standards, and knowing where they sit is the point: they are in the lodging and food service rules, and they reach water recreation facilities - swimming pools, spas and water slides - operated by a hotel and used by guests or the public, which must be designed, constructed and maintained to a named engineering standard. That is the same pattern as South Dakota's smoke-detector rules: a real requirement, scoped to licensed transient lodging, that does not reach an apartment building or a rental house. So if you let residential units with a pool, your obligation comes from the general duty rather than a pool code. You must keep the premises and all common areas in reasonable repair and fit for human habitation and in good and safe working order, and that cannot be waived - which for a pool means functioning gates and latches, intact fencing, working drains and covers, and no hazard you know about and leave. Local ordinances are the real source of barrier and fencing requirements in South Dakota and are not resolved here, so check your city's building and zoning rules before relying on the absence of a state rule. The cautious course is to fence and self-latch regardless, post rules and depth markings, prohibit unsupervised use by minors in the lease, and carry liability cover.

title: No Right to a Window Air Conditioner - and No Duty to Cool
bodyText: South Dakota gives a tenant no right to install a portable or window cooling device, and requires no lease term disclosing a restriction on one. It also imposes no duty to provide cooling at all: heating is named in the habitability statute and air conditioning is not, so a unit without air conditioning is not for that reason unfit, and a failed air conditioner you supplied is a repair item because you supplied it rather than because the law requires cooling. Whether a tenant may put a unit in a window is therefore entirely a matter for your lease, and if the lease is silent you are arguing about an implied right to alter the premises. Say so expressly. If you do permit window units, the terms worth setting are the ones that protect the building: professional or safe installation with proper brackets rather than a sash resting on the frame, no modification of the window or frame without consent, a prohibition on blocking an egress window, responsibility for water damage from condensate, removal at the end of the tenancy and restoration of the opening. Note two South Dakota points that bear on this. Electrical capacity is yours: you must maintain the electrical systems in good and safe working order and condition, non-waivably, so a circuit that cannot carry what a tenant plugs into it is your problem to assess rather than theirs. And any charge you impose for an unauthorised installation must be documented actual cost, since a fixed penalty for breach is void. The cautious course is a short written policy in the lease and consent recorded in writing.

title: No Tenant Right to Plug-In Solar
bodyText: South Dakota gives a tenant no right to install a plug-in solar device, a balcony panel or a battery, and imposes no portfolio-size threshold above which you must allow one. There is no notice-and-reasonable-restrictions mechanism, no utility provision letting a tenant install without utility approval, and no statute voiding instrument restrictions on solar energy systems as applied to a lease. South Dakota's solar provisions are about different things: it recognises a solar easement as a property interest, allows wind and solar easements and leases on school and public lands, and taxes solar facilities. None of that reaches a residential tenancy. So whether a tenant may install anything is governed by your lease, and a lease that prohibits alterations without written consent answers it. Two South Dakota points matter if you consider permitting it. An installation that feeds electricity anywhere beyond the device raises the question of selling or providing electricity, and South Dakota's exemption from utility status is written for electric-vehicle charging stations, not for tenant generation - so do not assume a tenant's arrangement is outside utility regulation. And the electrical system remains yours: you must maintain all electrical systems in good and safe working order and condition and cannot waive that, so a tenant's wiring into your panel is your exposure as much as theirs. The cautious course is to require written consent, professional installation and electrical permits where applicable, prohibit any connection to the building's wiring without your consent, require removal and restoration at the end of the tenancy, and put responsibility for damage on the tenant at actual cost.

title: No Duty in South Dakota Turns on How Many Units You Own
bodyText: This one is worth stating plainly because it is unusual and it simplifies everything else: no South Dakota landlord duty is tiered by portfolio size. There is no small-landlord exemption, no threshold at four units or five or ten, no two-limb exemption to read conjunctively, and no duty that switches on above a number of properties. The habitability duty, the deposit cap and timetable, the entry standard, the termination notices and the tenant's repair remedies apply identically to an owner of one duplex and to an owner of a thousand apartments. Two places where a number does appear are worth distinguishing, because they are not portfolio thresholds. Administrative rules require a smoke detector in each family living unit of a multifamily residence housing six or more families, and sprinklers throughout any new hotel, motel or multifamily residence housing six or more families - those turn on the size of the building, not on how many buildings you own, so a landlord with twenty fourplexes is outside both while a landlord with one six-plex is inside them. And the state's property condition disclosure statement, which applies on a sale and on a lease with an option to purchase, is limited to residential real property of not more than four dwelling units in one structure - again a building test. The cautious course is to stop looking for a small-landlord exemption in South Dakota and to read any building-size figure you meet as being about the building.

title: The Only Bond Runs Against the Tenant
bodyText: South Dakota has no possession bond for a landlord. There is no procedure for posting security and taking possession before judgment, no end-of-term possession bond, and no statutory confessed judgment for possession that a lease could invoke. The one security the eviction statute knows runs the other way and belongs to the tenant. No continuance may be granted for more than fourteen days unless the tenant applying for it gives you an undertaking, with surety approved by the court, conditioned on paying the rent that accrues plus costs if judgment goes against them. That is the closest thing here to a possession bond, and it is a condition on delay rather than a route to early possession. You do not need one, because the ordinary timetable is short: five days to appear, trial on two days' notice once the issues are joined, and execution for possession served in the daytime. Do not try to build the missing bond into your lease. A provision restricting a party from enforcing their rights by the usual legal proceedings in ordinary tribunals, or limiting the time to do so, is void here, with arbitration the only exception, and a confession of judgment is treated as deceptive in at least one consumer setting. On appeal the pattern repeats: if your tenant appeals a judgment for possession and wants to remain, the appellate bond conditions are that no waste be committed and that, if the judgment is affirmed, they pay the value of the use and occupation from the appeal until possession is delivered. Every security requirement here runs against the tenant who delays. The cautious course is to ask the court for the statutory undertaking whenever your tenant seeks a continuance, and to object if one beyond fourteen days is granted without it.

title: No Well-Testing or Results-Disclosure Duty
bodyText: South Dakota imposes no duty on a landlord to test a private well serving a rental, and none to give test results to tenants. There is no testing interval, no list of contaminants to test for, no reporting obligation and no disclosure of past results. A property on a private well is let on the same statutory terms as one on municipal water. That puts the whole weight on the habitability duty, and here the duty is doing real work rather than filling a gap. You must keep the premises fit for human habitation and in good and safe working order throughout the term, and maintain all plumbing systems in good and safe working order and condition, neither of which may be waived or modified. Water that is unsafe to drink is the clearest case of premises not fit for human habitation, and the fact that no statute tells you to test does not reduce that duty - it only means you have no checklist to show you met it. Note also that a lease cannot allocate this away: South Dakota has no mechanism, as some states do, letting a lease reduce the water-supply duty for a property without utility service. One adjacent disclosure point: radon in a well is one of the items on South Dakota's seller property condition disclosure statement, a duty that arises on sale - and a lease with an option to purchase is a covered transfer. The cautious course is to test annually for bacteria and nitrate, keep the results, give them to tenants without being asked, and treat any adverse result as an urgent repair.

title: No Statutory List of Tenant Prohibited Acts
bodyText: South Dakota has no statutory list of things a tenant may not do. States with a uniform landlord-tenant act usually set out the tenant's obligations - keeping the unit clean, not deliberately damaging it, not disturbing neighbours, using facilities reasonably - and make a breach an eviction ground. South Dakota has none of that, which means your lease is the whole of the tenant's rule book, with three statutory exceptions worth knowing. The tenant must preserve the premises, the appliances, the appurtenances and the other leased personal property, and must repair deterioration caused by the tenant's own negligent, wilful or malicious conduct, or that of someone under the tenant's direction or control - which gives you a damages claim for careless or deliberate damage without needing a lease term. Where premises are leased for a particular and specified purpose the tenant must not use them for another, and if they do you may hold the tenant responsible for the safety of the premises during that use or treat the contract as rescinded. And you may terminate before the end of the term where the tenant uses the property contrary to the lease agreement. Those are the bridge, and the eviction statute completes it: among the seven forcible entry and detainer grounds is a lessee who commits waste, or does or fails to perform any act which under the lease operates to terminate it. So because South Dakota implies almost no conduct rules, your own lease terms are what reach eviction - and they reach it directly rather than only through a prior termination. The cautious course is a specific, enforceable rules section - not a list of platitudes - covering noise, occupancy, smoking, pets, parking, waste and business use, with breach stated to be a default.

title: A Promise to Repair Need Not Be in Writing - Which Is the Problem
bodyText: South Dakota has no rule requiring a landlord's promise to clean, repair or improve a unit to be in writing, to carry a completion date, or to be given before the lease is signed. States with a rental-practices regulation often require all three, and treat a broken pre-lease promise as a deceptive practice. South Dakota requires none of it, which sounds like freedom and is actually exposure, because the promise is still enforceable - it is simply enforceable on whatever evidence the tenant can produce about what your leasing agent said at the showing. Two bodies of law give that evidence somewhere to land. A promise that induced the tenant to take the unit is a term of the bargain, and the lease chapter already treats the part of the premises the landlord had reason to believe was the material inducement as significant enough that its destruction lets the tenant terminate. And a misrepresentation in connection with a consumer transaction has its own statutory consequences under the deceptive practices chapter, which the library's own South Dakota rows address. The cautious course is to put every pre-lease promise in the lease or in a signed addendum, with what will be done and by when, and to make the lease say that no promise about condition or improvements binds you unless it is written and signed. That last clause is worth having precisely because South Dakota will otherwise let the question be decided on recollection. If you will not do the work, do not let it be promised.

title: No Chemical-Exposure Warning Requirement
bodyText: South Dakota has no chemical-exposure warning law of the kind that requires a posted or delivered notice about substances known to cause cancer or reproductive harm. There is no list of listed chemicals, no warning text, no posting duty for a building and no lease disclosure. Nothing obliges you to warn about garage exhaust, treated wood, building materials, pesticides applied on the property or anything else on that model. What fills the space is the ordinary law, and it is worth knowing which parts actually reach a chemical hazard. The habitability duty requires you to keep the premises fit for human habitation and in good and safe working order throughout the term and cannot be waived, so a genuine contamination or exposure problem is a repair obligation whether or not any warning was owed. A misrepresentation about the condition of the premises in connection with a consumer transaction may be reachable under the deceptive practices chapter, though whether that chapter reaches a tenancy is unsettled. And a recorded environmental covenant restricting the use of a contaminated property runs with the land, so where one exists its restrictions bind the occupancy and you should pass them on. Federal law supplies the one real warning duty a residential landlord has, and it is about lead paint in pre-1978 housing rather than chemicals generally. The cautious course is to disclose in writing any contamination, remediation or recorded environmental covenant you know of, give the federal lead pamphlet and disclosure where the building predates 1978, and tell tenants before applying pesticides.

title: No Property-Tax-Portion-of-Rent Statement
bodyText: South Dakota requires no statement telling a tenant what portion of the rent goes to property tax. There is no annual statement, none keyed to a rent change, and no lease provision that substitutes for one. Some states require this because their income-tax or renter-credit systems let a tenant claim a share of the property tax paid through rent; South Dakota has no state income tax, so the machinery that makes such a statement useful elsewhere does not exist here, and no analogous renter credit requires you to certify anything. Two points are worth drawing out for a landlord who is asked. You are free to tell a tenant what the property tax on the building is - it is public information from the county - but take care how you characterise a figure per unit, because an apportionment you calculate is your estimate, and a tenant who relies on it for any purpose is relying on you rather than on the county. And if you pass through a tax increase, that is a different question with a different answer: the pass-through exists only if the lease creates it, because deposit withholding reaches only rent defaults, other funds due to you under an agreement, and restoration. The cautious course is to answer a request by pointing the tenant to the county's own assessment and tax records rather than issuing a statement of your own, and to keep any contractual tax pass-through stated in the lease with its base figure and the tenant's exact share.

title: The Inquiry and Record Ban Exists, But It Turns on Purpose
bodyText:
South Dakota does have a protected-class inquiry and record ban, and landlords routinely miss it because it does not sit in the housing section. A separate section of the human rights chapter makes it an unfair or discriminatory practice for any person, by any means, trick, artifice, advertisement or sign, or by using any form of application, or by making any record or inquiry, or by any device whatsoever, to bring about or facilitate discrimination. That reaches you, your application form, your notes and your file, not just your decision.

Understand what it does and does not do. It is purposive, not flat: the question or the record has to work towards discrimination. South Dakota has no flat rule forbidding a protected-class question on a rental application the way it does for school admissions, where a separate section bans the inquiry, the form and the record outright. The housing section bans the decision and bans advertising or publicising that applicants of a particular class are unwelcome, and stops there. The state's human rights regulations add nothing: their interpretive chapters cover only employment, and the one inquiry rule in them is a hiring rule.

So a demographic question is not automatically unlawful in South Dakota, but it is evidence, and the record you keep of the answer is evidence too. The cautious course is to ask nothing about race, colour, creed, religion, sex, ancestry, disability, familial status or national origin on any application, note or file, with the single exception of what you need to assess a disability accommodation or service-animal request, and to keep that in a separate file used only for that purpose. Ask every applicant the same written questions and keep the list.

title: Leasing for a Specified Purpose Gives You Two Remedies
bodyText: South Dakota gives you a remedy most landlords never use, and it depends entirely on how the lease is drafted. If premises are leased for a particular and specified purpose, the tenant must not use them for other purposes; and if the tenant does, you may either hold the tenant responsible for the safety of the premises during that use, at all events, or treat the contract as rescinded. Read the two halves. The first shifts the risk of the unauthorised use onto the tenant absolutely - at all events, meaning without proof of fault - for anything that happens to the premises while it continues. The second lets you treat the lease as at an end. Both depend on the lease having specified a particular purpose; a lease that says nothing about use, or recites a vague purpose, gives you neither. There is a separate and overlapping route: you may terminate before the end of the term where the tenant uses the property contrary to the lease agreement. South Dakota has no statute voiding or annulling a lease because the premises are used for a prohibited or criminal purpose, so a lease does not dissolve by itself when something unlawful happens there - you have to act, and your lease terms are what let you. The cautious course is to state the permitted use specifically, as residential occupancy by named occupants, and to prohibit business, short-term letting and unlawful use expressly, so that both the risk-shifting and the rescission remedy are available rather than argued for.

title: No Radon Disclosure Duty to a Tenant
bodyText: South Dakota asks about radon, but only of a seller. The mandated residential property-condition disclosure statement puts radon gas in the house and radon gas in the well as separate items, each with a box for whether the condition exists and a box for whether a test has been performed, and it asks elsewhere whether the property has a radon system. That statement is owed to a buyer on a transfer. Nothing requires you to disclose radon to a tenant: there is no tenant disclosure duty, no testing mandate, no state pamphlet to hand over, no floor-level limitation of the kind some states use to confine the duty to ground and basement units, and no state radon programme in the statutes or the administrative rules at all. Nor is there a state radon-resistant new construction mandate. The state instead points local building ordinances at the 2024 model codes, so whether radon-resistant construction is required where you build depends on which edition and which optional provisions your city or county has adopted, which is a local question this answer does not resolve. The cautious course is to test. Testing is cheap, much of South Dakota sits in a high-radon geology, and a tenant who develops a concern mid-tenancy will ask you for a result you either have or do not. Where a test shows an elevated result, disclose it in writing before signing and either mitigate or price the unit knowing the tenant may argue that an unmitigated known hazard breaches your unwaivable duty to keep the premises fit for human habitation. Do not take a waiver of that duty in exchange for disclosure; it is void.

title: Recycling Is a Local Duty, Not Yours, So the Lease Has To Do the Work
bodyText: South Dakota puts recycling on local government and on waste districts, never on landlords. The state provisions create regional recycling and waste management districts, let counties and municipalities impose disposal fees, authorise a state waste reduction and recycling programme with source-reduction planning, and let a district bill for service, discontinue it, adopt designation ordinances and offer incentives to separate recyclable materials. Not one of them reaches a residential rental. You have no duty to provide recycling, no duty to tell tenants where or how to recycle on the premises, no notice to give at move-in and nothing to post. Two practical consequences follow. First, the requirement you are most likely to face is municipal, from your city or county ordinance or from your hauler's contract, and those sit outside state law, so read them before you write the lease. Second, because nothing is imposed, everything about waste and recycling at your property is a lease term and has to be written as one. If you provide containers and an enclosure, they are part of what the tenant has rented and part of the common areas you must keep in reasonable repair and in good and safe working order, which you cannot waive - an overflowing or unusable enclosure is a condition requiring repair. If you want to recover a hauler's contamination surcharge, remember that a fixed fee for breaking a rule is a contractual penalty and void in South Dakota. The cautious course is to name the service and who provides it, say in the rules what goes in which container and where the containers are, give that to the tenant with the lease, keep the enclosure serviceable, and recover only documented actual cost.

title: No Right to Redeem a Tenancy by Paying Up
bodyText: South Dakota legislates redemption heavily and never once for a tenancy. Whole chapters govern redemption from a sale on execution or foreclosure, short-term redemption mortgages, redemption from tax sales, and the redemption and marshalling of liens. Not one gives a tenant a right to redeem. There is no right to stop an eviction by paying the arrears, no pay-and-stay window before the writ, no rule that full payment of a nonpayment judgment bars execution, and no provision telling you whose money you must accept or forbidding you to restrict the method of payment. Nonpayment works differently here. An eviction ground simply exists once rent has gone unpaid for three days after it fell due, and no statute requires you to give notice or an opportunity to cure first. If you accept money after that, you are exercising a choice the statute does not regulate, and South Dakota gives you no mandated reservation-of-rights wording to protect the filing. The risk runs the other way: accepting rent can be read as waiving the default or renewing the tenancy, and that turns on your own conduct rather than a statutory formula. The cautious course is to decide the policy in the lease and then follow it exactly. Say that acceptance of a partial payment is not a waiver of any default and does not reinstate the tenancy or withdraw a notice, and that payments are applied to the oldest amount owed. Once you have filed, either refuse payment or take it under a written reservation in those terms and keep the receipt. Be consistent across tenants, because the only thing that will be examined is what you actually did. If you do reinstate, do it in writing and say so plainly.

title: No Religious or Cultural Display Right - but Religion Is a Protected Class
bodyText: South Dakota has no provision giving a tenant the right to display a religious or cultural object - no mezuzah rule, no doorframe exemption from a no-affixing policy, no protection for a seasonal or cultural display. Nothing requires you to permit one and nothing stops you prohibiting attachments to a door or doorframe. But this is one of the few places in South Dakota's landlord-tenant law where a protected characteristic bears directly on a house rule, and that changes how the rule should be written. Religion is a protected class in housing: it is an unfair or discriminatory practice to refuse to rent to a person, or to discriminate in the terms, conditions or privileges of a rental, because of their creed or religion. So a facially neutral no-attachments rule is fine, but a rule that in practice reaches only religious objects, or one enforced against a religious display and not against a wreath or a sports pennant, is the shape of a discrimination claim rather than a property-care decision. Disability is likewise protected, and an accommodation request connected to a display is possible. The practical approach is therefore the opposite of a prohibition: a neutral rule about what may be affixed and how, applied uniformly and documented, with a stated route for a tenant to ask for an exception. Permitting a small object fixed without damage costs you nothing and removes the argument entirely. The cautious course is to allow displays that do not damage the premises, require removal and making good at the end, and never to enforce selectively.

title: Concessions Are Unregulated - but Do Not Claw Them Back
bodyText: South Dakota does not regulate rent concessions. No statute defines a concession, requires you to disclose its terms, or limits how a move-in special or a free month is structured. How you write it, though, decides whether it survives. The common structure is the dangerous one: a lease reciting a higher rent, granting a discount or a free month, and providing that if the tenant defaults or leaves early the forgiven rent becomes immediately due. That is a sum payable because the tenant broke the agreement, which is precisely what South Dakota treats as a contractual penalty, and penalties imposed by contract for nonperformance are void. An agreed figure substituting for damages is enforceable only where actual damages would be impracticable or extremely difficult to fix, and forgone rent is neither - it is arithmetic. The safe structure is to make the discounted figure the rent. State the rent you actually expect to collect, for the term you are willing to grant it, and if you want a higher figure later use the mechanism South Dakota gives you: on a month-to-month tenancy you may modify the terms, rent included, on written notice given at least thirty days before the end of the month, with the tenant free to terminate effective the first of the next month by notifying you within fifteen days of receiving your notice. That gets you the same economics without a clawback to defend.

title: Nothing Bars You From Demanding Rent - Which Is Not the Same as Being Owed It
bodyText: South Dakota has no provision barring a landlord from demanding or collecting rent in any circumstance - no bar during a repair dispute, none while a unit is unfit, none after a vacate order, and none while a tenant is withholding. You may always ask. Whether you are owed the money is a separate question that South Dakota answers in several places, and the gap between the two is where landlords get into difficulty. A tenant who has given you notice of conditions requiring repair and waited a reasonable time may lawfully repair and deduct the cost from rent, or vacate and be discharged from additional charges of rent and from performing the other lease conditions, or - where necessary repairs would cost more than one month's rent - withhold the rent after written notice of the specific reason and hold it in a separate bank or savings and loan account until you make the repairs. In each of those situations the rent is lawfully not paid to you, so a demand is not wrongful but it is also not productive, and an eviction built on that non-payment meets a defence. The one real constraint on demanding is retaliation: a cause of action arises where you increase rent above fair market value after a tenant's good-faith code complaint, repair notice or tenant-union activity. The cautious course is to establish why rent is unpaid before demanding or filing - if it is a withholding, fix the condition and the money follows.

title: Escalation Clauses Are Unregulated - and There Is No Safe Harbour to Earn
bodyText: South Dakota does not regulate rent-escalation clauses, and - this is the part that matters - it offers no retaliation safe harbour that a lease clause could unlock. In states built the other way, a mid-term increase is lawful only if the written lease provides for it, so the clause is the landlord's entire protection. South Dakota has no such structure: there is no presumption of retaliation attached to a rent increase, no safe harbour for a market-rate increase during a term, and no rule measuring your notice of an increase against the notice the lease requires of the tenant. What South Dakota has instead is a retaliation cause of action with defined triggers, and a rent increase features in it only in one shape: a tenant may sue where the landlord increases rents above fair market value after the tenant has complained in good faith to a code-enforcement agency, has given written notice of a condition requiring repair, or has organised or joined a tenants' union. Note what that means for drafting. An escalation clause does not immunise you, because the claim turns on the increase being above fair market value and on what preceded it, not on whether the lease authorised it; and conversely the absence of a clause does not create liability. So a scheduled escalation in a fixed-term lease is simply a term of the bargain. The cautious course is to tie any escalation to something objective and verifiable, to document market comparables before any significant increase, and to avoid timing an increase close behind a repair complaint.

title: Thirty Days to Change Rent - on a Month-to-Month Tenancy Only
bodyText: South Dakota has one rent-change mechanism and it is easy to misapply. In a lease of lands or tenements from month to month, you may modify the terms of the lease - rent included - by giving written notice at least thirty days before the expiration of the month, to take effect at the end of that month. When served, the notice operates by itself to establish the new terms, rent and conditions as part of the lease if the tenant continues to hold the premises after the month ends. The tenant's counterweight is a short window: the tenant may terminate effective the first day of the next month by giving you notice of termination within fifteen days of receiving your notice of modification. Three limits define the rest of the picture. The mechanism is for periodic month-to-month tenancies, so it does not let you raise rent mid-term on a fixed-term lease - there, the rent is what the lease says until the term ends, and a mid-term increase needs the tenant's agreement or a clause the lease already contains. There is no separate nonrenewal-notice duty, so letting a fixed term simply expire requires nothing beyond what the lease provides. And South Dakota has no rent control and no emergency price-gouging cap on dwelling rents, so the amount is unregulated. One caution on the amount: raising rent above fair market value after a tenant's good-faith code complaint, repair notice or tenant-union activity is one of the defined retaliation triggers.

title: Rent Timing Is Yours to Set - the Default Is Rent in Arrears
bodyText: South Dakota lets you set rent in installments, and you should, because the statutory default is not what most landlords assume. Where there is no contract or usage to the contrary, rents of lodgings are payable monthly at the end of each month, other rents quarterly at the end of each quarter, and rent for a hiring shorter than those periods at the end of the hiring. The default is rent in arrears, not in advance. The opening words are the important ones: the default applies only in the absence of a contract to the contrary, so a lease that states rent is due in advance on the first of each month displaces it entirely. A lease that says nothing about timing leaves you collecting at the end of the month. No South Dakota statute addresses whether a scheduled installment counts as a partial payment of rent, so the consequences of accepting one are governed by your lease and by general contract law rather than by a rule written for this situation. Two drafting points follow. State the due date, the period each payment covers, and that payment is due in advance if that is what you intend. And if you accept rent after a default or after a notice to quit, say in the lease what that acceptance does and does not waive, because South Dakota's holdover provision presumes a renewal on the same terms when a lessor accepts rent from a tenant who stays on after the hiring expires.

title: No Rent Escrow to Raise a Defence - but a Long Continuance Needs Security
bodyText: South Dakota does not make a tenant pay rent into court to defend an eviction. There is no registry deposit as the price of raising a defence, no mandatory counterclaim rule specific to possession actions, and no rent-escrow condition on a jury demand. A tenant may defend and counterclaim under the ordinary rules of civil procedure, which make a counterclaim compulsory where it arises out of the same transaction, and nothing about the forcible entry and detainer statute changes that. There is one provision that does what a rent-into-court rule does, and it is worth knowing because it is your lever when a tenant plays for time. The tenant's time to appear and plead is five days from service, or thirty days after publication, whichever comes sooner. No adjournment or continuance may be made for more than fourteen days unless the tenant applying for it gives an undertaking to you, with good and sufficient surety approved by the court, conditioned on payment of the rent that may accrue together with costs if judgment goes against them. So a short delay is free to the tenant, but a long one is not: the price of a continuance beyond two weeks is security for the accruing rent. The practical consequence is that you should resist a long continuance by asking the court for the undertaking rather than by opposing the delay itself, and you should keep a running figure for accruing rent and costs so the amount is before the court.

title: You Cannot Split Collecting the Rent From Keeping the Place Habitable
bodyText: Some states say in terms that whoever receives the rent carries the habitability duty, so it cannot be separated from the rent by a lease, assignment, deed or security instrument. South Dakota has no such provision. What it has reaches most of the same ground by a different route. The habitability duty is imposed on the lessor in every hiring of residential premises, whether written or oral, and the parties may not waive or modify it - the one permitted reallocation being an agreement that the tenant perform specified repairs or maintenance in lieu of rent. Because the duty attaches to the hiring rather than to a document, an arrangement that routes rent to one party and leaves the duty with another does not extinguish it; and on an assignment the remedies travel, since whatever remedies a tenant has against the immediate lessor for breach of an agreement in the lease, the tenant has against the lessor's assigns. For a property manager or rent-collecting agent, the statute that defines the role is a licensing provision rather than a duty-transfer one: a property manager is a person who for consideration negotiates rentals or leases, lists rentals, or collects or attempts to collect rents for real estate. Collecting rent makes you a property manager who must be licensed; it does not make you the lessor for habitability, and it does not relieve the lessor. The practical point for an owner using a manager or selling subject to a lease: the management agreement can allocate who does the repairs and who pays, but it cannot move the tenant's statutory claim off the lessor, so keep the repair obligation funded whatever the paperwork says.

title: No Receipt Duty, Even for Cash - and the Risk Runs Both Ways
bodyText: South Dakota imposes no duty to give a tenant a receipt for rent, including rent paid in cash. There is no receipt requirement, no consequence for refusing one, no eviction defence built on a missing receipt, and no evidentiary presumption that earlier instalments were paid because you gave a receipt for a later one. If a cash-paying tenant later says they paid and you say they did not, the dispute is decided on whatever records exist. That absence cuts against you more often than it helps, because you are the one who has to prove non-payment to get possession: the eviction ground is a lessee who fails to pay rent for three days after it is due, and a tenant who testifies to cash payments you cannot disprove is a genuine problem in a summary proceeding where the hearing comes quickly. There is a second trap in accepting payment at all. If a tenant remains in possession after the hiring expires and you accept rent, the parties are presumed to have renewed on the same terms for the same time, not exceeding one year - so an unthinking acceptance of cash after a term ends can renew a tenancy you meant to end. The cautious course is to issue a dated, numbered receipt for every cash payment whether or not anyone requires it, keep a copy, prefer traceable payment methods in the lease, and never accept a payment after a termination notice without a written statement of what it is and is not accepted for.

title: No Rent-Reporting Rules Either Way
bodyText: South Dakota has no rent-reporting law. Nothing requires you to offer positive rent reporting, nothing sets a portfolio size above which you must, nothing requires a signature block for a tenant's election, nothing bars you from requiring participation, and nothing obliges you to notify a tenant in writing before reporting a late payment to a credit bureau. The subject is unregulated in both directions. If you choose to report, two things outside the landlord-tenant statutes shape how. Furnishing information to a consumer reporting agency makes you a furnisher under federal fair-credit law, which carries accuracy and dispute-investigation obligations of its own, and those are not resolved here. And South Dakota's breach-notification law does reach you: a person or business conducting business in the state that owns or licenses computerised personal information about residents must notify affected residents within sixty days of discovering a breach, report a breach affecting more than two hundred fifty residents to the Attorney General, and notify the consumer reporting agencies, with penalties of up to ten thousand dollars per day per violation. Reporting means holding more identifying data for longer, which raises that exposure rather than lowering it. The cautious course is to treat reporting as optional and say so in the lease, make a tenant's participation genuinely elective with a written election, report accurately and correct promptly when a tenant disputes an entry, and tell a tenant in writing before you report a delinquency - not because South Dakota requires it, but because the dispute you avoid is cheaper than the one you win.

title: No State Rental Inspection or Licensing - and Entry Still Needs Notice
bodyText: South Dakota has no rental inspection regime, no rental licensing or registration scheme, and no periodic-inspection requirement for private housing. Nothing conditions letting a unit on an inspection, and no state agency inspects residential rentals. The inspection powers that exist in the statutes are for transient lodging, food service and campgrounds, and for the fire marshal - not for an apartment. The topic's real question for a landlord is whether the lease can authorise a housing inspector to enter so the tenant must provide access without separate consent, and in South Dakota the answer runs through the general entry rule rather than an inspection statute. Except in an emergency or where it is impracticable, you must give the tenant reasonable notice of your intent to enter and enter only at reasonable times, with twenty-four hours' written notice presumed reasonable unless alternate methods of notification or times for entry are mutually agreed in the lease, and the notice must state the dates, a window in normal business hours, the purpose and a way to ask to reschedule. A lease term in which the tenant agrees to permit entry by a municipal inspector is therefore an agreement about entry, and it works on the same footing as any other - it fixes the agreed method and timing, but it does not displace the standard of reasonable notice at reasonable times. The cautious course is to say in the lease that inspections by a public authority may occur and that you will give notice when you can, then give actual notice each time.

title: You May Require a Renter’s Policy - but Not Force-Place One by Fee
bodyText: South Dakota has no renter's-insurance statute. Nothing requires you to let the tenant choose the carrier, nothing sets a proof deadline, nothing authorises force-placed coverage or an administrative fee for arranging it, nothing requires a written advisory that your insurance will not cover the tenant's property, and nothing requires a flood notice where the lease does not require insurance. Requiring a renter's policy is simply a lawful lease term. How you enforce it is where South Dakota constrains you. There is no statutory authority to buy cover for the tenant and bill it, so a force-placement charge rests on the lease alone, and a fixed sum the tenant owes because they let a policy lapse is a penalty imposed by contract for nonperformance and void. An administrative fee on top of a force-placed premium is the clearest example: it corresponds to no loss you can measure and is precisely the kind of term the agreed-damages rule refuses to save. The enforceable route is to treat a lapse as a breach of the lease and act on it, or to recover the actual documented premium you paid if the lease plainly permits you to buy cover and charge the cost. Even then, a charge is only collectible from the deposit if the lease makes it funds due to you under an agreement. The cautious course is to require a policy with a stated minimum liability limit, let the tenant choose the insurer, ask for a certificate at move-in and each renewal, and say in the lease, plainly, that your insurance does not cover the tenant's belongings or liability.

title: The Only Repair-Cost Threshold in South Dakota Runs Against You
bodyText: South Dakota does put a cost figure on repairs, and it is worth knowing exactly which way it points. Where the cost of the necessary repairs exceeds one month's rent, the tenant gets an extra remedy: after written notice stating the specific reason, the tenant may stop paying rent to you and deposit it instead in a separate bank or savings and loan account, held only for repairs, until you do the work or until enough has built up for the tenant to have it done. That is the whole of what the one-month threshold does. It is a trigger for the tenant, not a ceiling on your duty. You have no right to refuse a repair because it would cost more than the rent, more than the unit is worth, or more than you think reasonable, and no right to end the tenancy because a repair has become uneconomical. The habitability duty is flat, it runs for the whole term, and you may not waive or modify it. Your grounds for ending a lease early are the tenant using the premises contrary to the agreement and the tenant failing to make repairs the tenant is bound to make, neither of which is about your costs. The cost-driven escape that does exist belongs to the tenant, on destruction of the greater part of the premises or of what induced the tenant to lease. The cautious course on a repair you cannot justify is to negotiate an end to the tenancy or, on a month-to-month, use the ordinary termination route. Never make the repair a condition of staying, and never put a cost-based termination right for yourself in the lease.

title: No Way Out of the Rent-Escrow Remedy
bodyText: South Dakota gives the tenant a rent-escrow remedy and gives you no way to opt out of it. Where you neglect repairs for a reasonable time after notice of conditions requiring repair to make the premises fit for human habitation and to place them in good and safe working order, the tenant may repair and deduct the cost from rent, or vacate and be discharged from further rent. Where the cost of necessary repairs exceeds one month's rent, the tenant may withhold rent and immediately deposit it in a separate bank or savings and loan account maintained only for making the repairs, after written notice stating the specific reason for the withholding and with written evidence of the deposit given to you. Every notice duty in that scheme runs toward you, not from you. There is no exemption for small owners, no unit-count threshold, no registration or certification that switches the remedy off, and so no notice you could give to claim one. There is nothing to disclose and nothing to elect. Nor can you contract around it. The habitability duty itself cannot be waived or modified by the parties, these remedies are how that duty is enforced, and a lease term restricting a party from enforcing rights by the usual legal proceedings is void. The cautious course is to drop any exemption or waiver recital from your lease and put a working process in its place: one written channel for repair requests, a dated log of each request and your response, and a turnaround short enough that a reasonable time never runs out while you are still deciding. The one arrangement the statute does bless is the tenant performing specified repairs or maintenance in lieu of rent; put that in writing and describe the work.

title: Notice Starts the Clock, and Only Two of the Remedies Need It in Writing
bodyText: South Dakota conditions the tenant's repair remedies on notice to you, and the statute is deliberately uneven about the form that notice takes. For the two fastest remedies, repairing the condition and deducting the cost, and vacating and being discharged from further rent, the repair statute says only notice. No writing, no prescribed address, no prescribed wording. A phone call to your manager starts the reasonable time in which you must act, and so does a text message or a complaint made in person. Writing is required for exactly two things: withholding rent into a separate account, which needs written notice stating the specific reason for the withholding, and terminating the lease for your failure to put the premises into good condition or repair them, which needs a written request first. That unevenness decides the question landlords usually ask. A lease term requiring all repair requests to be in writing most likely cannot convert the bare-notice limbs into written-notice limbs, because the habitability duty behind them is one you may not waive or modify. The non-waiver sentence sits in the duty section, not the remedies section, so no statute settles this in terms; plan as if a court will not enforce such a term. Designating a verbal channel costs you nothing you ever had. Note too that your own right to end the lease for a tenant who will not make repairs the tenant is bound to make runs on a request after a reasonable time, with no writing specified either. The cautious course is to treat any complaint through any channel as notice, date it, log who received it, and answer in writing with what you will do and when. Ask for written requests as a convenience and never as a condition, and assume a tenant who gave you written notice of a condition requiring repair now has the retaliation statute available.

title: The Complete South Dakota Disclosure Picture
bodyText: South Dakota requires exactly one disclosure in a residential lease, and it is narrow. If you actually know methamphetamine was previously manufactured on the premises you must tell any lessee or prospective lessee, and in a multi-unit building the duty covers only the unit you know about. That is the whole of it. There is no state-prescribed lease form, no required page order, no type-size rule, and no statutory summary of tenant rights to hand over. FEDERAL: for target housing built before 1978 you must also give the lead hazard pamphlet, disclose known lead-based paint and hazards or state you have no knowledge, include the verbatim warning statement and signed acknowledgements, and keep the records three years. Almost every disclosure landlords expect elsewhere is absent - bed bug, mold, radon, flood, military air zone, submetering, certificate of occupancy, condemnation order, owner identity, foreclosure - and there is no rental registration. Do not conclude the state is indifferent to disclosure. It puts the obligation on sellers, through a long mandated property-condition statement covering radon, lead paint, mold, asbestos, buried tanks and flood plain, which does not reach a letting. Use it as your voluntary checklist, and never pair a disclosure with a waiver of your habitability duty, which cannot be waived. One exception matters more than all of this, and it is easy to walk into. The seller regime defines a covered transfer to include a lease with an option to purchase, a bare option, and a ground lease coupled with improvements. Add a purchase option to a lease of not more than four dwelling units in one structure and you must give the tenant-buyer that completed statement, in good faith, before they make a written offer - with liability if you do not.

title: No Required-Fee Disclosure List - Which Is Why the Lease Must Carry Every Charge
bodyText: South Dakota requires no list of fees in the lease. There is no duty to state each required fee with its purpose, no total-monthly-payment label, no notice period for adding a fee later, no cap on a markup over a third-party-billed service, and no bar on charging for maintenance of common areas. None of the structures other states have built exists here. The practical rule is the inverse and it matters more than a disclosure duty would. Your right to collect anything other than rent depends on the lease creating the obligation, because the deposit statute lets you withhold only amounts reasonably necessary to remedy defaults in the payment of rent and of other funds due to you under an agreement, and to restore the premises. A charge the lease never mentions is not funds due under an agreement. Worse, withholding it is a failure to comply with the section, and that forfeits all rights to withhold any portion of the deposit. So an unlisted fee does not merely fail - it can cost you the whole deposit. Adding a fee mid-tenancy has only one reliable route: on a month-to-month tenancy you may modify the terms on written notice given at least thirty days before the end of the month, with the tenant then free to terminate effective the first of the next month by notifying you within fifteen days. The cautious course is a single schedule in the lease naming every non-optional charge, its amount, its purpose and when it is due, and third-party-billed services recovered at the amount you were actually billed.

title: No State Rights Guide to Hand Over
bodyText: South Dakota publishes no landlord-tenant rights and responsibilities guide that you must give a tenant, and no statute requires you to deliver one, to deliver it again at renewal, or to collect a signed acknowledgment that the tenant received it. There is no statutory summary of the law to attach either - no prescribed recital of the deposit rules, the habitability duty or the entry standard. This is worth stating plainly because the absence is easy to misread in two directions. It does not mean there are no disclosure duties: the deposit statutes require a written statement of reasons when you withhold, and an itemized accounting on request, and the lease-option and association disclosures bite where they apply. What it means is narrower - there is no document the state has written for this purpose and no acknowledgment page to add to your signing packet. Nor is there a penalty attached to not providing one, since there is nothing to provide. A landlord moving from a state with a mandatory guide should take the acknowledgment page out rather than leave it in, because a signed receipt for a guide that does not exist invites an argument about what the tenant was told. If you want the tenant to understand the rules, write a short plain-language summary of your own and attach it as information rather than as a statutory notice, and keep it accurate. The cautious course is to say in the lease that the summary is informational and that the lease and the statutes govern.

title: No House-Rule Statute - Your Rules Bind as Contract Terms
bodyText: South Dakota has no house-rule statute. There are no enforceability conditions a rule must satisfy - no requirement that it promote convenience, safety or welfare, be reasonably related to that purpose, apply fairly to all tenants or be explicit enough to give notice - and no statutory limit on changing rules mid-tenancy. Nor is there a retaliation presumption for a substantial alteration in the terms of a tenancy. Your rules bind because the lease makes them terms of the agreement, and they bind to the extent the lease says so. Two consequences follow, and they point in opposite directions. Because no statute supplies enforceability conditions, a rule does not fail merely for being unreasonable - but it also gets no statutory support, so a rule the lease does not incorporate is not binding at all. Attach the rules, or describe them, and say the tenant must comply with them. Changing them mid-tenancy is where care is needed. On a month-to-month tenancy you have a real mechanism: you may modify the terms of the lease on written notice given at least thirty days before the end of the month, and the notice operates by itself to establish the new terms if the tenant holds over, with the tenant free to terminate effective the first of the next month by notifying you within fifteen days. On a fixed term you have no such power, so a new rule binds only if the tenant agrees in writing or it is made part of a renewal. The cautious course is to put the rules in the lease, reserve the statutory modification route expressly for periodic tenancies, and get written agreement for anything mid-term.

title: Selling the Property or Changing Who Manages It
bodyText: South Dakota answers the tenancy side of a sale with old conveyancing law and nothing more. A grant of the rents, the reversion or a remainder is effective without any attornment by the tenant, so your buyer needs nothing from the tenant to take over. The person to whom the property is transferred or devised gets the same remedies you had for recovering rent, for nonperformance of any lease term, and for waste or any cause of forfeiture. Conversely, the tenant's remedies for breach run against your assigns as well as against you, with one important exception: not on covenants against encumbrances or relating to title or possession. And a tenant's attornment to a stranger is void unless you consent or a court orders it, protecting a buyer against a tenant who starts paying the wrong person. What South Dakota does not do is impose any duty on you. There is no obligation to tell the tenant the property is for sale or sold, no landlord-identity or identity-change notice, no estoppel certificate scheme, no seller-disclosure duty to a tenant, and no statutory release of the selling landlord. One sale-specific rule is worth knowing: the extended two-month notice a tenant at will on active military service would otherwise get does not apply once you have sold the property or it has passed to your estate. The cautious course is to do by contract what no statute requires. Tell the tenant in writing who the new owner and manager are and where to pay, before the first payment is due. Assign the lease and transfer the deposit at closing against a written acknowledgment that the buyer has taken on the accounting duty, and keep your copy, because nothing else discharges you. Rent changes on a month-to-month tenancy still need the usual notice.

title: No Health-Code Variance to Disclose - Because There Is No Code
bodyText: South Dakota has no state sanitary or health code for residential rentals, so there is no variance mechanism and nothing to disclose. Nothing requires you to give a tenant a variance, to attach one to the rental agreement, or to tell a tenant that a condition has been permitted by an authority. States with a housing sanitary code typically have all three; South Dakota has none of them because the predicate code does not exist. The variance machinery South Dakota does have is in zoning rather than housing: county and municipal boards of adjustment consider variances in hardship cases, with expiry provisions for a special permitted use, conditional use or variance. Those concern land use and the position of buildings, not the habitability of a dwelling, and a zoning variance says nothing to a tenant about the condition of the unit. So there is no document to pass on. The duty that remains is the general one, and it is unaffected by any permission a local authority may have granted: you must keep the premises and all common areas in reasonable repair and fit for human habitation and in good and safe working order throughout the term, and that cannot be waived or modified. A variance from a local ordinance cannot reduce it, because the statutory duty is additional to any covenant imposed by law or ordinance rather than displaced by one. The cautious course, if a local authority has permitted something unusual about the property, is to disclose it in writing anyway and to keep the permission with the lease.

title: What South Dakota’s Lease Law Covers - and What It Leaves Out
bodyText: South Dakota has no residential landlord and tenant act, so there is no act whose scope you need to check - and that is the single most important fact about the state for you. What governs instead is a general leasing chapter applying to every hiring of real property, with residential-specific duties inserted into it, plus a separate forcible entry and detainer chapter and a separate chapter on estates at will. There is no population threshold, no local-adoption requirement, no list of covered counties, no lease-date gating of core duties and no multiple-dwelling definition, because there is no act to switch on. Several consequences follow for you. The habitability duty applies in every hiring of residential premises, whether in writing or oral, so your informal arrangement carries it. There is no mobile home park act: manufactured and mobile home communities are reached through the same general provisions, and the retaliation section expressly names a manufactured or mobile home community owner. Agricultural tenancies are not carved out of the leasing chapter but have their own provisions within it, including a twenty-year cap and a continuation rule for oral farm leases of forty acres or more. There is no long-term-lease exclusion, so a lease of any length is governed the same way. And tribal land is outside the scope of these entries entirely - a lease on or within a reservation, or on trust land, raises questions of tribal and federal jurisdiction that state law does not answer, so get advice directed at that before you let. Local ordinances are the real source of sub-state variation and are not resolved here.

title: No Seasonal Tenancy Category
bodyText: South Dakota has no seasonal tenancy category and no exemption for one. Nothing distinguishes a summer letting, a hunting-season rental or a winter-only tenancy from any other residential tenancy, and nothing reduces your duties because the letting is short or seasonal. That is the practical point: the habitability duty, the deposit cap and timetable, the entry standard, the termination notices and your tenant's repair remedies all apply to a seasonal residential letting in full, and the habitability duty cannot be waived. If your lease treats a seasonal cabin as outside the rules, it is simply wrong about the law. Two distinctions do exist and are worth keeping straight. Transient lodging is genuinely separate: hotels, motels, specialty resorts, bed and breakfast establishments, vacation home establishments and campgrounds are licensed and regulated as lodging, with their own fire-safety, sanitation and pool rules and their own ejection grounds - so a short-stay operation of yours may be a lodging establishment rather than a tenancy, which changes the whole analysis. And agricultural lettings have their own provisions within the lease chapter, including a twenty-year cap and a continuation rule for oral farm leases of forty acres or more, with notice by September first and termination the following March first. Neither of those is a seasonal-residential category. The cautious course is to decide which regime your short letting actually falls into - residential tenancy or licensed lodging - and to comply with that one fully, rather than assuming a seasonal letting sits somewhere between them.

title: Where You Keep the Deposit Is Up to You
bodyText: South Dakota tells you nothing about where to keep a deposit. There is no trust-account requirement, no escrow or segregation duty, no bar on mixing deposit money with your own, no obligation to use an interest-bearing or any other particular account, no duty to give the tenant the name and address of the depository, and no bond you may post in place of holding the money. There is no small-owner exception either, because there is no rule for an exception to carve out of. Chapter titles mislead here: the chapter on deposit of personal property is bailment law about goods, so your position is debtor and creditor - you owe the tenant the money, you do not hold it in trust. What constrains you is what you must do with the money, not where it sits. The ceiling is one month's rent, you must return it or furnish a written statement of your specific reasons within twenty-one days, you must give an itemized accounting within forty-five days on request, and any failure to comply forfeits all rights to withhold any part of it. The cautious course is to keep deposits in a separate account anyway: it costs nothing and stops the money being spent and then unavailable against a twenty-one-day deadline. A licence changes this. A licensed property manager or broker managing for you must deposit every security deposit in a federally insured financial institution and keep it as a separate ledger balance. Mixing others' money with the licensee's own is unprofessional conduct. So if a licensee holds your tenants' deposits, those rules govern the account.

title: No Interest Is Owed on a Deposit
bodyText: South Dakota requires no interest on a residential security deposit. No statute makes you pay interest, accrue it, credit it annually or at an anniversary, hold the deposit in an interest-bearing account, or account to the tenant for interest you do in fact earn. There is no rate, no formula and no index tied to a federal body, so none of the uncertainty that arises in states whose rate-setting reference no longer exists. There is no unit-count threshold and no guarantee bond you may post in place of paying interest, because there is no interest rule for either to modify. Interest earned on deposit money you hold is therefore yours. The cap limits what you may demand or receive from the tenant, and interest accruing in your own account is not money you demanded or received, which is the better reading of the cap even though the statute does not say so in those words. The real exposure is not the law but your own lease. If the lease promises interest you owe what you promised, and a promise to pay at a stated rate or to hold the money in an interest-bearing account binds you even though no statute would have required either. So say nothing about interest unless you mean it, and if you do choose to pay it, state the rate, the periods and when it is paid. Two further points. Interest changes none of the deadlines: the deposit, plus anything you have agreed to add to it, is returned or explained within twenty-one days and itemized within forty-five on request. And where a refund goes unclaimed, both the deposit and any interest on it are intangible property under the state's unclaimed-property act, which names interest and security deposits expressly.

title: No Non-Waiver Clause - but the Deposit Rules Defeat Evasion Anyway
bodyText: South Dakota's deposit sections contain no sentence saying the tenant may not waive them. They do not need one, because they are written so that a lease term cannot get around them. The cap and the definition work together: any money whose function is to secure performance of a residential rental agreement, or any part of one, is deemed to be a security deposit, and a landlord may not demand or receive a security deposit, however denominated, exceeding one month's rent. A larger deposit is permitted only where special conditions pose a danger to maintenance of the premises, and only by agreement. So a lease cannot escape the cap by renaming the money, and cannot escape it by a bare recital that the tenant agrees to a larger sum. The return rules work the same way, through forfeiture rather than prohibition: a landlord who fails to comply with the return section forfeits all rights to withhold any portion of the deposit, and bad-faith retention, or bad-faith failure to provide the written statement or itemized accounting, exposes you to punitive damages. A clause saying the tenant waives the itemized accounting, or agrees the deposit is forfeited on early termination, does not survive that structure - the first conflicts with a duty whose breach costs you the whole withholding right, and the second is a penalty for nonperformance, which South Dakota voids. The practical rule: the deposit rules are not a default you can contract out of, so write the lease to comply with them rather than around them.

title: How the Deposit Penalty Is Built - and What It Does Not Reach
bodyText: South Dakota's deposit penalty has three distinct parts, and the one that costs you most asks nothing about your state of mind. Any failure to comply with the return section forfeits all rights to withhold any portion of the deposit. Not the disputed portion, all of it, and not only where the failure was deliberate. Miss the twenty-one days, send a statement that does not give a specific reason, or ignore a request for the itemized accounting, and the whole deposit goes back whatever the tenant actually owes you. The second part does require bad faith: bad-faith retention of the deposit or any part of it, or a bad-faith failure to provide the written statement or the itemized accounting, exposes you to punitive damages. That figure is a ceiling of two hundred dollars rather than a multiple of the deposit, so South Dakota's punitive exposure is modest beside states that double or treble the amount withheld. The third part is what the statute leaves alone. It forfeits your right to withhold; it does not by its terms bar a separate action against the tenant for damage to the premises or for unpaid rent, and the chapter expressly preserves all other rights and remedies. A missed deadline therefore costs you the deposit as a source of payment rather than the claim itself, though you have surrendered your security and will be chasing a former tenant for it. Much larger exposure sits elsewhere in the chapter: unlawfully removing or excluding the tenant, or willfully interrupting electricity, gas, water or another essential service, costs you two months' rent plus the return of all advance rent and the deposit. The cautious course is to treat both dates as immovable and to give a specific written reason for every dollar you keep.

title: No Duty to Publish Your Deposit Standards
bodyText: South Dakota imposes no duty to publish, post or disclose the standards you use to set a deposit. Nothing requires you to hand your calculation criteria to an applicant before signing, nothing is triggered by owning more than four adjoining units or any other number of units, and nothing obliges you to charge every applicant the same amount. The statute controls the ceiling rather than the method: your deposit may not exceed one month's rent, and the only route above that ceiling is agreement with the tenant where special conditions genuinely pose a danger to maintenance of the premises. That exception is the closest thing South Dakota has to a differing-standards rule, and no posting or disclosure duty attaches to it. Two things should still shape how you set deposits. The exception is the only lawful way above one month, so when you charge more, record in the lease the specific condition that poses the danger, whether a pet, an unusual appliance or a business use of the unit, because that writing is the entire justification and an unexplained larger deposit is simply over the cap. And although no deposit-disclosure statute exists, state law makes it an unfair or discriminatory practice to discriminate in the terms, conditions or privileges of a rental because of race, color, creed, religion, sex, ancestry, disability, familial status or national origin. A deposit amount is a term of the rental, so varying it from applicant to applicant without a recorded reason tied to the unit or the tenancy is where the real exposure lies. The cautious course is to write your criteria down for your own use, apply them uniformly, and depart from them only for a documented condition of the premises rather than anything about the applicant.

title: No Mandatory Locks, Deadbolts, Peepholes or Rekeying
bodyText: South Dakota mandates no security hardware. There is no deadbolt requirement, no keyless bolting device, no window latch specification, no peephole or door-viewer rule for multi-unit buildings, no construction-date trigger, and no duty to rekey between tenancies. Nothing has to be installed and nothing has to be changed when a tenant leaves. The duty that does apply reaches hardware through its condition rather than its specification: you must keep the premises and all common areas in reasonable repair and fit for human habitation and in good and safe working order, and maintain the electrical, plumbing and heating systems in good and safe working order and condition - and you may not waive or modify any of it. A door that will not lock, a broken window latch or an exterior door that cannot be secured is a failure of that duty, so what you install is your choice but keeping it working is not. Two practical points. Rekeying between tenancies is not required but is the cheapest risk reduction available to you, because a former tenant's unreturned key is a liability you cannot see; and the lawful way to charge a departing tenant for it is documented actual cost, not a fixed fee, which would be void as a penalty. Second, remember what you may not do with locks: changing them to exclude a tenant costs two months' rent plus the return of all advance rent and deposit, and forcible exclusion from possession is measured at three times the compensatory sum. The cautious course is deadbolts on exterior doors, working window latches, rekeying at every turnover, and a written record of it.

title: No Work Card for Age-Restricted Housing Staff
bodyText:
South Dakota has no work card, staff permit, registration or mandatory background check for the people who work in age-restricted housing. Nothing of that kind exists anywhere in the state's law under any name. The Code carries many compulsory screening provisions and every one attaches to public employment or to a licensed occupation, not to the staff of a private landlord, and age-restricted housing is treated no differently from any other rental in this respect.

What South Dakota does regulate about senior housing is who you may exclude, not who you may employ. Discrimination on the basis of familial status is unlawful in housing, and familial status for that purpose means children under eighteen domiciled with a parent or custodian, including someone pregnant or securing custody. The age-restriction exemptions sit in their own short section and are the only thing that makes a seniors-only property lawful. They cover residences publicised as designated for older or disabled residents where a state or federal programme has designated them for the elderly, or where they are intended for and solely occupied by people aged sixty-two or older, or where the facilities and services are designed for the needs of the elderly and at least eighty per cent of the units are occupied or intended for one or more people aged fifty-five or older. The section says nothing whatever about staff.

The cautious course is to document the exemption you rely on and the occupancy percentage that supports it, review the figure annually, and screen anyone who will hold keys or enter occupied units because you have no statutory shield either way and negligent hiring is the real exposure. Federal rules for housing for older persons run alongside the state exemptions.

title: South Dakota's Only Military Rule Runs Against You, Not For the Tenant
bodyText:
