South Dakota has exactly one military provision in its landlord and tenant law, and landlords consistently get it backwards. It is not a tenant termination right. It is a longer notice you must give. Where a residential tenancy at will is the home of a tenant on active military service, or of a tenant whose spouse or minor child is on active military service, your notice to end it runs two months instead of the ordinary fifteen days. Two exceptions cut it back to the ordinary notice: sustained conduct that is disruptive, illegal, destructive, negligent towards maintaining the property, or a material breach; or your having sold the property or its having passed to your estate. The Legislature amended this section in 2024 and left the military limb in place.

Notice the limits. It applies to a tenancy at will, so it does nothing to a fixed-term lease. It defines immediate family narrowly, as a spouse or a minor child, so a parent or sibling on active service does not trigger it. And there is nothing else: South Dakota has no state Servicemembers Civil Relief Act, does not incorporate the federal one, extends nothing to Guard members on state orders, sets no deadline for deciding a servicemember's application, and gives no eviction stay keyed to a rent ceiling. The only other military provisions touching a tenancy are rental preferences inside public housing projects, which do not reach your units.

The cautious course is to ask on every application whether any occupant is on active service, record the answer, and check it before serving notice on a tenancy with no fixed end date, serving two months unless an exception plainly applies. A tenant's own right to break a lease on orders comes from federal law, not from South Dakota.

title: No Sex-Offender Disclosure Duty - and Your Agent Has None Either
bodyText: South Dakota imposes no duty on a landlord to tell a tenant that a registered sex offender lives on or near the property, and the legislature has addressed the nearest case in terms: licensed agents owe none. No licensee representing a seller or landlord has a duty to investigate, volunteer or disclose information regarding a registered sex offender residing on or near the property. So a property manager or listing agent you use carries no disclosure obligation, and no statute imposes one on you. The mirror provision is worth knowing because it is the one that can produce a conversation: a licensee representing a buyer or tenant likewise has no duty to investigate or volunteer, but on the client's inquiry that licensee must disclose any actual knowledge they have about a registered offender on or near the property. So the information can reach an applicant through their own agent, truthfully, and nothing you do controls that. What South Dakota regulates instead is where a registrant may live, and that duty is the registrant's: a person required to register may not establish a residence within five hundred feet of a school, a public park, playground or pool, a licensed day care centre, a licensed group family day care home, a registered family day care, or a domestic abuse or sexual assault shelter, subject to listed exceptions. The registry itself is public. The cautious course is to say nothing about offenders either way, answer an applicant's direct question by pointing them to the public registry rather than characterising it yourself, and never represent that a property or neighbourhood is free of registrants.

title: Community Safety Zones Restrict the Tenant, Not You
bodyText: South Dakota regulates where a registered sex offender may live, and it is worth knowing because the duty falls on the tenant rather than on you. A person required to register may not establish a residence or reside within a community safety zone, which means the area within five hundred feet of the facilities and grounds of a school, a public park, playground or pool, a licensed day care center, a licensed group family day care home, a registered family day care, a domestic abuse shelter or a sexual assault shelter, including the grounds themselves. There are exceptions - among them incarceration or a correctional placement in the zone, an assigned halfway house or supervised living centre, admission to a community homeless shelter by an appropriate official, placement in a licensed health care facility, an offence committed under eighteen and not tried as an adult, and a residence established and inhabited before the zone existed - and a long-standing registrant may petition for an exemption on clear and convincing evidence after ten years and if not a recidivist. Two things South Dakota does not do. It imposes no duty on a landlord to check the registry, to refuse an applicant, or to police proximity, and it makes no offence of knowingly leasing to registered offenders who live together. And it takes the question away from cities: no city, county, municipality or township may by local ordinance restrict or mitigate offender residence or community access inconsistently with the state scheme, so a local co-residence ordinance with a lease-statement safe harbour for owners is not something you will meet here. Screening applicants remains yours to do, within fair-housing limits.

title: No Single-Family Occupancy Disclosure
bodyText: South Dakota requires no disclosure that a dwelling is or is not a single-family residence, and there is nothing for such a disclosure to do here. In the states that mandate one, the disclosure exists because the landlord-tenant act carves single-family rentals out of some of its protections, so the tenant must be told which regime they are in; and because those statutes often dictate how the notice looks, requiring a relative type size or placement on the first page. South Dakota has no uniform residential landlord and tenant act, so there is no coverage line to disclose across. The residential lease statutes apply to the hiring of residential premises without regard to how many units the building holds, with two exceptions you should know rather than disclose. The methamphetamine disclosure, which is the state's one mandated lease disclosure, narrows in a building of two or more units to the unit you actually know about. And the state fair housing exemption for refusal to rent and discriminatory terms turns on a dwelling with living quarters for no more than two families where the owner occupies one of them, not on single-family status as such, and it does not reach discriminatory advertising. South Dakota also has no statutory lease form, no mandated first-page content and no type-size rule of any kind, so a separate signed page is a drafting choice rather than a compliance requirement. The cautious course is to describe the premises precisely in the lease, say how many dwelling units the building contains and what is exclusive to the tenant as against shared, and not to import another state's single-family disclosure language, which here would state a legal consequence that does not exist.

title: No Shoreline or Water-Access Disclosure Duty
bodyText: South Dakota requires no disclosure about shoreline, lakeshore or river access in a residential lease. Nothing obliges you to tell a tenant whether the property includes water access, whether access crosses someone else's land, whether a shoreline is subject to public use, or whether access may be lost when water levels change. Nothing requires a plat, a survey or a statement of riparian rights. For a lakeside or riverside rental the practical issue is not compliance but expectation, and South Dakota's lease law gives that teeth in one specific way. A tenant may terminate the lease before the end of the term if the part of the premises that was, and that you had reason to believe at the time of leasing was, the material inducement for the tenant to enter the lease is destroyed other than by the tenant's own ordinary negligence. A property marketed for its water frontage is one where the inducement is identifiable, and a lost or unusable shoreline is the kind of change that invites the argument. Add to that the general consumer-protection exposure for a misrepresentation in connection with a sale or lease. So the cautious course is to describe water access accurately and in writing - whether it is included, whether it is shared, over whose land it runs, and that levels and conditions vary and are outside your control - and to avoid promising a condition you cannot guarantee. Where access depends on a permit, an association or a neighbour's permission, say so and attach the document.

title: Showing Notice May Be Shortened by Agreement in the Lease
bodyText: South Dakota both sets an entry-notice standard and tells you how to vary it. The standard is that, except in an emergency or where it is impracticable, you must give the tenant reasonable notice of your intent to enter and enter only at reasonable times, and twenty-four hours' written notice is presumed reasonable. The notice must state the date or dates of entry, a period during normal business hours, the purpose, and a means for the tenant to ask to reschedule. The variation is in the same sentence as the presumption: the twenty-four-hour presumption applies unless alternate methods of notification or times for entry are mutually agreed upon between you and the tenant in the lease. So a shorter or different showing notice is lawful if the lease says so, and South Dakota requires no separate signed waiver document for it. Two cautions. What the agreement displaces is the twenty-four-hour presumption, not the standard behind it - reasonable notice, reasonable times - so an agreed alternative still has to be reasonable, and the shorter it is the harder that gets. And the agreement must be mutual and in the lease; a notice you hand out later announcing a new entry rule is not an agreement. The safe shape is a narrow term: shorter notice for showings only, confined to the closing weeks of the tenancy or after either party gives notice of termination, within stated daytime hours, with every other entry left on the ordinary notice.

title: No Rent Protection for Government Workers in a Shutdown
bodyText: South Dakota has no rent-timing protection for government employees during a federal or state shutdown. There is no grace period, no bar on late fees, no deferral right, no prohibition on filing an eviction, and no requirement to accept a payment plan. A furloughed tenant's rent is due when the lease says it is due, and the eviction ground matures when rent has been unpaid for three days. Nothing in South Dakota law changes that for any category of tenant. Two things remain available and are worth doing deliberately rather than by default. You may always agree a deferral, and the lease's own terms are the place to record it - a short written variation stating the deferred amount, when it will be paid and that you are not waiving your rights otherwise is better than an informal indulgence that later becomes an argument about whether you accepted a new arrangement. Be careful about accepting part payments without saying what they are for: South Dakota has no partial-payment statute, so the consequences of acceptance are governed by your lease and general contract law, and acceptance of rent from a tenant holding over after a term is presumed to renew the hiring on the same terms. There is also a federal protection worth remembering for a different group: a servicemember's protections on entering military service are federal and do not depend on a shutdown. The cautious course is a written short-term agreement, kept separate from the lease, with the figures and dates spelled out.

title: No State Limit on Renting in Single-Family Zones
bodyText: South Dakota places no limit on renting out a home in a single-family zone and imposes no owner-occupancy condition on doing so. There is no state cap on the number of rentals on a street or in a district, no registration or licence tied to a single-family zone, and no provision of the kind one state has enacted for a single county restricting new leases unless the owner lives on the lot. The subject is left entirely to local zoning, and that is where to look: a municipality or county may define districts and permitted uses, and some South Dakota cities regulate rental occupancy in low-density districts through occupancy limits, rental licensing or unrelated-occupant rules. Those ordinances are not resolved here and you should check your own city's before letting a house in a single-family district, particularly if the household will be unrelated adults. Two state-law points bound what a local rule can do to you once a tenancy exists. A lease is a contract for temporary possession and use of real property for reward, and the tenancy rules apply to it whatever the zoning says - the non-waivable habitability duty, the deposit cap and timetable, the entry standard and the termination notices all run normally. And a zoning problem is not itself a ground for forcible entry and detainer: none of the seven statutory grounds is a permitted-use or zoning ground. The closest is a lessee who does or fails to perform any act which under the lease operates to terminate it - so zoning reaches eviction only if your lease makes lawful permitted use such a term. The cautious course is to confirm permitted use before you let, because you cannot evict your way out of a zoning violation.

title: No Smart-Lock Statute - the General Entry Rule Still Applies
bodyText: South Dakota has no statute about smart locks, app-based entry, keyless systems or the data they generate. Nothing requires you to offer a physical key alongside an electronic credential, nothing limits what entry logs you may keep or how long, nothing obliges you to disclose that a door records access, and nothing bars using a remote credential to lock a tenant out. States are beginning to legislate here; South Dakota has not. The general law still governs two things that matter. Entry is entry whoever or whatever opens the door: except in an emergency or where it is impracticable, you owe reasonable notice of your intent to enter and must enter only at reasonable times, and a remote unlock is an entry. And using a smart system to cut off access is the serious risk. Unlawfully removing or excluding a tenant from the premises exposes you to damages equal to two months' rent plus the return of all advance rent and deposit, and a separate provision measures damages for forcibly excluding a person from possession of real property at three times the compensatory sum. Revoking a credential is quieter than changing a lock and is no safer legally. The cautious course is to treat the system as a lock: document what credentials exist and who holds them, do not disable a tenant's access for any reason short of a court order, give the tenant a means of entry that works if the network or a battery fails, and say in the lease who may hold credentials and what happens at move-out.

title: Smoking Is Already Illegal in Your Enclosed Common Areas
bodyText: Most landlords treat smoke drift as purely a lease question. In South Dakota part of it is already settled by statute, and not in the direction people expect. No person may smoke a tobacco product, or carry a lighted one, in any public place or place of employment, and a place of employment means any enclosed area under the control of a public or private employer. An enclosed common hallway, stairwell, laundry room or lobby of an apartment building managed by a company with employees is an enclosed area under an employer's control, so smoking there is already a petty offense. The exemption people remember - that the rules do not apply to a private residence unless it is used for day care - covers the dwelling unit, not the common areas. Two consequences follow. First, you have an affirmative duty: a person who owns, manages, operates or otherwise controls a public place or place of employment must inform violators of the prohibition, and failing to do so is itself a petty offense. Second, a lease term in which the tenant accepts or waives complaints about smoke cannot license smoking in those common areas, because a provision contrary to an express provision of law, or to the policy of express law, is unlawful. Inside the unit it is different: ch. 34-46 does not reach a private residence, so whether smoking is permitted there is yours to set by lease, and a drift acknowledgment about smoke from other units is an ordinary contract term. What it cannot do is cut off the habitability duty, which cannot be waived or modified, if drift is bad enough to make a unit unfit. Vapor products count: tobacco product includes a vapor product.

title: No Benefit-Delay Defence, and Collecting Against Benefit Income Is Mostly Federal
bodyText:
South Dakota gives a tenant no defence, continuance or reinstatement because a government benefit or a housing voucher arrived late. The eviction statute carries seven grounds and no benefit limb, and the only adjournment it allows is one the tenant buys by posting security for accruing rent and costs. Source of income is not a protected class, and the word voucher never means a housing voucher anywhere in the Code. A late benefit payment is simply late rent, and nonpayment for three days after it falls due is a filing ground.

Winning the judgment is the easy half. Collecting against a tenant whose income is a benefit is where the answer turns out to be federal, and that is the trap. The absolute-exemption schedule is a closed list of nine items - family pictures, a pew, a burial lot, the family Bible and library, clothing, a year's provisions and fuel, a narrow tax judgment, prescribed health aids and a small support award - and Social Security and public assistance are not on it. A separate million-dollar exemption covers retirement benefits, but only under employee benefit plans as that chapter defines them, which does not reach Social Security. Earnings are exempt only to the garnishment ceilings. So the shield over benefit income is federal: Social Security benefits are not subject to execution, levy, attachment or garnishment, and a bank must automatically protect recent direct deposits. One quirk cuts your way - the non-absolute exemptions do not apply to a debtor for the necessaries of life, but that list is only food, clothing and fuel, so rent is not among them.

The cautious course is to treat a benefit-funded tenancy as fully evictable but largely uncollectable, and to decide on that basis whether a money judgment is worth its filing fee.

title: No Source-of-Income Protection and No Voucher Mandate
bodyText: South Dakota does not protect source of income in housing, and nothing obliges you to accept a housing voucher or any other subsidy. The protected characteristics in South Dakota's housing provision are a closed list - race, colour, creed, religion, sex, ancestry, disability, familial status and national origin - and source of income, lawful source of income, receipt of public assistance and voucher participation appear nowhere in it or anywhere else in the Code. There is also no lease-statement duty about subsidy acceptance, which is the other half some states have. So declining an applicant because they would pay with a voucher is not prohibited discrimination under South Dakota law. Three cautions before you rely on that. Participation is voluntary only until you opt in: once you sign a housing assistance payments contract you are bound by its terms and by the agency's rules for that tenancy, including inspection and rent-reasonableness requirements, and those are contractual obligations rather than statutory ones. A policy that screens out voucher holders can still produce a disparate impact on a characteristic that is protected, which is a federal fair-housing exposure rather than a state one. And a city could in principle legislate in this area, so check local ordinances, which are not resolved here. If you do not intend to participate, say so consistently and apply the same income and screening criteria to every applicant, documented the same way, rather than making the voucher itself the stated reason.

title: No Special-District Rules for Rentals
bodyText: South Dakota has no provision giving a special district any role in a residential tenancy, and none requiring a landlord or tenant to deal with one. Special districts exist in South Dakota - sanitary districts, road districts, improvement districts and others - and they have their own governance, election and assessment powers, but none of them regulates a lease, requires a tenant form, or imposes a duty on a landlord as landlord. There is no district registration, no district inspection of rentals, and no district representation requirement in any proceeding. Where a district does reach a rental property, it reaches it as property rather than as a tenancy: through charges, assessments and service rules. That is where the practical risk sits, and it is worth connecting to the one real exposure South Dakota does create. A delinquent solid-waste fee levied by a municipality, county or subdivision may be certified to the county treasurer and must then be collected as a condition precedent to paying the real property tax on that parcel, and a delinquent municipal garbage collection fee is collected as a condition precedent to paying any other municipal utility charge. A district charge that goes unpaid therefore becomes the owner's problem regardless of who incurred it. The cautious course is to identify which districts levy against your property, keep those accounts in your own name where you can, build the cost into rent, and verify any tenant-held account is clear before returning the deposit.

title: No Sprinkler Disclosure Duty
bodyText: No South Dakota statute or rule requires you to tell a tenant whether the building has a fire sprinkler system, or to disclose that it does not. There is also no state grant or loan program for sprinkler retrofits in privately owned rental housing - nothing in South Dakota corresponds to the retrofit funding some states offer private owners. What South Dakota does have is the requirement itself rather than a disclosure about it: a sprinkler system must be installed throughout any new hotel, motel or multifamily residence housing six or more families, and a municipality may not require one in a detached one- or two-family dwelling or a townhouse of not more than three stories. Because there is no disclosure duty, the question is one of risk rather than compliance. If the building has no sprinklers, a short factual statement in the lease or a move-in packet costs nothing and forestalls a later claim that the tenant was led to expect protection the building does not have; the same goes for telling tenants not to hang anything from a sprinkler head where the building does have a system. Local ordinances are not resolved here, so check whether your city imposes a disclosure its own code requires.

title: Over One Year Must Be in Writing - Signed by You
bodyText: South Dakota's threshold is one year and the signature it demands is the landlord's. No agreement for the leasing of real property, or an interest in it, for longer than one year is valid unless the agreement, or a note or memorandum of it, is in writing and signed by the lessor or an agent authorised in writing. Three things in that sentence are easy to miss. The threshold is more than one year, not five or seven as in some states, so a two-year lease is already inside it. It is a validity rule, not a recording rule - an unwritten two-year lease is not merely unrecordable, it is invalid as an agreement for that term. And the signature required is the lessor's, with an agent's authority itself needing to be in writing, so a property manager signing without written authorisation is a real defect. What happens to an invalid long lease is the practically important part. The tenant in possession is not a trespasser; they hold under a tenancy the law supplies, and South Dakota's presumptions then decide its length - a hiring for an unspecified term is deemed renewed at the end of the term implied by law unless a party gives notice as long before expiry as the term itself, not exceeding one month, and a holdover whose rent you accept is presumed to have renewed on the same terms for the same time, not exceeding a year. So an oral long lease usually collapses into a periodic tenancy you can end on short notice - which may help you or hurt you. Put it in writing and sign it.

title: Every Number South Dakota Actually Fixes
bodyText: It is worth having South Dakota's statutory figures in one place, because there are few of them and landlords routinely assume caps that do not exist. The deposit cap is one month's rent, and a larger deposit may be agreed only where special conditions pose a danger to maintenance of the premises. The deposit clocks are twenty-one days to return the deposit or furnish a written statement of the specific reason for withholding, and forty-five days to give an itemised accounting if the tenant asks; bad-faith retention or failure to give the statement or accounting exposes you to punitive damages capped at two hundred dollars. Unlawful removal or exclusion, or wilful interruption of an essential service, costs two months' rent plus the return of all advance rent and deposit, and forcible exclusion from possession is measured at three times the compensatory sum. A residential tenancy at will ends on not less than fifteen days' written notice, or two months where the tenant or an immediate family member is on active military service. A reserved right of reentry needs three days' notice. Rent unpaid for three days matures the eviction ground; the appearance is five days from service; a continuance beyond fourteen days requires the tenant to give security for accruing rent. Rent changes on a month-to-month tenancy need thirty days' notice, with the tenant's fifteen-day termination right. The contract limitation period is six years. Abandoned property is presumed abandoned after ten days if worth five hundred dollars or less, and stored thirty days with a lien if worth more. And charging a gas or electricity consumer above the amount billed risks a five-hundred-dollar civil fine. There is no cap on rent, late fees, application fees or pet charges.

title: No Radiator Cover Requirement
bodyText: South Dakota has no steam radiator cover requirement. There is no duty to provide covers on request, no mandatory lease rider, no notice to tenants about requesting one, and no record-keeping obligation. Nothing in the statutes or the rules held for South Dakota mentions radiators at all. The duty that reaches a hot radiator is the general one, and it is worth being precise about its scope. You must maintain all heating systems of the premises in good and safe working order and condition, and keep the premises fit for human habitation and in good and safe working order, and you may not waive or modify that. A radiator that leaks, that cannot be controlled, that is overheating because a valve has failed, or that has an exposed steam pipe where the lagging has gone is a condition within the duty. A radiator that simply gets hot because it is a radiator is working as intended, and South Dakota imposes no obligation to shield it. So unlike a state with a cover statute, there is no request mechanism for a tenant to invoke and no safe harbour for you to meet. That makes a request worth honouring on its own merits rather than refusing on the footing that nothing requires it: a cover is inexpensive, a burn to a small child is not, and you have no statutory defence to point to if one happens. The cautious course is to supply covers where a unit will house young children, keep pipe lagging intact, make sure control valves work, and treat any report of an uncontrollable radiator as an urgent heating repair.

title: No Stigma Disclosure Duty - and None Needed for an Ordinary Lease
bodyText: South Dakota imposes no stigma disclosure duty on a landlord. Nothing requires you to disclose a death, a suicide, a homicide, a crime, a reputed haunting or any other psychological condition of a property, and nothing requires you to answer a prospective tenant's question about sex-offender registry information. Nor is there a provision protecting a landlord who does not disclose, which is what many states enact instead - the subject is simply absent. There is also no HIV or health-status provision in the rental context, though a diagnosis is health information and disability is a protected class, so making a tenancy turn on one is a discrimination problem rather than a disclosure problem. The disclosure machinery South Dakota does have belongs to sales. A seller of residential real property must give the buyer a completed property condition disclosure statement before a written offer, made in good faith, with liability for failing to comply. That matters to a landlord for one reason: the chapter's definition of a transfer includes a lease with an option to purchase, so if you let with an option, you are inside the disclosure regime and should complete the statement, in good faith, as a seller would. For an ordinary lease with no option you have no statutory disclosure duty at all, which puts the weight on not misrepresenting. The cautious course is to answer direct questions honestly, decline to speculate, and point a concerned applicant to the public registry rather than characterising what is on it.

title: No Duty to Supply a Stove or Refrigerator
bodyText: South Dakota does not require a residential landlord to supply a stove, a refrigerator or any other cooking or food-storage appliance. There is no provision making either a condition of habitability, and no rule about replacing one that fails. A unit let without them is not for that reason unfit. What the statute does require is the systems behind them: all electrical, plumbing and heating systems of the premises must be maintained in good and safe working order and condition, and the premises must be fit for human habitation and in good and safe working order throughout the term, none of which may be waived or modified. So the wiring and the gas line serving a kitchen are yours whether or not the appliance plugged into them is. If you do supply appliances, two consequences follow. They become part of what the tenant has rented, and the tenant's statutory duty to preserve the premises expressly extends to appliances and to repairing deterioration from the tenant's own negligent, wilful or malicious conduct - so careless damage is recoverable without a special lease term. And a broken appliance you supplied is a repair item under your general duty rather than a matter of grace, because the thing is part of the premises as let. One practical safety point: South Dakota treats the abandonment of an air-tight refrigerator or similar item as a hazard, so dispose of a replaced unit properly rather than leaving it in a yard or basement. The cautious course is a signed appliance schedule with condition noted at move-in.

title: Student Status Is Not Protected, and One Exemption You Probably Cannot Use
bodyText:
South Dakota has no student-housing regime. There is no licence, registration or certification for letting to students, no occupancy or inspection rule aimed at student lets, no cap on what a student may be charged, and student status is not a protected class, so you may decline an applicant for being a student. Nothing in the leasing law treats a per-bedroom or co-signed lease differently from any other lease.

There is one student provision, and it is narrower than it looks. The fair housing section carves out dormitory residences maintained by a public or private school, college or university for the educational benefit and convenience of unmarried students, and dwellings occupied by fraternities or sororities officially recognised by such an institution. Read that carefully before relying on it. It exempts housing maintained by the institution, or occupied by a recognised chapter, not privately owned housing let to students near a campus. A landlord who is not the institution and whose building is not a recognised chapter house is fully subject to the discrimination ban, and the sex-discrimination exemption for social fraternities and sororities that provide living quarters to members works the same way. The same section also preserves reasonable occupancy standards, which is what actually governs how many students you may put in a unit.

The cautious course is to treat a student let as an ordinary tenancy. Specify the term, because an unspecified hiring of lodgings is presumed to run for the rent interval and a hiring of real property is otherwise presumed annual. Keep total upfront security inside the one-month deposit cap however you label it, and charge documented actual cost for damage rather than a flat per-room fee, because a contractual penalty for nonperformance is void.

title: No Statutory Consequence for Refusing a Subsidy Inspection
bodyText: South Dakota attaches no statutory consequence to a landlord refusing an inspection in a subsidised tenancy. There is no provision making refusal a ground for anything, no penalty, no tenant remedy, and no rule requiring you to admit a housing agency's inspector. The refusal-to-inspect provisions South Dakota does have belong to licensing regimes for transient lodging and other regulated activities, where refusal can cost the licence - they do not reach a residential tenancy. The consequences of refusing a subsidy inspection are therefore contractual rather than statutory, and they are real: a housing assistance payments contract conditions payment on the unit passing inspection, so refusing access generally means the subsidy stops, and the agency's own rules govern abatement and termination of the contract. Those obligations arise because you signed up, and they are not resolved here. One statutory point does bear on access, and it runs the other way. Entry is governed by the general rule: except in an emergency or where it is impracticable, the tenant is owed reasonable notice of your intent to enter and entry must be at reasonable times, with twenty-four hours' written notice presumed reasonable unless alternate methods or times are mutually agreed in the lease. An inspector attends with you or with your consent, so your own entry obligations to the tenant apply to the visit - you cannot admit a third party on terms you could not admit yourself. The cautious course is a lease term acknowledging that an agency may inspect, plus actual notice each time.

title: No Statutory Rent Proration for Uninhabitable Periods
bodyText: South Dakota has no statute prorating or abating rent for the period a unit is uninhabitable, and none dealing with how a subsidy is apportioned when habitability fails. There is no formula, no per-day reduction, and no rule about who bears the loss between you, the tenant and a housing agency. What South Dakota gives the tenant instead is a choice of three self-help routes once you have had notice of a condition requiring repair and a reasonable time has passed. The tenant may repair it and deduct the cost from rent or otherwise recover it from you. The tenant may vacate, and is then discharged from additional rent and from performing the other lease conditions - which is proration of a blunt kind, ending the obligation rather than scaling it. Or, where the necessary repairs cost more than one month's rent, the tenant may withhold rent after written notice stating the specific reason and deposit it in a separate bank or savings and loan account, giving you written evidence of the deposit, holding it until you make the repairs or until enough accumulates for the tenant to have them done. Note what that third route is not: it is not a court escrow, no judge supervises it, and nothing requires the tenant to apply to anyone first. For a subsidized tenancy the money question is contractual - the housing assistance payments contract and the agency's rules govern what happens to the subsidy, and those are not resolved here. Ask the agency before crediting or withholding anything.

title: No Rule on Late Fees in a Subsidised Tenancy
bodyText: South Dakota has no provision about late fees in a subsidised tenancy. Nothing bars you from charging a late fee on the tenant's share of rent, nothing limits the amount, and nothing addresses what happens when a housing agency's portion arrives late. The state simply does not distinguish subsidised from unsubsidised tenancies for this purpose, so the general position applies: there is no cap, but a late fee must be a genuine estimate of what late payment costs you rather than a penalty, because a penalty imposed by contract for nonperformance is void. The real constraints in a subsidised tenancy are contractual rather than statutory, and they usually bite harder than anything South Dakota would impose. A housing assistance payments contract and the agency's own rules commonly restrict the fees an owner may charge a participating tenant, require the lease to be the agency's form or an approved addendum, and treat a charge outside the approved lease as unenforceable against the tenant. Those obligations arise because you signed up, and they are not resolved here. Two practical points. Never charge the tenant a late fee for the agency's portion arriving late - the tenant did not owe it and did not control it - and keep your fee calculation to the tenant's share only. And read the agency addendum before applying any fee, because where it conflicts with your lease the addendum generally controls, which is also how your own addendum-precedence clause is written.

title: No Receivership for Substandard Rental Property
bodyText: South Dakota has no receivership for substandard housing. No statute lets a court take your building out of your hands, appoint someone to collect the rents and spend them on repairs, or give that person a lien ahead of your mortgage. The state has a general receivership chapter and a court rule about receivers, but these are ordinary equity tools, available in a pending action to prevent loss of property, in a foreclosure, where a corporation fails, after judgment, or under the usages of equity. None addresses housing conditions, and none may be invoked simply because a rental is in bad repair. The only housing-specific receiverships in the Code protect a public housing bondholder and the state housing authority's loan, the opposite of a tenant remedy. Nor is there any state repair order for a rental, any rent-escrow scheme run by a court or agency, or any tenant action to have your property managed for you. What reaches you comes from three other directions. The state fire authority may make rules for abating unsafe structures within its scope, which for residences means multifamily buildings housing six or more families. County health boards may notify an owner of a nuisance, remove it on noncompliance and charge the cost, with a hearing and an appeal. And municipalities adopt building codes locally, so your real exposure is a city code officer, not a state scheme. The cautious course is to assume nothing protects you locally. Find out which code your city has adopted and whether it inspects rentals, answer a code notice within its deadline, and keep dated records of every repair. Your statutory repair duty cannot be waived, and your tenant's remedies include repairing and deducting and, where repairs exceed a month's rent, withholding rent into a separate account after written notice.

title: No Tax-Escalation Statute - It Works Only If the Lease Says So
bodyText: South Dakota has no statute permitting or regulating the passing of real estate tax increases to a residential tenant. There is no required formula, no duty to state the tenant's exact share, and no statutory obligation to refund the tenant's portion of an abatement - all of which some states impose. That means a tax escalation is purely a contract term, and it exists only to the extent your lease creates it. The deposit statute shows why the drafting matters. You may withhold from the deposit amounts reasonably necessary to remedy tenant defaults in the payment of rent and of other funds due to you under an agreement. A tenant's share of a tax increase is recoverable from the deposit only if it is money due under an agreement - which is to say, only if the lease actually obliges the tenant to pay it. A lease silent on taxes gives you nothing to collect and nothing to deduct. If you do pass taxes through, write it so it can be applied without argument: state the base year or base amount, the tenant's exact share as a percentage or a formula, when the statement is delivered and when the payment is due, and what happens on an abatement or a successful assessment appeal. On a month-to-month tenancy you have a simpler route: modify the rent itself on written notice given at least thirty days before the end of the month, which avoids a pass-through calculation altogether.

title: No Cable or Satellite Access Mandate - but Federal Law Reaches Dishes
bodyText: South Dakota gives a tenant no right of access to cable television, satellite or broadband service, and gives a provider no right to enter or wire your building. There is no mandatory-access statute, no forced-wiring provision, no compensation scheme for a provider's installation, and no bar on a rent differential between subscribers and non-subscribers. What South Dakota does have on the subject is criminal rather than regulatory: obstructing community antenna television transmissions is a misdemeanour, as is installing or possessing equipment to receive service without paying, with provisions for manufacture and distribution of such equipment and for seizure. Those protect the system and the provider's revenue, not a tenant's access. The real constraint on a blanket no-dish rule is federal, not state. The FCC's over-the-air reception devices rule limits restrictions on a tenant's installation of a small antenna or satellite dish within an area the tenant leases and has exclusive use of, such as a balcony or patio, which is why a flat prohibition in a lease is a poor idea even though South Dakota says nothing about it. The cautious course is to permit installation within the tenant's own exclusive area, prohibit penetration of the building envelope, roof and common areas without written consent, require professional installation and removal with restoration at the tenant's cost, and keep the charge at documented actual cost rather than a fixed fee, since a flat sum for a breach is void as a penalty.

title: When a Tenant Files for Bankruptcy
bodyText: No South Dakota statute says anything about what a tenant's bankruptcy does to a lease. There is no state provision on assuming or rejecting a lease, none on a trustee's time to decide, none barring a lease term that makes a filing itself a default, and none protecting a lease of a primary residence from rejection. This is federal ground, and the federal rules on assumption, rejection and the automatic stay govern. Treat a filing as a stop sign: the stay reaches an eviction already under way, and pressing one without relief from the bankruptcy court is the expensive mistake. Two things South Dakota does supply are worth knowing. The state has its own insolvency route outside bankruptcy, an assignment for the benefit of creditors, under which an insolvent debtor assigns the estate to an assignee who collects claims under court supervision. That matters to you because a separate leasing statute gives you the same remedies against the lessee's assignees, for a cause of action accruing while they are assignees, as you have against your tenant, excepting only an assignment made as security for a loan unaccompanied by possession. So an assignment of this kind does not strand you. South Dakota has also opted out of some federal exemptions and keeps its own homestead and personal property exemptions, which shape what a tenant's creditors can reach. The cautious course is practical. Do not write a term making a bankruptcy filing a default; it buys you nothing enforceable. Keep the deposit accounting exactly as the deposit statute requires, and treat the deposit as the tenant's money subject to your statutory right to withhold. On learning of a filing, stop collection activity, file a proof of claim for arrears, and ask the bankruptcy court before taking any further step toward possession.

title: One Confidentiality Duty, and It Is Narrow but Absolute
bodyText: South Dakota has no general rule barring you from disclosing information about a tenant. There is no consent requirement for sharing a rental history with another landlord, no restriction on confirming a tenancy, and no statutory limit on what you may pass to a debt collector or a prospective purchaser. But there is one duty, and it is easy to breach without noticing. Where a tenant terminates early because the tenant or a household member is the victim of alleged domestic abuse, unlawful sexual behaviour or stalking, and gives you a forwarding address or other contact information, you may not disclose that information to anyone except with the tenant's consent or as required by law. Note how absolute the prohibition is within its scope: the exception is consent or a legal requirement, not your good intentions. The practical trap is that you hold that address for an innocent reason - it is where the deposit refund and the itemized accounting go - and the obvious requests for it come from exactly the wrong people. Do not give it to the other occupant, a relative, a landlord taking a reference, a collection agency or anyone who says they have been asked to pass on mail. If you are served with something that appears to require disclosure, confirm that before answering. The cautious course is to flag such a tenant's file, keep the address out of general systems, and route any request to one person who knows the rule. And handle every tenant's data as if it will be breached, because the breach-notification duty does apply to you.

title: No Display or Signage Right for a Tenant
bodyText: South Dakota gives a tenant no right to display anything. There is no flag-display right, no protection for political signs, no provision letting a tenant as possessor authorise a temporary sign without the owner's permission, and nothing stopping an association barring an occupant's signs. The display provisions in South Dakota's statutes concern the state flag, tribal and POW/MIA flags at the Capitol, and campaign signs in municipal streets - none of them reaches a tenancy. So what a tenant may put in a window, on a door, on a balcony or in a yard is whatever your lease and rules say, and if the lease says nothing you are arguing about whether a sign is an alteration. Be explicit instead. Two boundaries are worth keeping in view when you write the rule. A restriction on what a tenant does inside the unit is different from one about the building's exterior and common areas: the tenant is entitled to quiet enjoyment of what they have rented, so a rule reaching into the interior is both less defensible and less necessary. And enforcement must stay away from the retaliation triggers - a tenant whose sign you dislike is not a tenant whose rent you raise above market or whose services you reduce, particularly where the display is connected to organising or to a complaint. There is also a federal limit for one kind of installation: satellite dishes and small antennas within a tenant's own exclusive area are protected by FCC rule. The cautious course is a short content-neutral rule about the exterior, written consent for anything affixed, and removal with restoration at the end.

title: Housing an Employee: No Special Regime, So They Are Simply Your Tenant
bodyText:
South Dakota has nothing on employee housing. No statute requires a signed disclosure of the occupancy and vacating conditions, none obliges you to offer a rental agreement when the job ends, none lets you treat an employee occupant as a licensee you can remove with the job, and no eviction provision names a caretaker or a person the owner placed on the property. There is no farm-labour or guest-worker scheme either.

The consequence is the one landlords dislike. Because nothing separates the two relationships, giving an employee a dwelling in exchange for work or at a reduced rent creates an ordinary tenancy, and ending the employment does not end it. If there is no agreed end date you hold a tenancy at will, which takes at least fifteen days' written notice, and two months where the occupant or their spouse or minor child is on active military service. If the occupant will not go, your route is the eviction statute, the same as for anyone else. Self-help is expensive here: excluding an occupant yourself exposes you to damages equal to two months' rent plus return of all advance rent and deposit, and separately to treble damages for forcible exclusion from possession.

The cautious course is a written lease separate from the employment contract, with a fixed term no longer than the job or a stated month-to-month term, rent stated as a figure even where it is set against wages, and an express term making the end of employment a ground to terminate on the statutory notice. Do not write a clause purporting to make the occupancy end automatically with the job, and do not try to contract out of the notice or the eviction process.

title: No Rules on Insurance Claims Between You and the Tenant
bodyText: South Dakota has no provision governing insurance claims between a landlord and a tenant. Nothing requires either of you to claim on your own policy before pursuing the other, nothing bars your insurer from subrogating against a tenant who caused a loss, nothing makes a tenant an implied co-insured under your policy, and nothing obliges you to tell a tenant that your insurance does not cover the tenant's own belongings. The allocation is left to the lease and to ordinary insurance law. Two things are worth doing about that. The first is to tell the tenant plainly, in the lease, that your insurance covers the building and not their possessions or liability, and to require a renter's policy. Tenants routinely assume the opposite, and the assumption surfaces after a fire when it is too late and expensive to correct. The second concerns subrogation. If your insurer pays for damage a tenant negligently caused, it may pursue the tenant, and whether the lease has altered that is a question your lease should answer deliberately rather than by silence - a waiver of subrogation protects the tenant and may need your insurer's agreement, while saying nothing leaves the tenant exposed to a claim they did not expect. Note the backstop South Dakota does supply: the tenant must preserve the premises and the appliances and repair deterioration caused by the tenant's own negligent, willful or malicious conduct, so the underlying liability for careless damage already exists without a lease term creating it.

title: You May Run a Portal - You May Not Make It the Only Channel
bodyText: No South Dakota statute authorises, requires or forbids an online tenant portal, and none says whether you may insist on payment or signatures through one. So the portal itself is a matter of contract, and you may offer it, promote it and build your operation around it. The limit comes from the electronic transactions act, and it is one of the few provisions in this area that a lease cannot touch. That act applies only between parties who have each agreed to transact electronically, judged from the context and the parties' conduct - and a party who agrees to one electronic transaction may refuse to conduct others, with the act saying in terms that this right may not be waived by agreement. A lease term binding the tenant to receive every notice and sign every document through your portal is therefore unenforceable to the extent the tenant later declines, and the notices that matter most are the ones you least want to have served defectively. Payment is on a different footing: nothing makes rent payable by any particular method, so a lease may specify portal payment as the agreed method, though a tenant's refusal to transact electronically makes an alternative route the prudent thing to have. A convenience fee is lawful as a charge for a service actually provided, but it cannot be a sum fixed for nonperformance. The cautious course is a portal clause that makes electronic notice voluntary, keeps a non-electronic route for notices and payment, and states any fee as an actual charge.

title: No Rent-Ledger Duty - but the Data-Breach Law Does Reach You
bodyText: Two halves to this, and landlords usually know neither. South Dakota imposes no record-keeping duty toward tenants: you need not provide a rent ledger on request, need not attach one to a nonpayment notice, and face no deadline for producing a statement of account. Nothing requires you to keep records at all, though the deposit rules effectively do, since you must give a written statement of your specific reasons for withholding within twenty-one days and an itemized accounting within forty-five days if the tenant asks, and failing either forfeits every right to withhold any part of the deposit. The other half is a real obligation and it is not in the landlord-tenant statutes. South Dakota's breach-notification law applies to any person or business conducting business in the state that owns or licenses computerized personal information about residents - which is you, as soon as you hold applicant or tenant data in any system. Personal information means a name combined with data elements including a Social Security number, a driver licence or other identification number, and account, credit or debit card numbers together with any code or password that gives access to the account. On discovering a breach you must notify each affected resident within sixty days, unless law enforcement needs longer or you investigate, notify the Attorney General and reasonably determine harm is unlikely - a determination you must document in writing and keep for three years. A breach affecting more than two hundred fifty residents must also be reported to the Attorney General. Whenever resident notice is due, the consumer reporting agencies must be notified without unreasonable delay. Enforcement is by the Attorney General as a deceptive act, with civil penalties up to ten thousand dollars per day per violation.

title: Repairs in Lieu of Rent - the Only Lawful Way to Shift Maintenance
bodyText: South Dakota lets you move repair work to the tenant in exactly one way, and the words matter. The habitability duty may not be waived or modified by the parties; however, the landlord may agree with the tenant that the tenant will perform specified repairs or maintenance in lieu of rent. Everything turns on those four conditions. The repairs must be specified, so a clause making the tenant generally responsible for maintenance, or for everything under a dollar figure, is a modification of the duty rather than an agreement about particular work. The consideration must be rent - repairs in lieu of rent - so trading work for a reduced deposit, a waived fee or a one-off payment falls outside the permission. It must be an agreement, which means the tenant's assent to those specific terms, not a recital in your standard form. And because the duty itself survives, the arrangement allocates who does the work and who pays for it, not whether the premises must meet the standard: if the tenant does not do the agreed work, the premises still have to be fit, and the duty is still yours. There is no separate-writing requirement, no single-family-only limitation and no second mechanism with different formalities - South Dakota has one provision, and it reaches every residential hiring. The cautious course is a short separate addendum: list the specific tasks, state the rent reduction attributable to them, state that you remain responsible for the habitability standard and may enter to inspect and perform the work if it is not done, and keep the tenant's maintenance obligations out of the lease's general terms.

title: Three Tenant Remedies, and No Court Supervision of Any of Them
bodyText: South Dakota gives a tenant three remedies when you do not repair, and the thing to understand is that none of them involves a court or requires the tenant to ask anyone's permission first. The trigger is the same for all three: notice to you of conditions requiring repair to make the premises fit for human habitation and in good and safe working order, and then a reasonable time in which you neglect to do it. After that the tenant may repair the condition and deduct the expense from rent, or otherwise recover it from you. The tenant may vacate the premises, and is then discharged from additional charges of rent and from performing the other lease conditions - so an unrepaired condition can end the tenancy and your rent stream without any termination notice from you. Or, where the cost of necessary repairs exceeds one month's rent, the tenant may withhold rent after written notice stating the specific reason for the withholding and immediately deposit it in a separate bank or savings and loan account, providing you written evidence of the deposit, and keep it there until you make the repairs, at which point it is released to you, or until enough has accumulated for the tenant to have the repairs done. There is no rent-into-court procedure, no certification of unfitness, no agency involvement, and no eviction bar during the withholding - the protections of states with court-supervised escrow are absent in both directions. The practical consequence: your window is the reasonable time after notice, and the cheapest remedy for you is almost always to repair within it.

title: No Organizing Right - but Retaliating Over One Is Actionable
bodyText: South Dakota gives tenants no right to organise. There is no right to form or join a tenants' association, no right of access for an organiser, no right to meet in common areas, no protection for a tenant representative, and nothing requiring you to recognise or deal with a tenants' group. You may decline to engage with one and you may apply an ordinary no-solicitation rule to your common areas. What South Dakota does instead is protect the activity after the fact, and the protection is specific enough to plan around. A cause of action arises in favour of a tenant and against a landlord of residential property, including a manufactured or mobile home community owner, for retaliation where the landlord increases rents above fair market value, decreases electric, gas, water or sewer services, or gives the tenant notice to vacate when the notice is not based on a breach of the lease - where any of that follows the tenant having organised or become a member of a tenants' union or organisation. Two details matter. The three retaliatory acts are a closed list, so the claim attaches to rent, services and possession rather than to every slight; and there is a defence where a notice to vacate was given more than one hundred eighty days after the organising, with a failure to renew expressly not retaliation. So the practical rule is that organising creates no obligation on you but does create a window in which the three listed moves are dangerous. The cautious course is one content-neutral solicitation rule applied consistently, and no change to rent, services or possession for six months after organising begins.

title: No State Tenant-Rights Summary to Hand Out
bodyText: South Dakota publishes no statement of tenant rights that you must give a tenant, and imposes no acknowledgment requirement. There is no state-agency summary to attach as the first page of a lease or a renewal, no signature required on each page, and no rule barring you from suing until such a document has been provided. Some states make the summary a precondition to enforcement; South Dakota has nothing of the kind, so your lease stands on its own terms and your remedies are not conditioned on any handout. That makes the lease the only place a tenant learns the rules, which is worth taking seriously for your own protection rather than theirs. The provisions a tenant is most likely to invoke are not in your lease unless you put them there - the twenty-one-day deposit return and the forty-five-day itemized accounting, the non-waivable repair duty and the three remedies that follow from a failure to repair, the entry notice standard, the fifteen-day termination notice for a tenancy at will, and the early-termination right for a victim of domestic abuse, unlawful sexual behaviour or stalking. A tenant who first discovers one of those from a lawyer tends to discover it along with an argument that you concealed it. The cautious course is a short, accurate summary of those points attached to the lease as information, clearly not a waiver of anything, and a signed acknowledgment of receipt kept with your copy - a document nobody requires, which is exactly why it is persuasive.

title: Tenant Screening Is Unregulated in South Dakota - Which Is the Problem
bodyText:
South Dakota regulates tenant screening not at all. There is no screening statute, no cap or disclosure rule for an application fee, no limit on what you may charge for a credit or criminal report, no rule about reusing a report, no requirement that a criminal-history look come only after a conditional offer, no look-back period, no bar on relying on an arrest or an expunged record, no minimum-income formula, no adverse-action notice of state origin, and no statutory immunity if you rent to someone with a record and another tenant is harmed. Screening is governed by the general discrimination law and by nothing else.

That makes the discrimination law do all the work, and it is where the exposure sits. Any criterion that sorts applicants by race, colour, creed, religion, sex, ancestry, disability, familial status or national origin is unlawful in the terms and conditions of a rental, and a separate section reaches the form, the record and the inquiry you use to get there. Two criteria landlords use without thinking are the usual failures: a blanket rule against households with children runs straight into familial status, and an income multiple applied to the rent rather than to the applicant's share can fail where a disabled applicant's income is structured differently. The law is explicit that a disability does not excuse an applicant from the financial terms, so a consistently applied income test is defensible.

The cautious course is to write your criteria down before you advertise, apply them in the same order to every applicant, record the reason for every decline against those written criteria, and keep any application fee to your documented actual cost, because a charge beyond cost looks like a contractual penalty and penalties for nonperformance are void in South Dakota.

title: The Tenant’s Statutory Duties Are Short - Three Sections
bodyText: South Dakota imposes three statutory duties on a residential tenant and no more. There is no list of tenant obligations of the kind a uniform landlord-tenant act supplies - nothing about keeping the unit clean, disposing of rubbish, using facilities reasonably or not disturbing neighbours. What exists is this. The tenant must preserve the premises, the appliances, the appurtenances and the other leased personal property, and must repair deterioration caused by the tenant's own negligent, wilful or malicious conduct or that of a person under the tenant's direction or control - so damage from carelessness or from a guest is the tenant's, without any lease term. Where premises are leased for a particular and specified purpose the tenant must not use them for another, and if the tenant does you may hold the tenant responsible for the safety of the premises during that use, at all events, or treat the contract as rescinded. And a tenant who receives notice of any proceeding to recover the property must immediately inform you and deliver the notice if it is in writing, being responsible for all damages you sustain from a failure to do so. That is the whole of it. Everything else a landlord expects of a tenant - cleanliness, noise, occupancy, pets, smoking, parking, business use - has to be a lease term, and the eviction statute will carry it: among the grounds is a lessee who does or fails to perform any act which, under the terms of the lease, operates to terminate it. The cautious course is a specific rules section, because the statute will not fill the gaps.

title: Nothing to Be Exempt From, and South Dakota Exemptions Never Come With a Notice
bodyText: There is no exemption notice in South Dakota because there is nothing for a property to be exempt from. The state has no rent cap, no just-cause termination regime and no tenant purchase right, so no lease statement tells a tenant that a rental falls outside any of them. What is worth understanding is the shape of South Dakota exemptions generally, because the pattern is consistent: where the law carves something out, you simply apply the carve-out, and no notice, election or filing is required. The deposit cap yields to a larger agreed deposit where special conditions pose a danger to maintenance of the premises, with no notice. The repair duty, which you otherwise cannot waive, yields where you and the tenant agree that the tenant will perform specified repairs or maintenance in lieu of rent, with no notice. Commercial lettings run on their own deposit timetable rather than the residential one, with no notice. A tenancy at will ends on the short notice unless active military service extends it, and the two exceptions to that extension apply automatically. Transient lodging has its own ejection grounds entirely. Even the utility regulator's jurisdiction excludes municipal utilities and rural electric cooperative electric service without anyone telling a customer so. The cautious course is to claim nothing in the lease that the law does not give you, and in particular never to paste another state's exemption statement into a South Dakota lease. A clause announcing that the property is not subject to rent limits or cause requirements cites law that has no application here, tells the tenant such limits exist somewhere in their tenancy, and gains you nothing a silent lease does not already have.

title: No Rent Cap, No Just Cause, No Tenant Purchase Right, So No Coverage Notice
bodyText: South Dakota gives you the opposite of a tenant protection act, and that is why there is no notice to give. Rent is whatever the lease says, and on a month-to-month letting you may change it, like any other term, by written notice given at least thirty days before the month ends, after which the tenant may leave effective the first of the next month by answering within fifteen days. Ending a tenancy needs no stated reason: a residential tenancy at will ends on fifteen days written notice, longer only where active military service is involved, and the eviction grounds are the ordinary ones. There is no rent limit for a lease to describe, no just-cause regime to disclose and no statement of cause required in a termination notice, and a separate statute goes further by forbidding any local government from controlling the rent charged for private residential property, so a city cannot create one either. Nor is there any tenant right to buy. Nothing gives a residential tenant notice of an intended sale, a first opportunity to purchase, a right of first refusal or a conversion notice. The condominium statute is a developer-registration regime whose notice of intent to sell goes to a state commission, not to anyone living in the building. A buyer takes subject to the existing lease, and a tenant may not attorn to a stranger without your consent or a court judgment. The cautious course is to leave all of this out of the lease and to resist copying another state's coverage notice into a South Dakota form. A notice that tells a tenant the state caps rent or requires cause, when it does not, cites law that does not apply here and can only be read against you.

title: Nothing Expires - No Repeal Clock on the Lease Chapter
bodyText: South Dakota's landlord-tenant law carries no sunset or repeal clock. No part of the lease chapter, the eviction chapter or the deposit provisions is scheduled to expire, and there is no dated repealer of the kind some states attach to a tenant-protection act, so nothing you build into a lease today becomes unenforceable on a future date by operation of a sunset. This is a more useful fact than it sounds, because it tells you where the risk of change actually sits: not in automatic expiry, but in ordinary amendment. The chapter is amended regularly and the recent example is a real one - the deposit return period was shortened by a 2026 act, so a lease or a procedure written to the old timetable is now wrong. The practical consequence is that a lease should avoid reciting statutory periods as fixed numbers wherever it can, and should refer to the period the statute requires instead. Where a figure must appear, date the document and review it against the chapter each session rather than assuming continuity. Two related points: emergency measures are a separate question, and South Dakota has none affecting tenancies, so there is no temporary regime due to lapse either; and the eviction and contract chapters that carry the real remedies are long-standing law with no expiry provisions. The cautious course is to track the legislative session rather than a calendar of expiries, and to review the deposit, notice and entry provisions annually before reissuing a lease form.

title: No Translation Duty and No Type-Size Floor
bodyText: South Dakota imposes no translation duty and no formatting rules on a residential lease. There is no requirement to provide a translated lease, no duty triggered by advertising or negotiating in another language, no prescribed verbatim lease text, no minimum type size and no conspicuousness standard for any lease term. English is not declared the controlling text of a lease because no provision addresses the question at all. So a lease in English is valid however the parties communicated, and a lease you also provide in another language is a matter of your own choice, with no rule about which version prevails - which means you should say so yourself. Two practical points follow. If you negotiate in a language other than the lease's, a tenant may later say they did not understand what they signed; that is a contract-formation argument about consent rather than a statutory violation, and the usual answer is a translated copy supplied for information plus a clause stating that the English text governs. And because no type-size or conspicuousness rule exists, a term is not unenforceable for being in small print - but the provisions that do constrain lease terms, such as the bar on penalties and the non-waivable habitability duty, apply regardless of how prominently they are drafted around. The cautious course is to keep one controlling language, say which it is, give a courtesy translation where it helps, and never rely on small print to carry a term the law would strike anyway.

title: How To Give a Trespass Notice, and Why It Rarely Reaches a Tenant's Guest
bodyText: Criminal trespass is South Dakota's route for barring someone who is not your tenant, and the notice makes it work. Notice against trespass may be given three ways: by actually communicating it to the person, by posting in a manner reasonably likely to come to a trespasser's attention, or by a fence or other enclosure a reasonable person would recognise as designed to exclude trespassers. A person who then enters or remains knowing they are not privileged commits the lesser misdemeanour, and defying an order to leave communicated personally by the owner or any other authorized person raises it a grade - so your manager can give it too. Two limits decide whether any of this helps in a corridor or a parking lot. A tenant is privileged to be there under the lease, so trespass is never the route against a tenant. And the chapter gives an affirmative defence to someone who reasonably believed the owner, or another person permitted to license access, would have allowed them to enter or remain; your tenant is such a person, so a guest the tenant still welcomes carries that defence into the common areas as much as into the unit. The open-to-the-public defence is narrower than it sounds: it runs only where the premises were open to the public at the time and the person met every lawful condition on access, so your common areas do not qualify once you have posted conditions and excluded the person by name. The cautious course is to put the ban in writing, name the person, deliver it and keep proof, post the common areas, treat a welcomed guest as a lease matter for the tenant, and never borrow the transient-lodging ejection grounds, which do not reach a tenancy.

title: No Truth-in-Renting Act - No Mandated Lease Content at All
bodyText: South Dakota has no truth-in-renting act and, more broadly, prescribes almost no lease content. There is no statutory list of terms a residential lease must contain, no prohibited-provisions section, no required statement of rights, no mandated form and no official notice to attach. The only content rule worth the name is a formality rather than a disclosure: an agreement to lease real property for more than one year is invalid unless it, or a note or memorandum of it, is in writing and signed by the lessor or an agent authorised in writing - and note that the signature the statute demands is yours, not the tenant's. What takes the place of mandated content is a set of rules your lease cannot escape by silence or by drafting. The habitability duty applies to every hiring of residential premises, written or oral, and may not be waived or modified. The deposit cap and the return timetable apply however the money is labelled. The entry standard, the termination notices and the tenant's repair remedies all apply whether or not the lease mentions them. So an incomplete lease does not reduce your obligations; it only reduces what you can prove and what you can collect, since a charge the lease does not create is not funds due to you under an agreement. The cautious course is to treat the lease as your own protection rather than a compliance exercise: state the figures, the dates, the notice addresses and every charge, because nothing else will.

title: Parking May Be Bundled or Priced Separately - No Rule Either Way
bodyText: South Dakota has no unbundled-parking statute. Nothing requires you to price parking separately from rent, nothing forbids it, nothing requires you to offer parking at all, and nothing entitles a tenant to give up a space for a rent reduction. How you structure it is a pricing decision, not a compliance question. Two consequences of that freedom are worth getting right in the lease. If parking is included in rent, it is part of what the tenant has rented, which means withdrawing a space mid-term is a change to the bargain rather than a management decision, and on a month-to-month tenancy the way to make that change is the statutory route - modify the terms on written notice given at least thirty days before the end of the month, after which the tenant may terminate effective the first of the next month by notifying you within fifteen days. If parking is a separate charge, say what it buys, whether a specific space is assigned, and what happens if the space is unavailable. The charge itself is ordinary rent or a fee due under the agreement, and is withholdable from the deposit as other funds due to you under an agreement - but only if the lease actually creates the obligation. Keep any enforcement charge at documented actual cost: towing is recoverable at what you pay, while a flat parking-violation fee is a penalty for nonperformance and void. Towing has its own statutory notice requirements, addressed separately in the library.

title: Interest on Money a Tenant Owes You
bodyText: South Dakota gives you interest on money a tenant owes without a word in the lease, and it is not a token rate. Unless an express written contract fixes a different rate, or the rate clearly appears on the bill, statement or invoice, interest runs at fifteen percent a year on moneys after they become due on any instrument of writing, on moneys lent, on a balance ascertained on a settlement of accounts, and on money received to another's use and detained from them. A rate that appears on a bill, statement or invoice may not exceed eighteen percent - which is the ceiling most likely to catch a landlord out, because a late charge printed on a monthly rent statement is a rate appearing on a statement. Where an obligation to pay interest carries no rate, the maximum is twelve percent from the date the debt is incurred, counted on a three hundred sixty day year. Judgments and statutory liens run at ten percent. And a legal rate stipulated by contract stays chargeable after a breach, as before, until a verdict or new obligation supersedes it. The striking feature is the freedom: unless a maximum is specifically established elsewhere in the code, there is no maximum interest rate and no usury restriction at all between parties who set the rate by written agreement. So you are not capped in the way you would be almost anywhere else. The limits sit in contract law instead - a penalty imposed by contract for nonperformance is void, and a sum fixed in anticipation of breach is void unless actual damage would be impracticable to establish. The cautious course is a modest stated rate running only from each amount's due date.

title: Letting by Someone Whose Own Interest Will End
bodyText: South Dakota has no usufruct; the concept belongs to civil-law jurisdictions and nothing here uses it or its vocabulary. The questions it answers elsewhere are handled by the law of estates, and the equivalent landlord is a life tenant. South Dakota classifies estates by the duration of their enjoyment: estates of inheritance, for life, for years and at will. An estate for years is a chattel real; an estate at will is a chattel interest, not liable as such to sale on execution. The owner of a life estate may use the land as a fee owner would, except that it must do no act injuring the inheritance, and must keep buildings and fences repaired from ordinary waste and pay the taxes and annual charges. Rent due on a lease for life is recoverable as on a lease for years, and rent depending on a person's life may be recovered after that person's death as well as before. A tenant for years or at will has no rights beyond those the instrument gives and a limited right to occupy and take the products. No statute says in terms that your lease ends when your own interest ends, but you cannot grant more than you hold, so expect it to. Two provisions matter either way: the tenant's remedies run against your assigns except on covenants about encumbrances, title or possession, exactly where a life tenant is vulnerable; and a lease terminates if the tenant acquires superior title.
