The cautious course, if you let as a life tenant or on any interest that can end, is to say so in the lease, keep the term inside your interest or make it month to month, disclaim any covenant as to title or continued possession, and name who takes over when your interest ends.

title: No Utility Allowance Rule - but Rebilling Is Capped at What You Were Billed
bodyText: South Dakota sets no utility allowance and has no statute barring you from passing master-metered electricity through to tenants except as part of fixed rent. There is no submetering statute and no allowance schedule. What there is, and what controls how you bill, is a flat cap on markup: knowingly charging a consumer of gas or electricity an amount greater than the utility actually billed exposes you to a civil fine of up to five hundred dollars. That is the operative constraint on every arrangement where you receive the utility bill and recover it from tenants. Dividing a master-metered bill among units is consistent with it so long as what you collect in total does not exceed what you were billed; adding an administrative margin, a per-unit flat fee above the bill, or a rounded-up charge is where the exposure lies. Electric-vehicle charging is the single express exception. The two clean approaches are to fold utilities into the rent as a fixed amount, so there is no per-bill charge to compare against, or to rebill at actual cost and keep the utility's bill available to show the arithmetic. One limit sits in the Public Utilities Commission's rules rather than the Code. A regulated gas or electric utility must meter each unit separately in a multi-unit building begun after June 13, 1980 (ARSD 20:10:26:03). Exceptions include a two-unit owner-occupied building, an older master-metered building not substantially remodeled since June 13, 1980, and central heating, cooling or water heating (ARSD 20:10:26:04). Otherwise the owner needs a Commission variance. Those rules govern how the utility meters a building, not what you may pass through.

title: No Apportionment Rule - but You May Not Bill Above What You Were Billed
bodyText: South Dakota has no rule about apportioning utilities among units and no provision making a lease term unenforceable because it charges a tenant for utilities that are not separately metered to that unit. Some states have just enacted exactly that; South Dakota has not, so billing a share of a master-metered bill is lawful here. One statutory limit decides how you may do it. Knowingly charging a consumer of gas or electricity an amount greater than the amount actually billed by the gas or electric utility exposes you to a civil fine of up to five hundred dollars. The cap is on the total you collect against what you were billed, so a square-footage or occupancy-based division of an actual bill is consistent with it, while a per-unit flat charge set above the bill, an administrative margin, or a rounded-up figure is where the exposure sits. Electric-vehicle charging is the single express exception to that cap. Two drafting points follow. Say in the lease exactly which utilities the tenant pays, how a shared bill is divided, and that the charge is the tenant's share of the amount actually billed - and keep the bills, because the arithmetic is your defence. And remember the other half of the bargain: cutting off electric, gas, water or another essential service to a tenant is not a collection tool, and willfully diminishing those services carries damages of two months' rent plus the return of all advance rent and deposit. If you would rather avoid the exercise altogether, fold utilities into a fixed rent.

title: A Utility Deposit You Collect Is a Security Deposit
bodyText: A utility deposit you collect from your tenant is a security deposit in South Dakota. The deposit statute does not turn on labels: any money whose function is to secure performance of a residential rental agreement is deemed a security deposit however it is denominated, and paying the utility bill is part of the tenant's performance whenever your lease makes it so. So money you take against unpaid utilities counts toward your one-month ceiling along with every other deposit you hold, must be returned or explained within twenty-one days of the tenancy ending and your receipt of the tenant's mailing address or delivery instructions, must be itemized within forty-five days if the tenant asks, and may be withheld only for rent defaults, other funds due to you under an agreement, and restoring the premises. There is no separate utility-deposit rule, clock or cap, so it is not a second pot outside the ceiling. Keep that distinct from the other kind of utility deposit. Where the tenant is the utility's own subscriber, the deposit is between the tenant and the utility and is not your concern: the utility holds it, and if the tenant never claims it, it is presumed abandoned one year after the service ends and goes to the state as unclaimed property, which is a markedly shorter clock than the one that applies to most unclaimed money. Where you are the account holder, the deposit the utility holds is yours to reclaim, while anything you collected from the tenant remains a security deposit subject to everything above. The cautious course is to state in the lease which of you is the subscriber, count any utility deposit toward the one-month ceiling, and account for it in the same written statement as the rest of the deposit.

title: No Required Utility Disclosure Attachment
bodyText: No South Dakota statute requires a utility disclosure to be attached to a residential lease, signed separately, printed in a prescribed form or type size, or placed on its own page. There is no state equivalent of the separate utility rider or availability statement some jurisdictions mandate. The only statutory rental-agreement disclosure of this shape in South Dakota concerns self-service storage, and it runs the other way, obliging the occupant rather than the operator. For a dwelling, what utilities the tenant pays, which are in your name, and how a shared bill is divided are all matters of contract, and silence in the lease is resolved against nobody by statute. That is precisely why the attachment is worth writing anyway. Two separate rules make vagueness expensive for you rather than for the tenant. First, if you hold the account and rebill, you may not knowingly collect more than the utility actually billed, on pain of a civil fine, so you need a documented basis for every charge. Second, if service is interrupted or willfully diminished, the remedy against you is heavy: injunction, possession or termination, plus damages equal to two months' rent and return of all advance rent and deposit. The cautious course is a signed utility schedule attached to the lease that lists every service, names who holds the account, who pays, the allocation formula where a bill is shared, and the transfer deadlines at move-in and move-out, charging documented actual cost rather than any flat amount. The Public Utilities Commission's gas and electric rules (ARSD 20:10:15 to 20:10:20) require no lease disclosure either.

title: You Can Ask To Be Copied on a Shutoff Notice, But Nothing Makes It Stick
bodyText: Start with the rule that matters most if a tenant's utility is about to be cut off: you must stay out of it. Willfully diminishing services by interrupting or causing the interruption of electric, gas, water or other essential service exposes you to damages of two months' rent plus the return of all advance rent and deposit, on top of an injunction, the tenant recovering possession, or the tenant ending the tenancy. South Dakota has no statute letting an owner file a separate document authorizing the utility to notify it of a tenant's pending disconnection, and none letting a tenant-customer name you as a designee to be copied on shutoff notices. Everything about how a regulated utility must notice a disconnection sits in the Public Utilities Commission's own rules rather than in statute, and those rules (ARSD chapter 20:10:20) provide for no landlord or third-party designee. The notice goes to the customer's billing or service address, so a copy to you depends on the utility's own policy. What those rules do say cuts the other way on the related question: where you are the customer, the utility must offer the tenant service in the tenant's own name where that is economically feasible, and may not condition the tenant's service on your unpaid bills. The cautious course is to put the authorization in the lease as the tenant's own direction to the provider, signed by the tenant, covering disconnection and final-bill notices; to ask the provider in writing whether it will honour it and keep the answer; and to treat it as a courtesy copy you may not get. Pair it with the tenant's duty to keep service on and to furnish evidence of the account, and never act on a shutoff notice by interrupting anything.

title: No Submetering Regime - and Interruption Is the Expensive Mistake
bodyText: South Dakota has no submetering statute and no interruption regime for landlord-submetered electricity. There is no procedure letting you disconnect a submetered tenant for nonpayment, no notice schedule, no reconnection rules, no required meter standards and no registration. Read that as a prohibition rather than a gap, because the general rule fills the space and it is severe. If a lessor of residential property unlawfully removes or excludes the tenant from the premises, or willfully diminishes services to the tenant by interrupting or causing the interruption of electric, gas, water or other essential service, the tenant may sue for an injunction, recover possession by suit, or terminate the rental agreement - and in any case recover damages equal to two months' rent plus the return of any advance rent and deposit paid. There is no exception for a submetered account, none for a tenant genuinely in arrears, and none for a service you are paying for yourself. In other words, in a state with no submetering disconnection procedure there is no lawful way to shut off a residential tenant's essential service, whatever the lease says, and a term purporting to authorize it is contrary to the policy of express law. Your remedies for unpaid utility charges are the ordinary ones: treat them as sums due under the lease, pursue them as rent or other funds due under an agreement, withhold from the deposit within the deposit rules, and terminate and evict if the default justifies it. Bill at or below what the utility billed you, and keep the meter readings.

title: When You Hold the Utility Account, the Tenant Has No Statutory Remedy - and That Is Your Risk
bodyText: South Dakota has none of the machinery other states build around a landlord-held utility account. A tenant cannot pay your unpaid utility bill and deduct it from rent, there are no liquidated damages for failing to identify your tenants to the utility, a master-meter owner has no statutory duty to notify the utility of anything, and tenants cannot petition for a rent receiver when you do not pay. A regulated gas or electric utility may not cut off your account at a rented address until it has offered the tenant service in the tenant's own name, where that is economically feasible (ARSD 20:10:20:09). It also may not make the tenant pay your bill. Beyond that, nothing requires it to warn each unit before a building-wide shutoff. That absence of tenant machinery is not comfort, because the consequence of your nonpayment lands on you through a different route. Service lost because you did not pay is a diminution of services, and willfully interrupting or causing the interruption of electric, gas, water or another essential service exposes you to damages of two months' rent plus the return of all advance rent and deposit, with the tenant also able to seek an injunction or terminate the tenancy. A shutoff for your unpaid bill will not look accidental to a court if you knew the bill was due. And because the premises must stay fit for human habitation and in good and safe working order - a duty you cannot waive or modify - a building without water or heat is a habitability breach as well, opening repair-and-deduct, vacate-and-be-discharged, or rent withheld into a separate account. The cautious course is to keep landlord-held accounts on autopay, never to let a shutoff notice run, and to tell tenants promptly and in writing if one arrives.

title: No Submetering Disclosure Statute - the Limit Is on the Amount
bodyText: South Dakota has no submetering statute, so there is no prescribed submetering disclosure, no type-size rule, no building-size threshold, no late-fee cap on a submetered bill, no ninety-day notice procedure for imposing charge-back mid-term, and no bar on eviction for nonpayment of a utility charge. What the state regulates is not the disclosure but the amount. Knowingly charging a consumer of gas or electricity more than the utility actually billed exposes you to a civil fine of up to five hundred dollars, with electric vehicle charging the one express exception. That cap is the real constraint on every arrangement in which you hold the utility account and recover the cost from tenants. Dividing a master-metered bill among units is consistent with it so long as the total you collect does not exceed the total you were billed; an administrative margin, a per-unit flat fee above the bill, or a rounded-up charge is where the exposure lies, and a flat penalty for late payment of such a charge is separately void because a statute voids contractual penalties for nonperformance. Because no statute prescribes a disclosure, the cautious course supplies one. State in the lease, on its own signed page, which utilities are measured by submeter or allocated, the formula or allocation basis, who reads the meters and how often, when the bill is rendered, and that the charge will never exceed your documented cost. Keep the utility's bill for each period. Never interrupt or diminish electric, gas or water service to collect, because the remedy against you for that is two months' rent plus return of all advance rent and deposit. The Public Utilities Commission's rules add no submetering disclosure, but they do limit metering. A regulated gas or electric utility must meter each unit separately in a multi-unit building begun after June 13, 1980 (ARSD 20:10:26:03). Exceptions include a two-unit owner-occupied building, an older master-metered building not substantially remodeled since June 13, 1980, and central heating, cooling or water heating (ARSD 20:10:26:04). Otherwise the owner needs a Commission variance.

title: No Opt-In Cutoff When the Tenant Does Not Transfer the Utilities
bodyText: Some states let a landlord, if the lease opts in, cut off a utility left in the landlord's name when the tenant fails to transfer it within a few days of taking possession. South Dakota does not, and attempting it is among the most expensive things you can do. Wilfully diminishing services to a tenant by interrupting or causing the interruption of electric, gas, water or other essential service lets the tenant sue for an injunction, recover possession, or terminate the rental agreement, and in any case recover damages equal to two months' rent plus the return of all advance rent and deposit. There is no exception for a service you are paying for yourself, none for a tenant who agreed to transfer the account and did not, and no lease term that can authorise it, since a provision contrary to the policy of express law is unlawful and one exempting you from responsibility for a violation of law is void. Your remedies are contractual and they are adequate. Make the transfer a lease obligation with a deadline, keep paying the bill if the tenant does not transfer it, and recover what you pay as a sum due under the agreement - billed at the amount the utility billed you, since knowingly charging a consumer of gas or electricity more than that carries a civil fine of up to five hundred dollars. If the failure persists, treat it as a breach and terminate on the statutory notice. What you must not do is let the service lapse or ask the utility to disconnect.

title: No Landlord Incentive for Renting to a Veteran
bodyText:
South Dakota offers a private residential landlord nothing for renting to a veteran. There is no tax credit, no property-tax abatement, no rent subsidy, no signing bonus, no damage-reimbursement fund, no risk-mitigation pool, no deposit guarantee and no landlord-incentive programme of any kind in the state's law. Veteran and military status are also not protected classes in South Dakota's fair housing list, so you may decline a veteran applicant on the same grounds as anyone else, and you may equally prefer one.

The veteran provisions that do exist sit elsewhere and are easy to mistake for incentives. The property-tax exemptions for disabled veterans and surviving spouses attach to a dwelling the veteran owns and occupies, so they are worth nothing to you as a landlord and in fact only reach your property if you sell it to a qualifying owner-occupier. The veterans' preference in employment binds public employers, not you. And the rental preference for servicemembers and veterans, together with the provision waiving admission conditions for them, belongs to county and municipal housing commissions operating public housing projects, not to private units.

The cautious course is to treat federal and local programmes as the only real money. A veteran applicant may hold a federal rental assistance voucher, and taking it is your commercial choice, because South Dakota has not made source of income a protected class and has no voucher statute at all. If you want veteran tenants, say so in your advertising, which is lawful because veteran status is not a protected class, and check with the county veterans service officer and the local housing authority rather than looking for a state incentive that does not exist.

title: No Water-Heater Temperature Requirement
bodyText: South Dakota sets no water-heater temperature for a rental. Nothing requires you to set a unit's heater to a maximum before a new tenant moves in, nothing sets a minimum, and no energy or building provision imposes a per-occupancy setting of the kind a couple of states have put outside their landlord-tenant acts. The general duty is what applies: you must maintain all electrical, plumbing and heating systems of the premises in good and safe working order and condition, and keep the premises fit for human habitation, throughout the term - a duty you may not waive or modify. A water heater sits squarely inside that, so the obligation is that it works safely and supplies hot water, not that it is set to a particular number. Two practical points. Scald risk is a liability question rather than a compliance one, and the absence of a statutory setting does not help you if a heater delivers water hot enough to injure a child; the model codes the state adopts for construction may address mixing valves and temperature limits for new work, and those are adopted by reference and not reproduced in the statutes, so check the adopted edition for anything you build or replace. And the duty runs to the system's safety as much as its function, which includes the relief valve and the venting. The cautious course is to set a unit-only heater to a sensible maximum between tenancies, record the setting and the date on your turnover checklist, and service the heater on a schedule you can show.

title: No Waterbed Statute - the Lease Decides
bodyText: South Dakota has no waterbed statute. Nothing stops you prohibiting a waterbed or other liquid-filled furniture, nothing requires you to permit one in a building of any construction type, and nothing lets you charge a special deposit, demand a particular insurance policy or impose an installation standard as the price of allowing one. Several states legislate all of that; South Dakota leaves it to your lease, and the ordinary rules then do the work. A prohibition is simply a lease term, enforceable as a term. If you allow one, the tenant's own statutory duty helps you: the tenant must preserve the premises, the appliances, the appurtenances and the other leased personal property, and must repair deterioration caused by the tenant's own negligent, willful or malicious conduct, which covers water damage from a bed the tenant installed or failed to maintain. Damage beyond ordinary wear and tear is deductible from the deposit as restoring the premises to their move-in condition, at your documented actual cost. What you may not do is attach a flat charge to the permission or to a breach of it: a fixed sum payable because the tenant brought in a waterbed, or a non-refundable waterbed fee, is a penalty for nonperformance and void, and money taken to secure performance is deemed a security deposit however you label it, counting against the one-month cap. The cautious course is a clear yes or no in the lease; if yes, require written consent, proof of the tenant's renter's insurance, and responsibility for all resulting damage at actual cost.

title: No Window-Guard Requirement or Lease Notice
bodyText: South Dakota has no window-guard law. There is no duty to install guards where a child lives, no duty to offer them, no lease notice in bold type, no model notice text by regulation, and no register of units with guards. Nothing in the state's statutes or in the rules held for it addresses window falls. The obligation that reaches an unsafe window is the general one: you must keep the premises and all common areas in reasonable repair and fit for human habitation and in good and safe working order throughout the term, and that cannot be waived or modified. A window that will not stay closed, a sash that falls, a missing or rotten sill, or a screen a child can push out of a frame is a condition within that duty - but note the limit of the analogy to a window-guard statute: a guard is an addition, and South Dakota's duty is about keeping what is there in good and safe working order rather than about adding protective hardware. So an insect screen is not a fall-protection device and your duty is to maintain it as a screen. Construction standards come from the adopted model codes rather than from a guard statute, and those govern new work. The cautious course, given there is no safe harbour to comply with: where a unit is above ground level and will be occupied by young children, install guards or restrictors that still allow emergency egress, say in the lease that screens are insect screens and not fall protection, and respond to any report of a defective window immediately.

title: Which South Dakota Notices Must Be in Writing
bodyText: South Dakota puts the writing requirement on the notice that ends a tenancy, not on the notice that starts an eviction. To end a residential tenancy at will the notice must be in writing, must specify a period of not less than fifteen days to remove, and must be served by delivering it to the tenant or to some person of discretion residing on the premises, or, if neither can be found with reasonable diligence, by affixing it to a conspicuous part of the premises where it can conveniently be read. You may neither reenter nor sue until that period has expired. A commercial tenancy at will takes the same written notice with one month instead of fifteen days. Where the lease reserves a right of reentry, three days' previous written notice of intention to reenter is enough, served the same way, and an action for possession on a reserved reentry needs no notice at all. Modifying a month-to-month tenancy takes written notice at least thirty days before the month ends, and the tenant's answering termination must come within fifteen days of receiving it. Ninety days' written notice to vacate and remove is required where leased land holding a mobile or manufactured home is developed for an alternate use. A farm tenancy needs written notice by September first. A tenant needs written notice only to withhold rent into a separate account or to end the lease for your failure to repair; repairing and deducting, or vacating, needs only notice. For unpaid rent, no notice is a condition of filing. But a written notice to quit, with a demand for possession, is what unlocks the double-yearly-value measure for a wilful holdover, so serve one anyway and keep proof of service.

title: Checks Marked 'Paid in Full'
bodyText: South Dakota follows the Uniform Commercial Code rule on checks marked 'paid in full' (SDCL 57A-3-311). If a tenant, or anyone else you have a claim against, gives you a check or other payment instrument for less than you claim, with a conspicuous statement, on the check or in a writing with it, that it is offered in full satisfaction of the claim, then cashing it settles your whole claim, the unpaid balance included. This applies only when the payment was offered in good faith and the amount was not yet fixed or was subject to a genuine (bona fide) dispute, so writing 'paid in full' on a short check for rent nobody disputes does not by itself settle the rent owed. Writing 'under protest' or 'without prejudice' when you endorse the check does not save the balance: the rule on reserving your rights does not apply to an accord and satisfaction (SDCL 57A-1-308(b)). There are two ways out. If you are an organization (for example an LLC) and, within a reasonable time before the check, sent the tenant a conspicuous statement that communications about disputed debts, including checks offered in full satisfaction, must go to a named person, office or place, the claim is not settled if the check or the writing with it was not received there. And whether or not you are an organization, the claim is not settled if you offer to repay the amount of the check within 90 days after it is paid; an organization that sent the statement just described cannot use this second way out. Neither way out works if you, or your agent responsible for the disputed debt, knew within a reasonable time before the check was collected that it was offered in full satisfaction. South Dakota's general contract law adds that part performance of an obligation, expressly accepted by the creditor in writing in satisfaction, extinguishes it (SDCL 20-7-4). The cautious course: don't cash a check for less than you claim that is marked as payment in full of a disputed amount; return it, and if one is cashed by mistake, offer the money back within 90 days.

title: Duty of Good Faith
bodyText: South Dakota's landlord-tenant statutes impose no general duty of good faith of the kind in the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act (SDCL ch. 43-32 searched); good faith appears only in specific rules. Courts in many states read a covenant of good faith and fair dealing into every contract, a lease included; whether and how South Dakota's courts do is case law this library has not reviewed, so act as if the duty applies. In practice: give notices, enter, handle the deposit, enforce lease terms and end a tenancy honestly and for the purpose the law or the lease gives you the right, not as a pretext.
